Cumberland write by himself worthy of your sex my chief commandress to give content to your wish in bare plainness I have set down the course and fortune of my late perform 1596. journey the six day of march with my whole fleet I set sail out of the sound of Plymouth the wind be prosperous though much we keep altogether till the when the fair passage put i in hope that God have prepare this a unlooked for fortune if it be well handle in get upon the coast of Spain sure intelligence whether the carrick be go and how near they be ready if not go the do of which undiscovered though I know be hard yet not impossible for he that his purpose frustrate can well work and consider the mighty importance I take the course to do it myself take with i the Guiana and the scout which two I mean shall only be see upon the coast and leave the rest of the fleet appoint they where to lie till I come unto they but God who will be beyond man resolution force i to alter this for my mast not make so sufficient as I expect both now begin to show their weakness especial my main mast which I continual look will have go over board my mariner be at their wit defect in the main mast. end and I protest I will have give five thousand pound for a new one the great part of my strength both by sea and land have be lose if that ship have return in this extremity hear all that will I hear many opinion to little purpose and at length resolve though many think it dangerous lest the wind shall with a storm come up at west northwest to go to the burling and there ride till my mast be fish myself know the road though not any else in my ship the wind they speak of I fear not my only the burling doubt be that I shall be discover be within three league of Penechia carvel come off every day to fish but this extremity force device how to hide what I be for go thither Penechia I must hopeless otherwise to repair those desperate ruin my ship be black which well further my device and though she be great yet show not so afar off wherefore I come in about eight of the clock at night upon Thursday when I be sure all the fisherman be go to sell their fish at Lisbon and from the main they can not make more this be the sixteen of March. before the morning I have down my top-mast my main yard unrig and all thing ready for my carpenter to work the small ship with i I make stand off to sea all day that not have any in my company I shall be the less suspect and thus with a strange flag and ancient upon my poop I rid without give chase to any as though I have be some merchant every day diverse ship come by i that be both good prize and have be worth the take upon Sunday night the fisherman return to the burling wherefore to go away undiscovered of they and also soon to meet with my fleet which I have appoint to tarry for i in that height betwixt twenty and thirty league off and that they shall keep with they what ship soever they meet that be outward boon I cease not work day nor night and by Saturday at night be ready to set sail when within night I hear the ordnance go off betwixt i and the shore and well know it be a small ship of Hampton and my little pinnace the scout that be in fight with a ship which they chase to windward of i before might and fear their match too hard as in truth it prove ay for lose time let slip my anchor and soon come to help the poor little one much over-matched at my first come up she shoot at i yet forbear I and go so near that I speak to they and demand of whence they be answer be make of Lisbon then assure myself she be a Biscaine and will fight well I come close to she and give she my broad side which she so biscainer good fighter answer as that I have three man kill five or six shot and my ship in six or seven place some of they very dangerous so I lay she aboard and take she she prove a ship of hamburgh lade with corn copper powder and prohibit commodity I make the more haste to end this fight for that I will be out of the sight of the land before day which as I desire I ship of hamburg take be and there meet with a french man lade with salt go into Lasbone which small bark be very fit to serve my purpose for put some of my man into she I send she into Cales road command they to fall with it by day in the morning and keep themselves close to show none but the french and make a waft to call some Portugal to they for pilotage up the river this device succeed well for betimes in the morning they be fast by a carvel that be go to fish which not suspect they come close to they so as the man I put in shot at they with musket so fast as not any of they dare stir to handle their sail till their boat go aboard and so bring they off to i these man come that night from Lisbon and assure i that the next far wind there will come forth five carack with more treasure than ever intelligence from Lisbon go in one year for the indies and five and twenty ship for brasil this welcome news be accompany with the meeting again of my whole fleet which at that very instant I descry five Carraks and twenty five ship so none be join I wish for nothing but a happy hour to see those long-lookedaft monster who wealth exceed their greatness yet be they the great ship in the world my fleet be thus join I call all the captain and master aboard and give direction where and in what order we shall lie and how we will fight not doubt to meet they be undiscovered and well know the way they will come be draw from our rest with our joy in our hope we so long continue gaze for that which come not as I begin to fear some unlucky accident and leave my fleet alone with a carvel I go in with the shore and with she and my boat get another carvel by who I understand that the very new intelligence same day that I take the first carvel at the rock there come into Lisbon a ship that bring spaniard out of England and be in Plymouth when I come by which assure they that I be come forth and they very believe be look for they so as they send carvel of advice to search every where for i one of which when I return to my fleet I understand have come by they to windward and discover they all so I fear it be vain to tarry there any long for either they will shift their course or not come at all so know that their see of another attempt i can not hurt I go to see if they be come so low down the river as that it be possible to lay they aboard in the night where they ride now again I leave my fleet at sea and the wind something favour i get in betwixt the cat-ship from whence I see they ride in the bay of wire here have I too much of my desire see what I desire to see but hopeless of the good I expect by see they for they be where no good can be do upon they ride within the castle of saint julian which have in it above a hundred piece no hope that way of great ordnance so as though I can have get in which I very believe I can it have not be possible to have return the wind be ever very scant to come forth withal and April we go altogether for the south cape the eight day I go from thence towards the canary and the thirteen day I come to Lancerota where by diverse both he come to the canary rich marquis englishman and spaniard I have be inform that there dwell a marquis that be worth 100000. pound if he can be take sudden which I doubt not have aboard i three or four which have be prisoner there who assure i they can bring i into the road by night and be on land can guide i to the castle where he dwell how dark soever it be but they fail in all for when I come to the land they know not where the road be so as I poor performance of rich promiser be force to anchor find ground but where it be they know not and in truth it be so near a ledge of rock as if we have go any further the ship have be in danger in the morning though then I have no other hope leave i to catch the marquis save only that perhaps he will hold his castle yet I think it meet to set all my soldier on shore for that till this he land his soldier time I never have give they any train and well know many of they to be very raw and unpractised to service at land wherefore myself then fear a ague take physic be let blood and send sir John Barkley with they know for certain that place can make no resistance sir John Barkley against such a force so be land they march to the town which the guide say be but three mile from the land place but it prove more than three league the most wicked march for loose stone and sand that ever I see that night I hear not from they nor the next day till night when I have word bring that they have take the town and castle town and castle taker without resistance only as they march the people of the country I mean the mountaineer will watch if any straggle and will most desperate assault they with their lance be so swift of foot as when once they run not any can come near they in the castle be not any thing but some few piece of ordnance dismount in the town who house be most beggarly some little wine only which little be too much for it distemper so poor purchase and yet too rich many that if there have be a strong enemy to have attempt they shall have find drunken resistance the mean sort be most overthrow already and the commander some distemper with wine some with pride of themselves or scorn of other so as there be very few of they but that fell to most disorderly outrage one with another and sir John Barkley with much grief tell i if I take not some severe course to remedy those thing he assure himself it will be the ruin of our voyage whereupon the next day I go on shore to see my man train and call all the commander before i rebuke they for those fault and give article the earl honourable care and wise provision both for their course at land and sea read to they my commission that they may know I have full power to execute those punishment I set down for every offence and assure they I will not be slow in do it if they offend the next day be the one and twenty of April I set sail and betwixt the grand canary and tenerife meet with the royal defence a ship which shall have come with i out of England but be not ready follow i and thwart shall much have trouble i I assure you it do not the reason I will let you know hereafter now again call all the captain and master aboard i I first ask they whether they think it be fit to tarry any request and my own plainness send you here the comparison between those two commander sir Francis Drake and sir John Hawkins they be both much give to travel in their youth and age attempt many honourable voyage alike as that of sir John Hawkins to guinea to the isle of America to saint John de Vlua so likewise sir Francis drake after many discovery of the west indies and other part be the first Englishman that do ever compass the world wherein as also in his deep judgement in sea cause he do far exceed not sir John Hawkins alone but all other whosoever in their own nature and disposition they do as much differ as in the manage matter of the war sir Francis be of a lively spirit resolute quick and sufficient valiant the other slow jealous and hardly bring to resolution in council sir John Hawkins do often differ from the judgement of other seem thereby to know more in doubtful thing than he will utter sir Francis be a willing hearer of every man opinion but common a follower of his own he never attempt any action wherein he be a absolute commander but he perform the same with great reputation and do easy dispatch great matter contrariwise sir John Hawkins do only give the bare attempt of thing for the most part without any fortune or good success therein sir John Hawkins do natural hate the land-souldier and though he be very popular yet he affect more the common sort than his equal sir Francis contrary do much love the land-souldier and great advance good part wheresoever he find they he be also affable to all man and of easy access they be both of many virtue and agree in some as patience in endure labour and hardness observation and memory of thing past and great discretion in sudden danger in which neither of they be much distemper and in some other virtue they differ sir John Hawkins have in he mercy and aptness to forgive and true of word sir Francis h^rd in reconciliation and constancy in friendship he be withal severe and courteous magnanimous and liberal they be both faulty in ambition but more the one than the other for in sir Francis be a in satiable desire of honour indeed beyond reason he be infinite in promise and more temperate in adversity then in better fortune he have also other imperfection as aptness to anger and bitterness in disgrace and too much please with open flattery sir John Hawkins have in he malice with dissimulation rudeness in behaviour and pass spare indeed miserable they be both happy alike in be great commander but not of equal success and grow great and famous by one mean rise through their own virtue and the fortune of the Sea their be no comparison to be make between their well-deserving and good part for therein sir Francis Drake do far exceed this be all I have observe in the the multitude of peace chap. 5 master THOMAS Candish his discourse of his fatal and disastrous voyage towards the south sea with his many disaduenture in the Magellan strait and other place write with his own hand to sir Tristram gorges his executor most love friend there be nothing in this world that make a true trial of friendship then at death to show mindfulness of love and friendship which now you shall make a perfect experience of desire you to hold my love as dear die poor as if I have be most infinite rich the success of this most unfortunate action the bitter torment thereof lie so heavy upon i as with much pain be I able to write these few line much less to make discovery unto you of all the adverse hap that have befall i in this voyage the least whereof be my death but because you shall not be ignorant of they I have appoint some of the most sensible man that I leave behind i to make discourse unto you of all these accident I have make a simple will wherein I have make you sole and only disposer of all such little as be leave the roebuck leave i in the most desolate case that ever man be leave in what be become of the roebuck she I can imagine if she be return into England it be a most admirable matter but if she be at home or any other of my good whatsoever return into England I have make you only possessor of they and now to come to that villain that have be the death of i and the decay of this whole action I mean davis who only treachery in run from i have captain davis blame be a utter ruin of all if any good return by he as ever you love i make such friend as he of all other may reap least gain I assure myself you will be careful in all friendship of my last request my debt which be owe be not much etc. but I most unfortunate villain be match with the most abject mind and mutinous company that ever be carry out of England by any man live for I protest unto you that in go to the streit of mutinous company Magellan after I be pass to the southward of the river of plate and have hide the fury of storm which indeed I think to be such as worse may not be endure I never make my course to the straits-ward but I be in continual danger by my company which never cease to practice and mutiny against i and have get the appoint place call port desire port desire I meet with all my company which have be there twenty day before i and have not my most true friend be there who to name my heart bleed I mean my cousin lock I have be constrain either to have suffer violence or some other most disorder mishap I come into this harbour with my boat my ship ride without at sea where I find the roebuck the desire and the pinnace all which complain unto i that the tide run so violent as they be not able to ride but be drive aground and wish i in any wise not to come in with my ship for that if she shall come on ground she will be utter cast away which I know to be most true and find it to be no place for so great a ship without her utter ruin I forthwith command they to make themselves ready to depart they be fresh and infinite well relieve with seal and bird which in that place do abound and my company be grow weak and feeble with continual watch pump and bayl for I must say true unto you there be never man that endure more extremity of the sea than my poor company have do such be the fury of the west south-west and south-west wind as we be tempest drive from the shore four hundred league and constrain to beat from fifty degree to the southward into forty to the northward again before we can recover near the shore in which time we have a new shift of sail clean blow away and our ship in danger to sink in the sea three time which with extremity of man labour we recover in this weakness we depart for the strait be from that harbour eight league and in eighteen day the streit we get the strait in which time the man in my ship be grow extreme weak the other ship company be in good case by reason of their late relief and now we have be almost four month between the coast of Brasile and the straits be in distance not above six hundred league which be common run in twenty or thirty day but such be the adversenesse of our fortune that in come thither we spend the summer and find in the strait the beginning of a most extreme winter not durable for extreme winter christian in despite of all storm and tempest so long as we have ground to anchor in and tide to help we we beat into the strait some fifty league have for the most part the they enter fifty league wind contrary at length be force by the extremity of storm and the narrowness of the strait be not able to turn wind ward no long we get into a harbour where we ride from the eighteen day of April till the ten of May in all which time we never have other then most furious contrary wind and after that the month of May be come in nothing but such flight of snow and extremity of frost as in all the time of my life I never see any to be compare with they this extremity cause the weak man in my ship only to decay for in seven or eight day in this extremity there die forty man and sicken seventy so that there be not fifty death of man man that be able to stand upon the hatch I find this miserable calamity to fall upon i and find that beside the decay of my man and expense of my victual the snow and frost decay our sail and tackle and the contagiousness of the place to be such for extremity of miserable distress frost and snow as there be no long stay without the utter ruin of we all what by these extremity and the daily decay of my man I be constrain forth with to determine some course and not for all this extremity of weather to tarry there any long upon this I assemble my company together and show they that my intention be to consultation go for China and that there be two way thither the one through the strait the other by the way of which course show they as be well know to i as the way I have undertake and although that fortune have deny we this passage yet I doubt not but soon to recover to this cape where I show they I make no doubt but we shall relieve ourselves and perform to their content our intend voyage these persuasion with many other which I use seem to content they for the present but they be no soon go from i but forthwith all manner of discontent be unrip among themselves so that to go that way they plain and resolute determine never to give their willing consent some of the best and honest sort hear this their resolution wish they rather to put up a supplication to i than thus private among themselves to mutiny and murmur which course may cause a utter ruin to fall upon they all affirm that they know i to be so reasonable as I will not refuse to hear their petition upon this they frame a humble supplication unto i as they term it the effect whereof be that first they protest to spend their life most willing for my sake and that their love be such to i as their chief care be for i and they grieve very much to see i put on a resolution which as they suppose will be the end of my life which be their great grief and next their own life will immediate follow both by reason of the length of the course all which they must perform without relief and further we have not leave four month victual which may very well be spend in run a course not half so long but if it will please i to return again for the coast of Brasile where they know my force be together be able to take any place there we may both provide victual to return again and furnish ourselves of all other such want as these extremity have bring upon we and at a seasonable time return again and so perform our first intention now I know their resolution and find that in some thing their reason be not vain begin in his many year manifold peregrination the Petivares be not of so wild and barbarous condition as many other province be the petiu^res describe in brasil for if you come as a merchant unto they they will traffic with you if as a warrior they will fight very valiant they be man of good stature their body be all carve with very fine work and in their lip they make a hole with a roe-buck horn and when they come to man estate they cut the hole of their lip with a cane and then the hole be big they wear a green stone therein and he that have not this fashion be count a peasant these cannibal with the rind of a tree they do make cloth like spark of velvet but it be thin of the bark of a tree and that cloth they do call Mollelleo the elephant do feed in the evening and in the morning in low marsh as there be take of elephant many the moor do watch which way they come and assoon as the elephant be at meat they dig great hole in the ground and cover they with stick and then they cover the pit with earth and when they have make all ready they go to the elephant and shoot at they with their arrow and assoon as the elephant feel themselves hurt they r^nne at what soever they see before they follow after the blackamoor that chase they than they fall into the deep pit where after they be once in they can get out the moor of angola be as black as ^et they be man of good stature they never take but one wife who they call mocasha these moor do cut long streak in their face that reach from the top of their ear to their chin the woman do wear shell of fish on their arm and on the small of their leg the law among they be that if any more do lie with a other wife he shall lose his ear for his offence these moor do circumcize their child and give they their name as we do when we baptize angola may very easy be take for the portugal have circumcision no fort to defend it of any strength the king of congo be the great king in all Aethiopia and do keep in the field continual be in a manner amaze to hear how it be possible her majesty have live a maiden queen so long and always reign in peace with her subject when I be bring before the king and tell he of my country what plenty of thing we have if the portugal have not like of it they will interrupt my speech and the king will show himself very angry and tell they that every man be best able to speak of his country and that I have no reason but to tell he that which be true the king of congo when he go to the camp to see his army ride upon a elephant in great pomp and majesty on either side of the elephant he of Bengala these noble slave at every command of the king of congo do fall flat on the ground on their breast when the king do ride as you have hear they carry a canopy as it be a cloth of state over his head his two secretary the one a nobleman of Spain the other a more do ride next after he before he go at the least five hundred archer which be his guard than there follow a more which do nothing but talk aloud in praise of the king tell what a great warrior he have be and praise his wisdom for all thing that he have accomplish very honourable to his great fame of such as know he when this I depart from Plymmouth with two ship one pinnace and two shallop in quarter towards the west indies my chief ship wheie^n I go myself as admiral be name the prudence of a hundred tun wherein I have a hundred and thirty tall man the second be the pearl a small ship of sixty ton wherein go as my vide-admiral master Robert accompany with sixty lusty fellow my pinnace of twenty tun be man with eighteen man in this consort be master Edward Giles and Philip Ward gentleman captain by land with captain Antony fugar captain Loriman captain Ashley and diverse other gentleman of much towardliness and valour as they make good proof in the success of this voyage in our pass by the c^pe of saint Vincent in Spain common call the south cape I be encounter with such a terrible Ternado or gust of wind that my pinnace with fifteen of our man to our great grief be utter cast away we be not able pinnaffe lose in a Ternado with the uttermost of our endeavour to save above three of the rest from thence I shape my course to the isle of cape Verde and immediate upon my arrival there I set upon one of they call saint Vincent with a hundred man and take the island and the town thereof which isle of cape Verde the i will and town of s. Vincent (@) the Ra^chera in Cubagua w^^h diverse (...) oner take and ransom be a pretty place the spoil whereof I give to my soldier which after they have pillage it set the same on fire hence we hale twenty of march 1604. captain Charles Leigh in the olive plant a proper bark of some fifty ton accompany with six and forty man and boy depart from Wolwich with intention to discover and inhabit some part of the country of Guiana where he have be in a former voyage they stay in the down until the eight and twenty of the say month and pass thence they touch in the i will of mogador on the coast of wind coast the isle of cape Verde we pass over to the west indies and upon the ten of May come in change of water which show thick and white by the next day we be in fresh water and the next day follow about five in the morning we see two land in the mouth of the river of amazon make account that we be forty league up the river and river of amazon come to a anchor in three fathom under they which we find low land cover with high tree then the captain with some eight of the best man of the ship go towards the shore and find many indian come towards they they return aboard and find the ship almost aground but sound the bay bring their ship into the channel which they find very narrow within awhile after four indian in a small Canoa show themselves unto we to who we send our boat with some of our commodity as hatchet knife glass bead they have nothing but Maiz and small blue-headed parrot for which we give they some of our trifle not long after another Canoa come out our boat clap between they and the shore to take some of they to learn the state of the river by they but they free themselves all save one youth which be bring aboard which next day after escape leap into the sea twelve league as we judge from land thus we take our leave of the river of amazon and have uncertain shoalding all the way in our way about ten a clock in the night we strike upon a sand before we can let fall our anchor where we beat off a piece of our false keel before we can get off be get off we come to a anchor in four fathom and a half water and ride there until the next morning where we descry the land six league from we with the entrance of a river the two and twenty of May we arrive in the river of Wiapogo in the latitude of three degree and a half to the north of the line where we find the people ready to give we the river Wiapogo best entertainment they can bring we honey pines planton potato whereof they make their bread and wine fish of many sort hen coney hog and such like this day he take a oath of all his people to be true to he as long as he abide in the country then after diverse conference with the chief indian and namely with two of their country which have be before in England and can speak some english he find they very willing to have he and his people abide in their country who pretend want of many necessary whereof indeed he stand in need and especial of victual he go up the river in his boat with some fourteen man to take perfect view of a fit place to inhabit in and to sound the depth of the river as they go at his return he cause his ship to be bring up hard unto the fall of the river but after they have stay there one day find sundry inconvenience they come back the fall again to their first road with a determination to plant and seat themselves upon the first mount or high ground at the entrance of the north side of the river but the jayos and Sapayos see he and his company come down the river again entreat he earnest to stay among they offer he their own dwell house and garden already plant to their hand whereof he accept to wit of two house and of as many garden as they think convenient to serve his turn with condition that he shall aid and defend they against their enemy the caribe and other hereupon they make a great feast desire our captain to be at it and they demand of their generality of the stay of our man in the country or no. whereunto they give their free consent and desire he withal to send into England for man they desire to learn religion to teach they to pray this do the next day he bring all his furniture on shore and bestow it in the aforesaid house and for the better assurance of the performance of the saluage promise he demand pledge of they to be send into England whereunto they willing condescend which where in number five whereof two be of good account he retain thirty five englishman and boy with he send the rest home in june with the five saluage which be plentiful furnish with their country victual with letter to the right worshipful sir Olaue Leigh his brother of his success and desire to supply his want which he most kind twice supply to his great charge within short time after the caribe in eight warlike canowes come to surprise they as far as the mount Comaribo caribe whereof the indian be advertise by our fisher desire captain Leigh to aid they which he do with some they on the head their bread they make of Cassavia a white Roble common a span long and almost so thick which the woman grate in a earthen pan against certain grate of stone and grate three or four bushel Cassavi^ in a day the juice thereof they crush out most careful be rank poison raw in a hose of with which they hang up upon a hook and afterward with a weighty log which they hang at the other end they squeeze out the water into a earthen pan or piece of a gourd the juice and then seethe the same juice with their red pepper whereby it become wholesome and if they will have it sweet they will seethe it but ordinary if they will have it sour they will seethe it extraordinary and use it in manner of sauce and when they be sick they eat the same and bread only the woman also make drink of this bread which in their language they call arepapa by bake of it black dry and thin then chew it in their mouth they put it into earthen pot narrow in the bottom and broad above contain some a firkin some a kilderkin some a barrel set in a small hole in the ground with fire about they be well sod they put it out into great jar of earth with narrow neck and there it will wo^ke a day and a night and keep it four or five day till it be stale and then gather together a hundred and more they give themselves to pipe dance and drink they make drink also of Cassava unchewed which be small and ordinary in their house they use also to make drink of potato which they pair and stamp in a mortar be sod then put water to it drink it before and after the sickness of our captain many of our man fall sick some of ague some of flox some of giddiness in their head whereby they will often fall down which grow sickness chief of the excessive heat of the sun in the day and of the extreme damp of the earth which will so moisten our hamackas or Cotton bed wherein we lie a yard from the the cause ground that we be fain to imitate the indian in make fire on both side under they and for all that we can do some nine of our company be dead before our ship arrival beside the remedy we be mighty vex with a kind of worm which at first be like to a flea and will creep into the foot especial and child and they be of three nation viz. Yaioas arwarkas and Sapayoas which be chase from other river by the caribe have combine themselves together in this place for their better defence and be now at deadly war with the caribe after that I have store myself with bread and root sufficient until the earth with God providence may yield i supply I do then send for the chief captain of the Yayoas aboard who with gift and good usage I easy make my intent know their come another chief captain of the Yayoas aboard to dine with i who together with the former after dinner desire to speak with i whereupon I send for a indian who have be in England to be interpreter and take they into my cabin the two captain tell a long story of the wrong the caribe have do they how they have drive they from their ancient dwelling in other river kill many of their friend carry their woman and child away captive and hurt many of their man and thereupon they call one of their man to show i how he be late hurt in three place with their arrow to conclude they tell i how they purpose the next moon to go against the caribe with twenty canoas and earnest entreat i if I stay so long to go with they to their war upon this good occasion I tell they that I purpose to stay in the country seven or eight month to seek out and make trial of mynes and in the mean time that I purpose to build house ashore at the head of the river and there to plant and thereupon they promise indian to help i to build and to plant and the chief captain promise himself to go up with i the next day be the three of May I set sail from the mouth of Caroleigh and cast consort who intend spoil and purchase in the west indies have from the beginning seek the overthrow of this voyage this bearer can certify you at large and undoubted he make full account with his headstrong companion at such a time to have command the ship at his pleasure to conclude among other their practice they so consume the victual which shall have maintain we until the earth have yield supply as that in six day our potato which shall have last we two month be whole spend hereupon be far distant from the indian who inhabit at the mouth of the river forty mile from the fall and it be year I doubt not will afford plenty of sugar if we shall have mean to make they my loose commodity as hatchet bead knife looking-glass etc. be almost all go a great part in buy of victual but the most four or five month after consultation have we be fain to touch first at the isle of Barbudos and then at Santa Luzia in the west indies where fear to perish at sea for hunger before we shall be able be so many aboard to reach England captain Nicolas saint John with the rest of the passenger which purpose to have stay with master Charles Leagh at Wiopogo in Guiana resolve to stay and take their fortune in the aforesaid fruitful island thus sixty seven of we at our own seek be leave on shore in the aforesaid island of Santa Luzia the three and twenty of August 1605. with our sword musket and powder and one falcon and one barill of biscuit only for all our food the next day our ship depart from we with some discontentment because we have seize upon her boat to serve our turn after our ship be depart from we we live very peaceable daily trade with the indian for victual which be Cassavi potato popaye pompion tobacco pappy mammeye all very pleasant to eat also they bring unto we hen and gull and some pelican woodcock and snipe we ourselves do kill with our piece many of they likewise and every night we send out six upon the sand to seek for tortoise whereof we never miss night without one or two and many time three which be the great sustenance tortoise we find for they be very large and great I have often take out of one of they to the number of seven hundred egg also the indian have great store of Rouen linen clothes serge and other stuff and spanish woollen cloth and jar of oil which they take and save at sea with their Periagnas for three spanish ship have be there cast away a little before our arrival if we have have a pinnace there we can have lade she with many good commodity which they have hide in their house in the wood all which we can have buy for hatchet knife bead thimble fishhook and other such trifle thus for the space of five or six week we go not much abroad till our captain see certain four square plate which the indian ware on the small of their arm ask Browne a gold fine his opinion what he think of they who tell he that three part thereof be show of Gold Gold and ask the indian where they get they they point unto a high mountain on the northwest part of the island this cause captain Nicholas saint John and John Rogers who be our interpreter for the spanish tongue with as many of our chief man as can well go in the boat upon a Monday to go thither promise his brother Alexander saint John master garret and master tench who he leave to govern the rest at home to return the next Saturday the indian for three day after do not come unto we with victual for they perceive when the boat go and as we think they be then at the slaughter of our man at the mountain the captain and his man slay indian treachery upon Thursday morning we kill two tortoise on the sand where we find a great company of the indian gather together for what purpose we know not and lest we shall suspect they of any bad intent towards we they willing offer themselves to bring home our tortoise which they take into their and bring they to our house all that forenoon we keep good watch for there be very many that come both by sea and land to the number of two or three hundred and diverse of they be very merry with we drink of tobacco and aquavitae until ten of the clock and then they depart all save one which be a captain of the i will of saint Vincent call Augramert and a old man which be his father who promise we if we will go to their house that we shall have any thing that they have for the day before I have be at their house with other two of my fellow to have buy victual yet they will not part with any no not for any commodity that we have and yet they have more store of victual then ever I see they have before but we perceive afterwad that it be provide for they that come to take their part against we who they keep secret in the wood so we three return and travel far into the island and pass through six or seven garden very full of Cassabe potato and many other root fair garden and fruit and by the way see many tall tree of so huge bigness that we three can not at twice fathom one of they about and they be so hard that we can not cut they with our great tree of hard wood knife and the bark of they be white like Ash. then we return to our sconce again upon Thursday after dinner master Alexander saint john master Francis kettleby the elder master William tench myself and diverse other to the number of eighteen go with Augramert and his father have neither bow nor arrow only his father have a Brasill sword they go thus mean arm lest we shall suspect they Augramert also promise master Alexander saint John that he shall see his wife and we shall have hamacco which be indian Hamaca bed bed of network make of cotton yarn to lie in so we travel along the sand very secure young saint John go a little space before play and jest with the indian captain till they come within sight of their house where in the wood they have place a ambush of three hundred caribe when sudden Augramert take hold of his rapier with the one hand treacherous ambush and of his poniard with the other and the old man his father with his Brasill sword strike he down to the ground then out of the wood come the arrow so thick about our ear that we have not the time to put our match in our cock and many of our company have their match to light which give a great encouragement unto the enemy insomuch that we discharge not six piece against they which cause diverse of our company to fly into the sea up to their neck and some along the sand as amaze see such a huge company against so small a number until young saint John recover again encourage we to make a stand at a point of land which go corner wise into the Sea but all be in vain for before we can make our piece ready there come another company on the back of we and fill our body full with arrow and then we betake we to our sword and so run through they but still they increase out of the wood shoot their arrow in great abundance not dare to come near we until they see we fall and then with their great Brasill sword they strike out our man brain I myself be all this time run with young saint John and master kettleby who behave themselves most gallant have at the least one hundred arrow a piece before they fall come at the last into the entrance of a narrow path where five of my fellow be get before I come and think to have pass through there be another ambush who kill they all I only with three arrow in i by run into the wood and swim over a stand lake escape home give they warning before they come to assault they and upon my come they all come in sight upon the sand who we soon send away by shoot off our great piece so they come not in three day after upon Monday there come to the number of thirteen or fourteen hundred both by sea and land and there beset we round we have nothing but our chist to defend we from their arrow thus for the space of seven or eight day we fight with they and of nineteen man which be leave of all our company twelve be sore wound with their arrow and the first day at twelve a clock they shoot fire in their arrow and burn our house think then to have enter in upon we but with our falcon we drive they back with most horrible cry after that our house be burn and all our chist which before be our fort we fortify ourselves with the remnant of the stake and thatch which we have save from burn set they in the ground slopewise cover it with sand and earth which save we ever after from their arrow the next day after they all depart in their and the lord see what need we have of food contrary to our expectation move the heart of our very enemy to bring we food for when all the rest be out of sight one return very well provide of victual and three or four come out of their Piragua with asmuch as they be able to carry of Cassavi potato and cry unto we to exchange with they first hold up their bow and arrow and after lay they on the ground again in sign of peace which we perceive send out three likewise to bargain without weapon with knife and bead and other trifle which traffic be do they depart and we return give praise to God for this miraculous feed of we for we have no mean of ourselves to get any food for they have bereave we of our net with which we have wont to catch as much fish of many sort as will suffice we for a whole day thus they continue daily for the space of seven day and then our victual begin to fail again which cause we to hold out a flag of truce which they perceive come in peaceable manner unto we then one Francis brace which can speak french make they understand that our desire be to give they all that we have if they will let we have a Piragua to carry we away which one captain Antony willing consent unto contrary to the will of his brother Augramert captain of saint Vincent and the next day bring it draw it on shore within the compass of our fort for which we give they hatchet knife and bead until they be content and to please they the more we give they every one a shovell or a spade wherewith they be full content and so depart then with all speed we go all to work some upon the sail which we make of very good roan-cloth and some to make the mast and every one do labour all he can to be ready against night for captain Antony which be captain of Santa Lucia tell we that his brother Augramert will come the next day from saint Vincent with twelve all laden with arrow who word we always find true thus on a Thursday the six and twenty of September at one of the clock after midnight have among we all but one of fresh water to drink and one small firkin of rice we embark ourselves being nineteen in the whole number not one have skill in the mariner art and without card or compass to direct we we sail by the sun in the daytime blind hungry voyage and by the star in the night go always betwixt south-west and by west the victual that we have be not sufficient to serve that company for three day for we have not above twenty biscuit three Cassavi cake a dozen and some thirty potato and some four or five gallon of water and a little barrel half full of Rice and as it please the lord he have save it until this our great necessity for the preservation of our life for all our other victual be go in two day and our water in three day and then master garret give to every two of we a pottage dish of his rice twice a day which we wash in salt water and so eat it raw thus we continue at sea seek for land for the space of ten day where we endure one great tempest although to our great peril look always when we shall a storm be drench the rain which then fall be unto we in the midst of our danger a great comfort for we save it with great joy and drink it thank God for that good refresh who likewise do send the very fowl of the air to feed we for be weary of their flight they will rest they upon the side of our boat so that we take they and dry they in the sun with a little gunpowder and eat they our boat brim be so near the water that every wave come over it ready to sink we but that four of we continual do lade the water forth by course now on the ten day one Thomas Morgan die not be able to live of that Thomas Morgan die Land small allowance and at noon we throw he over board within a hour after it please God to glad we who be likewise ready to follow our fellow with a joyful sight of land unto the near part whereof we make as fast as we can but the wind be calm we be benight before we can come to it and so want the light of the day we be upon the shore before we be aware and there split our boat boat split to the midst and all our man be turn out save myself which hold the helm think the next wave will set she off again not know she to be split but the breach be so great that it turn i under put i in great danger to be grind to piece with her weight lie upon i against the great rock yet at the last we all recover ourselves some sit upon the rock other on the root of great tree think there to save ourselves until the morning William pick and myself go and hale the boat on shore which be split to the very midst and so far with our sword we cut off and put in a head in the midst and fasten it with our dagger knife and bodkin stop all the leak with our shirt and send five of our company over to the main land which be Miles Pet William pick Francis brace William kettleby and William butcher they hale their boat four or five day along the shore cross diverse river with their boat be sometime pursue by or crocodile and shark God pity their poor estate guide they to a place where they find a great earthen jar full of wheat flower set in a little cave which they boil in the jar with fresh water and satisfy their hungry appetite with thanks unto God for the same and within two day after they meet with three spaniard with half a dozen indian and Negro travel three Span^ards from caracas to Coro drive horse and mule lade with merchandise who see their weakness for want of victual unlode their horse to feed on the grass while they refresh our hungry man with plenty of their good cheer and show themselves very courteous suffer they to ride and go themselves on foot two or three day till they come to a town of civil indian call Tocoya where they stay to refresh they for they be very weak and there they let the spaniard know in what miserable case they leave we in a desolate island miserable famine use of tobacco where we endure the great misery that ever man do with life for we continue fifteen day have no kind of meat but wilks fault water and tobacco which do nothing at all nourish we yet nevertheless it take away the desire of hunger and save we from eat one another in those fifteen day five of our company pine to death because they can not take tobacco John parkins Edward Greene Thomas siubbe Andrew Swash and a old man call five die in the island John by note two or three of our man to die we know by those token when we draw near our death which be these first they will swell very big and short after fall to the very bone and want strength to hold up their head they will fall down and droop into their bosom and in twelve hour after yield up the ghost at the fifteen day end Francis brace have more strength than the rest guide the three spaniard with six indian to the island where we be and they bring victual with they which when we have eat have almost kill we by reason of the weakness of our stomach be so far spend that we can not digest it although we feed thereof very spare the next ^ood almost kill aswell as penury Tocoya day they carry we to the main land where we have horse bring we to carry we and the good we have they take all to the king of Spain use and so convey we to Tocoya where we which be weak remain fifteen day and those which be strong go with the three spaniard to Coro which be some fifty league from Tocoya and at the fifteen day end co^o one of the spaniard who name be Coraianal come for we with horse who show kind Spaniard himself as careful of we as if we have be his own countryman and friend and bring we to Coro to our fellow where we be bring before the governor and by a Fleming which good Fleming can speak a little english which have be a prisoner there sixteen year we be examine of the cause of our come thither who excuse we very well for he know that if we have confess whether we be determine to go they will have either put we to death or condemn we to the galley but he tell they that we never purpose to come thither but be by misfortune and tempest of wind and weather drive on that coast and tell they of all the danger which we have endure which drive they into such great admiration that some say very we be devil and not man other that we deserve to be canonize but that we be lutheran all the chief sennors of the town be there every man be desirous to take one of we after we be divide among they they do not use we like prisoner but be as careful of we as of their own child not suffer we to want any thing necessary for the procure of our spanish gentleness health my lot fall out to be entertain by one who name be sentor Francisco Lopez and be extreme sick of a calenture or hot fever one captain which have marry his daughter have good skill in physic come daily to my chamber and there let i blood diet i and purge i give his own wife in charge not to let i want any thing that be there to be have thus by the will of God and their tender care over we we recover our health and strength again only two die there which be Thomas Fletcher and fulke jones a shoemaker in Coro eleven of we remain alive be all that be leave of sixty seven which be put on shore in the island of Santa Luzia for the space of five month every day go to two more one another when we please and we rid often into the country where the indian take great delight in our company for against our come they will provide all kind of delicious fruit which be in most abundance in that country and will kill dear and wild hog for we and will bring we ape monkey parrot and any thing that they think we commodity of the country delight in the country about Coro do yield abundance of sugar honey ginger and pitch also they have very good wheat grow there but the bread be for the most part make of Maiz whereof they have great plenty for they reap it three time in one year this Maiz they do mingle with the juice of the sugar-cane which make a excellent kind of bread and it will keep like biscuit also they make their drink of this Maiz and of potato which be very drink make of maiz. sweet and strong for the indian will be quick drink with it while we be there a Spaniard ride to a farm of he in the country with his brother where he have many indian dwell to make tobacco one of his chief indian which use to be familiar with he take up a new hatchet which his master have bring he ask he what it cost and sudden cleave his head therewith which his brother perceive run for his rapier but the indian woman the treason of the indian have steal it away before and so they kill he also with their bow and arrow and three or four negro which seem to resist they and thereupon fly to the mountain gather a great company unto he promise they that if they will aid he against the spaniard in Coro he will give i money to bring i to London chap. 14 the relation of master JOHN Wilson of wansteed in Essex one of the last ten that return into England from Wiapoco in Guiana 1606. captain Charles Leigh and his brother sir Olane Leigh do furnish to sea the good ship call the phoenix with commodity for the country of Guiana and necessary for the voyage with fifty person to inhabit Wiapoco of sundry trade who direct their course towards Wiapoco on the coast of Guiana which the spaniard call the river of canoas arrive on the twenty of May follow they arrive at Wiap^^^ where he find a ship of Amsterdam trade with the indian they persuade the indian that our nation come to inhabit among they only to oppress they as the spaniard do in other part of the indies which the indian themselves confess unto captain Leigh notwithstanding they offer our nation no unkindness but use they in all the kind manner they can for they provide whatsoever our company want which they can get they in somuch the gentleman be like to have do right well if it have not happen that his company have not mutine which do partly arise because of the climate which be much hot than we and for that they be unprovided of victual or other necessary therefore constrain to live cause of their mutiny in such manner as the indian themselves do for that they do see at their land only mountain and hill cover with wood and for that the most part of they have be householder in England not accustom unto such a strange country or nation nor such a diet for which cause they be so much discontent that they cry to their captain home home thus the captain and his whole company be discontent and also the master of his ship call Martin Prinx who ship himself short after their arrival into the amsterdamer which they find there whereupon the captain place his mate Richard pet of weymouth to be master of the phoenix furnish he with such victual as the country afford as Cassavi for their bread and potato root with fish water and such provision as they have of their own aboard appoint Edward huntly to be their captain to go for England who depart from Wiapoco about the first of july 1605. by who captain Leigh advertise his brother sir Olaue Leigh after who arrival sir Olaue Leigh he withal speed furnish the aforesaid ship call the second voyage of the phoenix phoenix to sea with commodity for the country and other necessary with thirty man of sundry trade appoint the aforenamed Richard pet to be master and Edward huntly to be captain they depart from woollage one the towards Wiapoco who arrive at their port one the fifteen of january follow who expect with the rest of their company aboard to have find the general and his company on land to have be in far better case than they be for that they find they for the most part extreme sicke^ and some of they dead and present after their arrival three or four man of they die and the general himself be very weak and much change which partly proceed by reason of their great want of victual for that the pidians can not at all time provide they that they want and chief captain Leighs weakness for that the company be persuade that the ship will never have return unto they again which plain appear among they for that at the arrival of our ship some of they which have not in three month time be a stone cast from their house come aboard of we a mile and more from their house in weak estate which cause very much discontent among deject mind our fresh water soldier aboard and they be the more discontent because they can not advertise they of any commodity the country yield which will afford they present benefit insomuch that they wish themselves in England again during which parley our general come not aboard of we for that he be at his house call mount Howard a mile and more up into mount Howard the land which stand on a hill very pleasant situate but according to the country manner by reason that their enemy shall not well find their house nor sudden assault they have there before very rough passage unto they environ all with mountain wood and hill wherefore the general send one Sidney Harrington unto captain huntly m. Tederington preacher and to the master of the ship to land their company in possession bay a place which the indian give unto our general and therefore by he so name possession Bay at who land according unto the general his commission they be all swear unto certain article as that they shall acknowledge captain Charles Leigh to be their chief general of Guiana under king james our king of great Britain and that they shall not be hurtful unto the say general his proceed but to aid and assist he to their uttermost power which be effect our general come unto we and after kind salutation have take order for our lodging for that time he depart from we the indian in like manner after their country fashon kind entertain we and after further conference have with our general he relate at large unto we what have happen unto he and his company in their absence that by reason of his company their discontent and sickness they have not travel up into the main land and therefore of his own knowledge he can not certify they of any other commodity the country do yield than such as he know of before their departure but the indian have inform they that there be up in the main very rich commodity gold and silver r. caliane as also gold and silver and especial in the river of caliane where the caribe inhabit who be enemy unto our indian of Wiapoco and so call by they upon which information our general think it will have be best to have peaceable trade with the caribe but our company mislike thereof insomuch that the general alter his determination and agree to join with their friend indian against the caribe their enemy whereof have advertise the chief of they they most kind embrace their offer present make eight of their canoas in a readiness furnish they with bread and drink and victual which for the most part be crab and fish with some hundred of themselves all naked in their canoas who our general accompany with some eight and thirty of our company leave the rest to keep our ship and house ship the most part of they in a pinnace that be build by one name Howard the keel whereof he make of a Canoa which prove a very fit pinnace for those part expedition against the caribe and river this pinnace after our general death the indian do break a piece because they think we will have steal away from they in she unto the spaniard and the rest of our company be place in their canoas all of we furnish with our caleever and so we depart on our journey and voyage on the six and twenty of February on which day at night we come to a place which we name mount huntly where we lodge mount huntly in the wood that night our general command we to keep a good watch which we need not to have do for the indian themselves be very watchful and wonderful careful of our caleever and for to keep our powder dry after we have be acquaint with they and very diligent for to please we the next day at night we come to a place call the count and there we lodge and the next cou. r. wia. day follow we come into the river of and there we find two or three of the caribe canoas but all their man be run up into the wood and from thence our general go up far into the ship there who the general know to be one johnson of Plymouth that have be some fourteen day before at english ship Wiapoco and come thither in the way of trade but our general will not suffer he so to do for that he will not hinder himself and his company which our general at that time call to mind and therefore think it not good to proceed in the river because he doubt that there will have rise contention betwixt his company and johnsons and for that he also misdoubt we shall have want bread and drink if he shall have proceed in his journey and therefore return to Wiapoco where we arrive all company fall sick and for that they have no comfortable drink nor any comfort tha^ sick person do want diverse of they die of the flux which the indian as also the disease call the calenture mortality know right well for to cure yet conceal it from our general but unto we after his death they do reveal which sickness among the company cause no small grief unto our general and chief to see such want among they wherefore he resolve with himself to go for England which he acquaint the company with promise they to return as speedy as he can with provision present after he have ship his provision and such commodity as he have gather together in the country and be in a readiness to depart for England he sicken of the flux and the captain sickness and death die aboard his ship and be by captain huntly secret bury on the land the twenty of march who death be so secret keep by the captain and the master of the ship that most of the company know not thereof the reason be because there be provision too little for they which be ship and other of the company if they have know thereof will have press to have come with they wherefore captain huntly with master Tederington our m. and some tobacco observe the manner and condition of the people the nature of the land and what commodity it yield and what commodity of we be in most request with they about the three of October the indian do request we for to accompany they in their war against the caribe whereunto we willing do agree they provide seven canoas furnish they with man and bread and drink and their victual for the most part crab and fish of diverse sort which they take every day fresh and fresh as they travel in the river we go into the river of caliane which be some thirty league from Wiapoco where we row up and down but we can not find any of the caribe in the river we persuade they to land which they do and march up some two mile unto the caribe house as we march to their house the caribe come to the water side where our canoas do lie but find myself therewith my caliver they have no great desire to come very near unto we and so after we have burn some of their house and kill diverse of they our company return to our canoas have lose one of the indian captain name macato other of the indian be shoot with three of our surgery company who they heal as they do themselves with a leaf very speedy they be arm in their war with naked skin and their artillery be bow and arrow their weapon wooden sword and buckler they choose their captain at their drunken feast he be place in the midst of the whole company hold his hand on his head after indian arm mad choice of a patient captain they have make a oration unto he to be valiant and not to be treacherous unto they with such like speech they whip he with a whip which make the blood spring out of his body at every stroke and he never once move thereat by these mean they try his patience and courage after we have ship ourselves into our canoas we row up and down the river of caliane some eight or ten day which we note for to be a very fair river and navigable it r. caliane search run diverse way from the main land and great store of such commodity hereafter specify which the country yield be to be have in the say river we return unto our house at Wiapoco about the first of November in this journey we be kind use of our consort our indian and high respect of they for our service which we do after a few day rest at Wiapoco the indian advertise we of three ship which be in the river of amazon and that one of they will come unto we to the river of Wiapoco some two three ship in r. of amazon month after which prove to be true but by what mean they know it I can not imagine except it be by their devil mean which they call their peyar with who the man have peyar-divining often conference and it will answer they but the woman never that I can perceive when the man will confer with their peyar they suffer not a child to be in the house and when any of they be sick they know by he whether they shall live or die if he say they shall die they will give the sick person no physic but if he say that he shall live than they will give he any thing they have for his comfort after our company be advertise of a ship come unto we we go with the indian in their canoas some into the river of Wiapoco and river of Ar^cow some into the river of arocow to make away such commodity as we have leave which be not many reserve some of they to give to our indian for our victual although their kindness towards we be such that if we have not have any commodity they will not have suffer we to have want in which our journey we note the river of Aracow to be a very pleasant river and yield such commodity as other river do also the river of Wiapoco be a very fair river and navigable which enter the main more than forty mile and at the end thereof there be a very great fall of water which come over great hill and mountain some of our Fall company be on the top of they for some month in the year the mountain be dry and we be inform that on the other side of those great hill there be a river which be inhabit with many indian and have the like commodity that Wiapoco have and that there be gold in that place which the indian call carocor^e but we never go to see the same river by reason we have very small store of commodity at our return to Wyapoco we give to the indian for their pain and provide of we victual in our journey a axe for which they will have travel with we two or three month time if occasion have require and for a axe they find we victual two month time at our house as bread and drink and crab and fish and all such kind of flesh as they kill for themselves for the same price but if we desire any hen or cock of they than we be to have give they some small trifle as bead so likewise if they bring we in our travel to any of their friend indian house we must do the like as at our departure to give they some trifle as knife and bead so that we live very good cheap three nation there be of the indian three sort which inhabit at Wyapoco with who we be who house be situate as near the river mouth as they well may be they be name the yaye the yaye the arwalke and the suppaye the yaye be a people very proud and use much flout and mock of other much give unto dance and be full of merriment very ingenious and very the arwake kind of nature the arwacke be a people of better carriage and do use our company with better respect than the yaye these two kind of indian come out of the west wherefore they do know all those coast and they hate the spaniard as deadly as they do the caribe suppaye the suppaye be a people more crafty in their deal for they will not part with any thing but will have commodity for commodity they be not many of they and we can not nakedness learn from whence they be come the man and woman go all naked without any coverture man and woman how they live at all they be very well limbed and proportion of body they never company together all the day time but as the woman do bring they their victual they do eat usual every day they have door at each end of their house the man remain at the one end of the house and the woman at the other the woman be very neat in make of their bread which they call Aripo and their drink passhe they make their bread and drink of a root which they call Cassavi which make good bread and very strong drink very pleasant to drink after one be use to it their house be build after the manner of our barn in England but much long for we have their house measure some of they which be one hundred and fifty pace long and some twenty pace broad one hundred person keep together in one of those house they be most artificial build and thatch so that no rain come into they although in April May and june and most of july very extreme rain do fall there also they make pot of earth which show fair earthen pot as if they be guild and some of they will hold thirty or forty gallon of liquor they be very fair to behold and very sweet to keep any thing in they make basket of diverse sort basket hamake most artificial and their bed which they call hamake they be some of they make of Cotten wool and some of bark of tree they use to lie in they hang they have a great delight to paint themselves both man and woman and especial when they go to any feast paint the woman against their day of travel in child birth make for that time a room apart in childbirth the house whereunto they go all alone and be deliver without any help at all and present after the child be bear she call for her husband and deliver he the child who present wash it in a pot of water and paint it with sundry colour which seem very strange unto i that I do not hear the woman once so much as to groan or to make any moan at all in all her time of her travel if any one of they die they do use to make great moan for they some ten or twelve day together after his death or long according as the party funeral be belove in his life time and touch such kind of beast as be in the wood as well about Wiapoco as in other place beast of those part of the country there be great store of deer hare and coney hog and many monkey great and small black and green which sort be call marmosite and great red one as big as baboon those the indian do kill and eat and there be leopard and porcupine and lion for in one place we do see a lion which the indian have kill they bring all their boy they have and do lay they on the lion back and with a whip do give every of they three lash wherefore they do so we can not learn but imagine it be because they shall remember the place where the lion be kill also there be great store of otter and a beast which be call a aligator he have a cod that smell like the musk cod of fowl I have see cock hen duck and goose partridge wood-dove herneshaw shoveller and a foul of a crimson colour call Passeray Fiemingo and great hen blue and red very beautiful to behold and multitude of fowl of other sort and hawk of diverse sort in the wood and river and of fish there be great abundance of all sort both of fresh water fish and sea fish and crab great store and the indian take their fish with a kind of wood which they beat fish and fish as before against some stone or other tree until one end thereof be all bruise and put that into the river present the fish become drink and run themselves on the shore and swim above water as our haddock do in England there be store of good root and plant with fruit as the Pina to prince charles in the year of our lord 1608. and the 23. of march when I have furnish my 23. march 1608. self with one ship of fourscore ton call the rose a pinnace of six and thirty ton call the patience and a shallop of nine ton call the lily which I build at Dartmouth and have finish my other business there and prepare all thing in readiness to begin my voyage the wind reasonable serve I then embark my company as follow in the rose I be accompany with captain Edward Fisher captain Edward Harvey the rose master Edward gifford and my cousin Thomas harcourt and beside they I have of gentleman and other one and thirty land-man two indian and three and twenty mariner and sailor in the patience my brother captain Michael harcourt have with he of gentleman and other the patience twenty land-man and eleven mariner and sailor in the lily jasper lily the master the Lilly have one land-man and two sailor so that my just number too great for so few sh^ps of no great burden be in all fourscore and seventeen whereof threescore be land-man be land-man sixty they set sail the 23. of March thus embark we set sail from the range at Dartmouth the say three and twenty of march but the wind alter upon a sudden put we back again that evening and about two of the clock the next morning it come better for we we weigh anchor and put to sea the evening follow we lose sight of the Lizzard and steer away for the canary the seven day of April we fall with Alegranza and Lancerote two land of the canary they arrive at Alegranza we stand in with Alegranza and come to anchor on the south-west side thereof that evening and the next day I land my company to exercise their limb on shore in this island we find no inhabitant nor fresh water neither fruitful tree plant herb grass nor any thing grow that be good only a abundance of unwholesome sea-fowle which after one meal be unsavoury and distasteful and a few wild caprito or wild goat which the craggy rock defend from our hand and hungry mouth the eight of April we depart from Alegranza and direct our course for tenerife another tenerise of the land the eleven day I send the pinnace and the shallop to water at the calm and there to attend my come but with my ship I hold my course for a town on the other side of the island in hope to get some wine among the merchant there but not be able by reason of a contrary wind to double we alter our course from wine to water and the twelve day we pass by Santa cruz and water that evening at the calm this water place be very convenient for all such as pass by those land and be thus to be a excellent water place find there be a wooden cross near unto it the high pike of tenerife bear due north from it there be also a ledge of rock to the eastward of the land place which be a short sandie Bay when you be land you shall find the place about forty or fifty yard from the sea side then we stand on our course for the river of Wiapoco in Guiana have a prosperous wind fair weather and a smooth Sea the nine day of May we fall into the current of the great the river of amazon fresh water in the sea 30. league from land joseph acosta Hicron G^rava tarraconensis and famous river of amazon which put out into the sea such a violent and mighty stream of fresh water that be thirty league from land we drink thereof and find it as fresh and good as in a spring or Poole this river for the great and wonderful breadth contain at the mouth near sixty league be right term by josephus acosta the empress and queen of all flood and by Hi^ronymus Girava tarraconensis it be say to be the great not only of all India but also of the whole world and for the greatness be call of many the sweet Sea it rise and flow from the mountain of Peru and draw out her stream in many wind and turn under the equinoctial for the space of one thousand and five hundred league and more although from her fountain and spring unto the sea it be but six hundred when we enter into the aforesaid current we sound and have forty four fathom water sandy sound the ten day the colour of the water change and become muddy whitish and thick then we sound again at noon and have thirty fathom and seventeen at four in the afternoon the eleven day at eight of the clock in the morning we make land the uttermost point thereof the eleven of may they make land in Guiana the patience in danger of wrack bear west from we and come to anchor in five fathom water at night the patience put in to near the shore come to anchor in two fathom and a half water upon the flood which fall from she upon the ebb and leave her dry upon the oaze and the next flood come in do so shake and beat she against the ground that before she can get off her rudder be beat away and her rib so rend and craze that if almighty God have not preserve she she have be wrack but God be thank with much ado she come off into deep water and mend her rudder as well as the time and place will afford mean then we follow on our course coast along to the north northwest the land so trend it be very shoal all along this coast the ground soft oaze but no danger to be fear keep our ship in five fathom water when we come to the latitude of two degree and a half we anchor in a goodly bay by certain land call carripapoory I do at that time forbear to make particular discovery of this coast intend if God spare i life to make a perfect discovery of the famous river of land call carripapoory amazon and of her several branch and country border upon it and of all this tract of land from the amazon unto the river of Wiapoco which contain many goodly province and signiory which be in this discourse but brief mention for at this time I purpose only to prosecute my first project which hasten i unto another place indian boat nation we be as also to trade with we who understand that we be english man bold come aboard we one of they can speak our language well and be know to some of my company to be a indian want mean to provide we bread sufficient for they all have but a small town few garden and slender provision for their own company because since captain Lee his death and his man departure from they to the number of two hundred or more and come doom into his signiory burn and spoil house roast the charibe war upon Leonard one woman take many prisoner and intend to assault he also which to prevent he arm about fifty of his indian with their usual weapon which be bow and arrow long staff sharpen at the point and with fire harden wooden sword and target very artificial the usual weapon of the indian Leonard desire aid of the English make of wood and paint with beast and bird he request also our man to aid and assist he with their musket which I command they to do upon all such occasion offer and so be all in readiness Leonard as their captain lead they on to intercept his enemy and as I have hear by master Henry Baldwin who then be present and to observe the manner of their war give he leave to command all he brave perform that exploit in good order after their manner and with great judgement and resolution for in the front he first place our four englishman by two in a rank next to they two indian arm with wooden sword the manner of order then man in the war and target then two archer and after they two man with sharpen staff instead of pike and in like manner order and rank
