VILLAGAGNON ann. 1557. and 58. @. i. of the beast and other live creature and plant of Brasill before I proceed any further present in the begin of this chapter I think good brief to admonish the reader that no live creature of the kind of fourfooted beast be find in all the Brasilian world altogether like unto we in shape and that the use not but very seldom to bring they up tame at home but that I may general describe the wild beast which the barbarian call so I determine to begin with they which be apply to the use of man it seem that that be to be set in the first place which also be most common they call Tapiroussou of a reddish and long shaggy hair great resemble a kow in bigness and shape yet see it want horn and have a short neck with long and hang ear and more wither and slender leg with a whole hoof very like unto the hoof of a ass a man may right say it participate the nature of the kow and ass notwithstanding it differ very much from either both because it have a very short tail here the reader be by the way to be admonish that very many beast be breed in America which have no tail at all and have much sharp tooth nor may any danger be therefore procure unto man by this beast see it use to repose safety rather in flight then in strength the barbarian kill they as also many other shoot they through with arrow or use to catch they in a hollow trench or with other manner of trap and gin ingenious and cunning make but that wild beast be great esteem by the barbarian by reason of the skin which as soon as they have take away cut the back of the hide in a round circle they dry it in the sun and fashion it like unto a target of the bigness of the bottom of a indifferent vessel wherewith they repel the arrow of the enemy receive in the war and the skin dry in the sun become so hard that I easy believe that it can be pierce through with the stroke of any weapon although it be cast with great violence I careful desire to bring two such target into France but the famine so oppress we return that all the provision of victual be spend not except monkey and parrot and other live creature or the same kind which we bring with we out of that country those two target be lay upon the coal be also eat to expel hunger unto the which the rest of the skin that be in the ship as I shall declare in their proper place be add moreover the flesh of the Tapiroussou come almost near unto the taste of beef this the barbarian broil after their manner and in their country language call it boucanare but because I have now use that word and that hereafter it shall be often repeat lest the reader shall any long remain doubtful occasion be offer I will declare what this thing be the american fasten four wooden fork in the ground of the thickness of a arm three foot asunder in the figure of a square and almost of the equal height of three foot lay stick across over they two finger distant each from other and so make a wooden grate this in their language they name Boucan they have many such grate in their house whereon they Boucan and the barbarian kitchen lie flesh cut into gobbet or piece and make a soft fire of dry wood that there may be no smoke almost at all they suffer they to be broil as long as they please after this manner have twice turn they in the space of a hour and because they do not powder meat with salt as the manner be here they use the only remedy of broil for the preserve of the manner of preserve meat among the american they therefore although they have take thirty wild beast in one day such as we will describe in this chapter they will lay they all cut in piece upon those grate as soon as it may be do lest they shall be taint and corrupt and there be often turn they be sometime broil and scorch above four and twenty hour together until the inside of the flesh be as well roast as the outside and by this mean they be all preserve from corruption nor be there any other manner of dress or preserve fish which when they have get they dry they in great plenty to make meal especial those which in their country meal of fish language they call Piraparati which be the very true and natural mullet of the which I shall hereafter speak in another place and these grate among the barbarian be right to be account the shambles and storehouse and therefore you shall scarce come to their village but you may see they lade with the flesh of wild beast and fish and it usual happen also very often as we shall hereafter speak if you come unto the barbarian that you shall man flesh lay upon Boucan behold these grate fill with man flesh which I think they bring as spoil take from the conquer enemy to be slay and eat but that I may prosecute the intend description of wild beast the second degree of bigness seem to be give unto a certain kind of deer which they name Seovassou but herein they d^ffer from we both that they be much low and have lesser horn and also in Seovassou a kind of deer Taiassou a boar this that they have as long shag hair as our country goat but the american boar which they call Taiassou be very like in shape unto those which be breed with we in bulk of body ear head and foot very hurtful also through his long and sharp tooth yet see he be more lean and slender and terrible gnash and grind his tooth together he be notorious also through that deformity he have a hole in the back by nature as the sea-swine have in the head whereby he draw in breath and let it out these three be their great beast swine with a hole in their back there be also among the american a certain red wild beast which they name Agouti of the height of a wean pig of thirty day old with a cleave foot a very short tail and with the nose and ear almost of a hare most delightful to the taste there be also other of two or three kind which they call not much unlike our hare but somewhar of a reddish a kind of hare hair they catch great rat also in the wood of the bigness and hair of squirrel which come near unto the delicate taste of coney reddish Miso pag or Pague for after what manner they pronounce it you can scarce or not at all understand pag a beast mark with spot be a wild beast of the indifferent height of a hound with a deform head the flesh come near unto the taste of veal with a very fair skin distinguish with white russet and black spot so that it will be of great price with we if they be to be get there be another also find which they call Sarigoy which the barbarian eat not by reason Sarigoy a stink beast of the noisome stink thereof but flay some of they and take away the fat of the kidney whence that stink proceed we eat they without loathe for they be both tender and also excellent flesh there be also that which they call Tatou this be not very well able to run yet as hedgehog Tatou arm with scale the armadillo with we creep through the briar and bush she be arm with very hard scale so that she can be pierce with a sword if also you wrap the skin together be take off wherewith the barbarian make very many chist which they call Caramenos you will say they be warlike gauntlet it be of a white flesh and of a excellent taste moreover unto these beast which be most common with the american crocodile call be add of the bigness of a man thigh and proportionable length but they be so jacare or crocodile keep tame far from do any hurt that the barbarian house be full of these jacare and the little child play with they without any danger those crocodile which I happen to see have a very wide mouth long leg with a tail neither round nor sharp but very small at the end and whither as some have write they move the upper chap I free confess that I have not observe moreover the american take lizard they call they tovous not green but russet tovous lizard and of a spot skin like our country small lizard and although they be four or five foot long and proportionable in bigness and therefore of a terrible form yet notwithstanding like frog they abide in the river and marsh hurtful unto none furthermore the skin be pluck off if they be bowel and sodden they be very delicate meat so that I the great lizard in America edible have not taste any thing more sweet in America for they be of as white a flesh as capon be with we delicate tender and sweet that nothing excel they yet in the beginning I abhor the taste thereof but afterward when I have taste they better as touch meat the lizard be chief commend of i the have also very great toad which they eat be roast without toad eat in America bowel but see both physician teach and it be also common know and apparent that the flesh and corrupt blood and whatsoever else belong to the toad be deadly any one although I hold my peace may easy conjecture that by reason of the temperateness of that country or some other cause whereof I be ignorant it happen that toad there be not venomous and dangerous at all as they be with we they eat serpent also of the bigness of a man arm five foot long almost moreover the american use to eat very great serpent I have observe that the barbarian as I mention concern crocodile bring home a certain kind of they particoloured with black and red and cast they down among their wife and child so secure that they handle they with their hand these monstrous land-eele they cut into piece and dress but they be unsavoury and of very little taste diverse and smoke tatatin I think it needful that I declare the excellent manner of kindle the same they have two kind of wood whereof the one be very soft but the other very hard which they use after this manner to kindle fire they sharpen a twig of a foot long of that hard wood at the one end like a spindle and stick the point thereof in any piece of that soft wood then lay it on the ground or upon a stock they turn that twig swift about with the palm of their hand as if they will pierce a hole through the piece of wood which lie under through that so swift and violent motion smoke be not only raise but also fire put cotton unto it or certain dry leaf in stead of our country tinder fire be very apt engender whereof I myself have make trial after that the guest have refresh themselves with meat and lodge after the manner how stranger requite their host. which we have declare if they be liberal they use to give unto the man knife scissors and pincers fit for the pluck out of the hair of their beard to the woman comb and looking-glass and to the child fishhook but if the guest want victual when he have agree of the price he may carry they away moreover because they want all kind of seem to a discourse of the scurvy or Scor^^^^ be a kind of dropsy and reign most in this climate of any that I have hear or read of in the world though in all sea it be wont to help and increase the misery of man it possess all those of which it take hold with a loathsome slothfulness that even to eat they will be content to change with sleep and rest which be the most pernicious enemy in this sickness that be know it bring with it a great desire to drink and cause a general swell of all part of the body especial of the leg and gum and many time the tooth fall out of the jaw without pain the sign to know this disease in the beginning be diverse by the the sign swell of the gum by dent of the flesh of the leg with a man finger the pit remain without fill up in a good space other show it with their laziness other complain of the crick of the back etc. all which be for the most part certain token of infection the cause be think to be the stomach feebleness by change of air in refresh ourselves with the fowl of these land they be of diverse sort and in great plenty as pengwin wild duck gull and gannet of the principal we purpose to make provision and those be the pengwin good provision in the strait the description of the Pengwin the Pengwin be in all proportion like a goose and have no feather but a certain down upon all part of his body and therefore can flee but avail himself in all occasion with his foot run as fast as most man he live in the sea and on the land feed on fish in the sea and as a goose on the shore upon grass they harbour themselves under the ground in burrowes as the coney and in they hatch their young all part of the island where they haunt be undermine save only one valley which it seem they reserve for their food for it be as green as any meadow in the month of April with a most fine short grass the flesh of these pengwin be much of the savour of a certain fowl take in the land of Lundey and Silley which we call puffin by the taste it be easy discern that they feed on fish they be very fat and in dress must be flay as the they be reasonable meat roast bake or sodden but best roast we salt some dozen or sixteen hogshead which serve we while they last instead of powder beef the hunt of they as we may well term it be a great hunt the Pengwin recreation to my company and worth the sight for in determine to catch they necessary be require good store of people every one with a cudgel in his hand to compass they round about to bring they as it be into a ring if they chance to break out then be the sport for the ground be undermine at unaware it fail and as they run after they one fall here another there another offer to strike at one lift up his hand sink up to the armpit in the earth another leap to avoid one hole fall into another and after the first slaughter in see we on the shore they shun we and procure to recover the sea yea many time see themselves persecute they will tumble down from such high rock and mountain as it seem impossible to escape with life yet as soon as they come to the beach present we shall see they run into the sea as though they have no hurt where one go the other follow like sheep after the bell-wether but in get they once within the ring close together few escape save such as by chance hide themselves in the borrow and ordinary there be no drive which yield we not a thousand and more the manner of kill they which the hunter use be in a cluster together be with their cudgel to knock they on the head for though a man give they many blow on the body they die not beside the flesh bruise be not good to keep the massacre end present they cut of their head that they may bleed well such as we determine to keep for store we save in this manner first we the keep for store split they and then wash they well in sea-water than salt they have lie some six hour in salt we put they in press eight hour and the blood be soak out we salt they again in our other cask as be the custom to salt beef after this manner they continue good some two month and serve we in steed of beef the gull and gannet be not in so great quantity yet we want not young gull to eat the guls. all the time of our stay about these land it be one of the delicate food that I have eat in all my life the duck be different to we and nothing so good meat yet they may serve for necessity duck they be many and have a part of the island to themselves several which be the high hill and more than a musket shoot over in all the day of my life I have not see great art and curiosity in creature void of reason then in the place and make of their nest all the hill be so full of they that the great mathematician of the world can not devise how cunning architecture to place one more than there be upon the hill leave only one pathway for a fowl to pass betwixt the hill be all level as if it have be smooth by art the nest make only of earth and seem to be of the selfsame mould for the nest and the soil be all one which with water that they bring in their Beakes they make into clay or a certain daub and after fashion they round as with a compass in the bottom they contain the measure of a foot in the height about eight inch and in the top the same quantity over there they be hollow in somewhat deep wherein they lie their egg without other prevention and I be of opinion that the sun help they to hatch their young their nest be for many year and of one proportion not one exceed another in bigness in height nor circumference and in proportionable distance one from another in all this hill nor in any of their nest be to be find a blade of grass a straw a stick a feather a moat no nor the fill of any fowl but all the nest their neatness and passage betwixt they be so smooth and clean as if they have be new sweep and wash one day have end our hunt of pengwin one of our mariner walk about the island of seal or sea-woolue discover a great company of seal or sea-wolue so call for that they be in the sea as the wolf on the land advise we that he leave they sleep with their belly toasting against the sun we provide ourselves with staff and other weapon and seek to steal upon i with great courtesy and compassion even with tear in his eye the mildness of a general after victory and word of great consolation and command i to be accommodate in his own cabbine where he seek to cure and comfort i the best he can the like he use with all our hurt man six and thirty at least and doubtless as true courage valour and resolution it requisite in a general in the time of battle so humanity mildness and courtesy after victory while the ship be together the mainmast of the dainty fall by the board and the people be occupy in ransack and seek for spoil and pillage neglect the south-west from panama and run many land to the southwards near thirty league they be many and most inhabit and those which have people have some negro slave unto the spaniard which occupy themselves in labour of the land or in fish for pearl in time past many enrich themselves with that trade but now it be grow to decay the fish for pearl manner of fish for pearl be with certain long Pinnasses or small bark in which there go four five six or eight negro expert swimmer and great diever who the spaniard call Busos with tract of time use and continual practice have learned to hold their breath long under water for the better achieve their work these throw themselves into the sea with certain instrument of their art go to the bottom and seek the bank of the oyster in which the pearl be engender and with their force and art remove from their foundation in which they spend more or less time according to the resistance the firmness of the ground afford once lose they put they into a bag under their arm and after bring they up into their boat have load it they go to the shore there they open they and take out the pearl they lie under the uttermost part of the circuit of the oyster in rank and proportion under a certain part which be of many plight and fold call the ruff for the similitude it have unto (@) ruff the pearl increase in bigness as they be near the end or joint of the oyster the meat of those which have these pearl be milky and not very wholesome to be eat in 1583. in the island of Margarita I be at the dreg of pearl oyster after the manner we dreg oyster in England and with my own hand I open many and take out the pearl of they some great some less and in good quantity they be find in diverse part of the world as in the west indies in the south sea in the east the place where pearl be find indian sea in the strait of magellane and in the scottish Sea those find near the pole be not perfect but be of a thick colour whereas such as be find near the line be most orient and transparent the curious call it their water and the best be a clear white shine with fiery flame and those of the east India have the best reputation though as good be find in the west India the choice one be of great value and estimation but the great that I have hear of be find in these land of pearl the which king Philip the second of Spain give to his daughter Elizabeth wife to Albertus archduke of Austria and governor of the state of great pearl Flanders in who possession it remain and be call for the rareness of it be as big as the pommel of a poniard in this navigation after our surrender the general take special care for the good entreaty the general continue his honourable usage towards the sick and wound of we and especial of those who be hurt and God so bless the hand of our surgeon beside that they be expert in their art that of all our wound man not one die that be alive the day after our surrendry and many of they with eight ten or twelve wound and some with more the thing that ought to move we to give God almighty especial thanks and praise be that they be cure in a manner without instrument or salve for the chest be all break to piece and many of their simple and compound throw into the sea those which remain be such as be throw about the ship in break pot and bag and such as by the divine providence be reserve at the end of three day by order from the general be command to be seek and gather together these with some instrument of small moment buy and procure from those who have reserve they to a different end do not only serve for our cure but also for the cure of the spaniard be many more than those of our company for the spanish surgeon be altogether ignorant in their profession and spanish surgeon ignorant have little or nothing wherewith to cure and I have note that the spaniard in general be nothing so curious in accommodate themselves with good and careful surgeon nor to fit they with that which belong to their profession as other nation be though they have great need than any that I do know at the time of our surrender I have not the spanish tongue and so be force to use a interpreter or the latin or french I begin and endeavour to satisfy the general and the better sort in the po (...) it be I dare intermeddle and especial to persuade by the best reason I can that we may be send present from panama with they but the what a pirate be english have neither peace nor truce with Spain but war and therefore not to be account pirate beside Spain break the peace with England and not England with Spain and that by which of all kind of defiance be most reprove and of least reputation the ransom of prisoner and that by the canon be more honourable but above all the most honourable be with trumpet and those who range the sea without licence of their prince who when they be meet with be punish more severe by their own lord then when they fall into the hand of stranger which be notorious to be ^ore severe prosecute in England in time of peace then in any the kingdom of Christendom but the english have all licence either immediate from their prince or from other thereunto authorize and so can in captain with sir RICHARD Hawkins in his voyage through the straight of MACELAN begin the nine of April 1593. concern the say straight and certain place on the coast and inland of Peru. the second of February 1593. we fall with the land of in 50 degree fifty five league off the straight of Magelan which land lie east and by north or east north-east from the straight which be a part of from which land we enter the straight upon the west south-west course then we run ten league west northwest other ten league west south-west than eight league south-west and come to a anchor on the starboard side in a hook where you may Moor any ship in twelve fathom water from thence we run south-west and by south seven league where we come to a island call penguin island and take in five or six ton of penguin and flay they and salt they thence twelve league south south-west penguin island and find good ride in twelve fathom fine sand from thence to port famine the new town of Pedro sarmiento five league south-west then west northwest sixteen port famine league where we anchor in good ride then northwest and by west till we come to the river of on the starboard side eight league then five league northwest the river of then northwest and by west thirty league till we come out of the straight which be in length one hundred and eleven league the mouth or entrance of the straight be in thirty two degree and a half and the outlet be in the same height the middle be in fifty four degree and a terce after we be come out of the straight we go away northwest and by north forty league into the sea then north until we come to the island of Mocha which be in thirty Mocha eight degree and thirty minute where we have good trade with the people this i will be three league long where great relief of mutton and other thing may be have from the indian this i will be twelve league from the main Land from thence we go north and past by the i will of saint Marie from thence unto valparaiso which stand in thirty three maria. Valparaso degree into which haven I go with our boat and take four ship in which we have wine and other good provision and there we remain the space of twelve day and in this time I go on shore and take five house which be full of wine and other good thing and in this time there come a ship by the harbour which the general go to take but he do not yet I with twelve man do take she and within one hour the general come to we the ship have clothes of cotton for man to wear of the indian make and some Gold Gold valparaiso be a port and a (@) in the bottom of the bay where they make excellent wine from thence eighteen league into the land be saint jago a great town of spaniard from thence we pass to arica which be in twenty degree as I take it all arica Pisco this coast lie north and south from thence we pass to Pisco and where the general and the master Hugh Cornish go to go on shore but they do not here we meet with six of the king ship which come to seek we but at that time we escape six of the king ship they these place be in fourteen degree and a half from thence we pass by the city of lima which be in twelve degree and a half from thence by Paita which be a haven Lima. in spanish contain more particular than this have or else it may be of Lewis Vaez etc. petition which by i have be present to your majesty view to persuade the conduction of some colony unto the land which your majesty have command to be discover in the part of australia and yet to this hour no resolution be take neither have I receive any answer or hope whereby I may rest assure to obtain my dispatch although I have attend fourteen month in your court and have employ fourteen year in this discovery without any profit or other respect but the benefit thereof with which notwithstanding infinite contradiction I have go 20000. league by land and by sea and have diminish and sink my estate I have travel with many affliction in my person and suffer such strange and extraordinary cross that they seem almost incredible to myself and all that so religious a undertake shall not unworthy be abandon in regard whereof I do most humble beseech your majesty in the bowel of the divine charity that you will be please to take order that I be not deprive of the fruit of this design which with such instance I do desire and which with so much justice be due unto my continual pain and travel nor that I be debar from the effect of so considerable and well ground a request who principal scope be the glory of God and of your majesty and from whence infinite benefit be likely to issue forth which will live as long as the fabric of the world shall subsist and after the dissolution thereof will remain to all eternity 1. touch the extent of these region new discover ground my judgement on that which I have see with my own eye and upon that which captain Lewes paez de torres admiral of my fleet have represent unto your majesty the length thereof be as great as all Europe and Asia the less unto the sea of Bachu Persia and all the isle aswell of the ocean as of the mediterranean sea take England and island into this account this unknown country be the four part of the terrestrial globe and extend itself to such length that in the print discourse so I call it rather than translation in english call it the five part but the spanish have the four perhaps account the east indies for a second America the three and this the four reckon all the first know part for the first description of the people probability it be twice great in kingdom and seignory than all that which at this day do acknowledge subjection and obedience unto your majesty and that without neighbourhood either of turk or moor or of any other nation which attempt war upon confine country the land which we have discover be all seat within the torrid zone and a great tract thereof reach unto the equinoctial circle the breath may be of 90. degree and in some place a little less and if the success prove answerable unto the hope they will be find antipode unto the better part of Africa unto all Europe and to the great portion of Asia but you must observe that as the country which we have discover in 15. degree of latitude be better than Spain so the other which be oppose to their elevation must by proportion and analogy prove some terrestrial paradise 2. all those quarter swarm with a incredible multitude of inhabitant whereof some be white other black and in colour like Mulatos or half moor and other of a mingle complexion some wear their hair long black and scatter other have their hair cripse and thick and other very yellow and bright which diversity be a apparent argmument that there be a apparent argument that there be commerce and communication among they and this consideration together with the bounty which nature have bestow on the soil their inexperience of artillery and gun and their unskilfulness in labour in mine with other semblable circumstance do induce i to infer that all the country be well people they know little what belong to artificial trade for they have neither fortification nor wall and live without the awe of king or law they be a simple people canton into partiality and exercise much disagreement among themselves the arm which they use be Bowes and arrow which be not poison or steep in the juice of venomous herb as the custom be of many other country they do also carry club truncheon pike dart to hurl with the arm all which be frame only of wood they do cover themselves from the waste or girdle place down to the half of their thigh they be very studious of cleanliness tractable cheerful and wondrous addict to be grateful unto those that do they a courtesy as I have experience many time the which do build in i a belief that with the assistance of God if they may be gentle and amiable entreat they will be find very docible and easy of manage and that we shall without much work accommodate ourselves unto they and it be most necessary to observe this way of sweetness especial in the beginning that the inhabitant may be draw along to this so holy and save a end whereof we ought to take a particular care and zeal aswell in small thing as in matter of more importance their house be build of wood cover with palmtree leave they have pitcher and vessel make of earth they be not without the mystery of weave and other curiosity of that kind they work on marble they have flute drum and wooden spoon they set apart certain place for oratory and prayer and for burial place their garden be artificial sever into bed border and pale mother of pearl and the shell which contain pearl they have in much use and estimation of which they make wedge razor saw culter and such like instrument they also do make thereof pearl and great bead to wear about their neck they that do dwell in the land have boat very artificial make and exceed commodious for see of their boat in Ma^^es voyage sail which be a certain three sort of root which grow there in great abundance neither do they employ much labour in make this bread for they do only roast the root until they be soft and tender they be very pleasant to the taste wholesome and nourish they be of a good length there be of they of a ell long and the half of that in bigness there be great store of excellent fruit in these country there be six kind of plane tree almond tree of four sort and other tree call Obi resemble almost in fruit and greatness the melacatone store of nut orange and Limonds they have moreover sugarcane large in size and in great plenty they have knowledge of our ordinary apple they have palmtree without number out of which there may easy be draw a juice which will make a liquor allude much to wine as also whey vinegar and honey the kernel thereof be exceed sweet and they have fruit which the indian call which be green do make a kind use of the Coco of twine and the pith be almost like in taste unto the cream of milk when they be ripe they serve for meat and drink both by land and sea and when they wither and fall from the tree there sweat out a oil from they which be very good to burn in lamp and be medicinable for wound and not unpleasant to be eat of their rind or bark there be make bottle and other like vessel and the inner skin do serve for calk of ship man do make cable and other cordage of they which be of sufficient strength to draw a canon and be fit for other domestic use but that which be more special they do there use the leaf of palmtree which they a mass together to make sail of they for vessel of small bulk and burden they make likewise fine thin mat of they and they do serve to cover the house without and for hang within and of they they do likewise make pike and other sort of weapon as also oar to row with and utensil for the house you be to note that these palmtree be their vine from whence they gather their wine all the year long which they make without much cost or of vinegar spicery and other sauce that serve for delicacy and to awake the appetite and you must oberue that many of these thing be the same with those which we have in our part and possible they be be able to nourish and furnish not only the inhabitant of the same and those of America but give a accession unto Spain itself both of riches and extent of command and this may be accomplish after the at this time make no mention I be not able to survey all which I desire neither can I in a full month have see all that which I be of myself inclinable to view you be not to make your judgement of the practice for they do not bestow themselves on those thing which with such vexation and torment we here labour to obtain 5. there be find in this country as many commodity both for the support and great store of silk mine of gold silver stone and pearl the country be very well inhabit so that it be think there be no part of the world better the king of Spain because he have many other country under he he do little esteem of this country but do take out of it all thing that be for his profit have use those people with great cruelty and take of they much tribute this land have many port in the north sea and much more in the south sea the principal port in the north side be saint juan de lua at this place do he discharge the armada that come from Spain and from this place they carry their merchandise to the great city of Mexico which city be sixty league within the land and know by the parish in the same to have a hundred and fifty thousand fair house of indian and six thousand fair house the spaniard have in it the fear and reverence that they use towards the spaniard be such that one Spaniard may go among a thousand of they and strike the chief of they and use his pleasure without any word give by the indian to the contrary such be the fear that these silly people have of the spaniard but now thanks be to almighty God the indian of that country and kingdom be become christian yet notwithstanding now and then the old man have not forget their former law do use their idolatry which be know be very cruel correct by the friar for the same offence the people of this kingdom be of a sharp wit and good understanding for whatsoever it be science or other art these people be very apt to learn it with small instruct the indian of this country do make great store of woollen cloth and silk silk and clothes so that they now begin to carry of these silk for Spain and have all other thing necessary that any other kingdom of the christian have only wine and oil which the king of wine and oil deny vineyard port and ship Spain deny to have make there but such as come from Spain because of his custom notwithstanding the king do allow they to plant vineyard for to eat of the grape this land be great commend not for that above mention nor yet for the gold and silver mynes that it have but for the great number of port for ship it have in the south sea where they make Francis pizarro Diego almagro and Fernand luque a priest enter into a league of triumvirate for the southern discovery lib. 3. c. 1. triumvirate and therein to share equal both the care charge and gain they procure ship and convenient provision and with two hundred and twenty soldier pizarro and almagro in first voyage the year 1526. one a little after the other set sail for panama pizarro have sail three hundred mile go on land and be repel by the indian himself wound and many slay hereupon he return to panama almagro go up a river in another region and be kind entertain and bring thence three thousand ducat of gold with which in his return he come near to the place where pizarro have receive his bad entertainment and himself in fight with they lose one of his eye and many of his soldier be come to panama with second voyage those show of gold they redintegrate their design and with two hundred soldier and many indian slave set sail land in another place where they also be beat back to their ship and many slay thence they go to the i will Gorgon a small and desert island six i. their woman be in common and brutish our father the sun this be the manner of speech because they derive their pedigree from the sun and for any beside the to say so be blasphemy and incur stone see man live in this fashion take pity on they and send from heaven a son and a daughter of his own to instruct man in the knowledge of our father the sun and to worship he for their god to give they law also and precept of humane and reasonable course of life in civil fashion to dwell in house and town to husband the earth to sow and set to breed cattle with these ordenance our father the sun place these his two child in the lake eighty league from cusco and give they a bar of gold two finger thick and half a yard long for a sign that where that bar shall melt with one blow on the ground there they shall place their residence and Court last he command that when they have reduce the people to serve he they shall uphold they in justice with clemency and gentleness behave themselves as a increase the season to be fair and encompass the world once every day that they shall imitate he and become benefactor to the nation be send to the earth for that purpose he constitute also and name they king and lord of all the nation which they shall instruct and civilize after these instruction he leave they and they go up from travel to the north still as they go strike with that bar of gold Ocllo which found Cosco which signify a navel and subject those nation the second Ayar Cachi or salt the three Ayai V^hu a kind of pepper the four Ayar Sanca that be mirth and content these fable they allegorise also and some spaniard will here find the fable and allegoriser eight person which come forth of Noah ark wherewith I meddle not nor with the other fable which other indian nation have of their progenitor there be no honourable stock conceit of the original of all chief family which be not derive from some fountain or lake or lion tiger bear eagle or other bird of prey or hill cave etc. but I by the say relation and of many other and indian of those town which the say Inca Manco Capac people in the space of twenty year which I there live receive notice of all that I write for as much as in my childhood they relate their story to i as they use to tell tale to child and after be grow in age they give i large notice of their law and government compare this spanish with the old tell i how their king proceed in peace and war and how they handle their subject and as to their own son they recount to i all their idolatry rite ceremony sacrifice feast use superstition much whereof I have see with my eye it be not whole leave when I be twelve or thirteen year old who be bear eight year after the spaniard have get my country I also purpose to write a story of these thing do write to my schoolefellowe for their help to give i particular information of the several province of their mother each country keep their annal and tradition which report my intent to their mother and kindred that a indian a child of their own land mean to write a history thereof search their antiquity and send they to i whereby I have notice of the conquest and act of every Inca. Dominico ourselves of certain necessary thing and principal of horse there we leave more than a hundred and forty of our man which will stay by promise and agreement which they of the village make with they depart thence we arrive at saint jago or Giacomo which be a haven in the island of Cuba and repose ourselves there certain day the captain furnish the haven of s. James himself with man munition and horse it happen in that place that a gentleman call Uasques Parcalle neete unto the town of the trinity which be in the same island offer the governor to give he certain victual which he have in the say town of the trinity which the trinity be a hundred league off from the say port of saint jago whereupon the governor depart with all the fleet towards that town but arrive half the way at a haven which they call the cape of Santa cruz it seem good unto the governor to abide there and send one ship only to receive those victual and so he appoint one captain Pantoxa to go thither with a haven call the cape of saint Cruz. his ship and that for the great security I also shall go with he and he remain still there with the four ship we have now get another in the island of saint Domenica be arrive with our five ship at the haven of the trinity the captain Pantoxa go with vasquez Porcalle to receive the victual at the town which be one league distant from the haven one hour after I be land the sea begin to be outrageous and the northwind be so strong a huracano or tempest notable both at sea and Land that the boat dare not go aland nor can they with the ship in any sort put to the contrary side the wind be in the prow whereupon with very great travail with two contrary season and with much rain they continue all that day and the Sunday the night approach the sea and tempest begin so much to increase that it no less torment those on the land then they at sea for all the house fall down and all the church and we be enforce to go seven or eight man embrace one another arm in arm together to be able to resist the wind that it may not carry we away and to avoid the ruin of the house fly unto the forest the tree give we no less cause of fear than the house have give we because they fall hold we in continual fear that they will kill we in this tempest and danger we pass all the night without presage find any part or place where for one half hour only we may stand secure but principal the midnight before we hear noise and great cry and the sound of bell flute and drum and other instrument which continue until the morning that the tempest cease in those country so fearful a thing have never be see whereof I cause a testimonial and true certificate to be make which I have send unto your majesty on Monday morning we go down to the haven and find not the ship there but see some of their furniture in the water whereby we know that they be cast away and so we purpose to go along the coast search if we may find any thing but find nothing we determine to search by the mountain and have go about a quarter of a league of from boat place upon tree by the tempest the water side we find the boat of a ship set upon certain tree and further beyond ten league along the coast they find two person of my ship and certain cover and roof of house and those two man be so actual transfigure and change with weatherbeating both of the shore and of the sea that they can not know who they be we find also a friar habit and a coverlet tear in piece and find no other person or thing any more threescore man be lose in those two ship and twenty horse and those that remain alive be thirty person only who the same day we arrive in that haven go aland together with the captain Pantoxa we remain in such manner for certain day with much trouble and great necessity because the sustenance and provision of that people be all lose and destroy with certain wild beast and the country remain in such sort that it move great compassion in the beholder the tree be fall the mountain burn and remain without leaf or grass and so we pass until the five day of November that the governor five of November of our fleet come thither to we with his other four ship who also themselves have pass great danger and torment and be escape because in good time they have retire themselves unto some place of safety the man which he have bring with he and those that he find there be so much affright and terrify with the loss and danger past that they resolve to embark themselves no more in the winter and beseech the governor that he will suffer they to repose and rest themselves in those place he perceive their mind and the desire of the inhabitant do so and give i the charge of the ship and the man which shall go with i to winter at the haven of go far within the land and find they all shallow and dangerous and so we go thirty day and sometime find some indian fisher a poor and miserable people and at the end of these thirty day when our necessity for want of water be extreme go to the coast one night we perceive a Canow come and see she we expect that she will have arrive but although we call unto she she will not come nor behold we and because it be night we follow she not but hold on our course when day begin to appear we see a small island and go thither to see if we can find any water there but we labour in vain because there be none while we stay there a mighty tempest arise upon we whereupon we abide there six day not dare to put out to sea again and have pass five day without drink our thirst be so great that we be force to drink the sea-water and some drink so large that five of our man die sudden we go out the same way which we have see the Canow go the night before we depart thence this day we see our miserable thust self many time drown and so cast away that there be none of we who do not assure himself of death but it please our lord God who in the great necessity use to show his favour that about sun set we weather a point which the land make where we find it very calm and quiet here many canowes come towards we and the indian that be in they speak unto we and without wonder at we return they be a people of a great body and well set and carry neither bow nor arrow some of we follow they unto their house which stand near unto the water side and leap aland and before the entrance of the house we find many pot of water and great quantity of fish and the lord of that country offer it all unto the governor and take he by the hand bring he to his house their house be of mat very well make and after we enter into the house of their cazique or lord he give we much fish and we give they bread of corn which we bring and they eat it in our presence and demand more which we give they and the governor give the cazique many small trifle and abide with he in his house about half a hour within night the indian assault we and the rest of our man who ride very ill be cast upon that coast they assault also the house of the cazique where the governor be and with a stone smite he on the face and take the cazique but he have his man so near escape away and leave a mantle of he of the skin of the Martinet sable which in my judgement be the best of all the world and have a scent whereunto the scent of Ambergrise and musk be not comparable rich fur and sweet mardole Zibelline and the scent thereof be smell very far off we see also other but none like unto that now see the governor wound we set he aboard and cause he to bring with he the great part of the man unto the boat and fifty of our man only remain on land to fight with the indian who that night assault we three time and with so great violence that every time they make we retire a stone cast so that there be not one of our man that be not wound after this we return to embark ourselves and sail three day and have take a little water as much as the few vesiel we have be able to carry we return to fall into the same necessity wherein we be first and go on our voyage we enter into a straight where abide we see a Canow of the indian come and as we call unto they they come and the governor to who boat they be near governor and many other labour to dissuade he yet he will needs go thither and carry a negro with he and the indian leave for hostage two of their man those indian return in the evening and bring we our vessel without water but bring not our two christian again and those two man of they who remain for pledge as soon as they speak unto they will have cast themselves into the water but our man who near thereunto where many small land be and there we all meet together and take fresh water within the sea because the river run into the sea continual and with great violence and that we may be able to bake a little Maiz which we bring because for two day before we have eat it raw we go aland on that island but find no wood there we agree to go unto the river which be behind the point one league from thence and as we go the current of the river be so great that by no mean it suffer we to arrive but current drive we back from the Land land 2 misery pursue they at sea and betray they to the indian their miserable life and death we sail four day every one eat half a handful of raw Maiz a day by at the end of these four day a tempest take we which make we recover the boat of captain tell and through the great mercy which God show to some of we we be not whole drown and be winter and exceed cold and so many day wherein we have sustain hunger with many blow which we receive from the sea the day follow the man begin very much to faint in such manner that when the sun go down all those that be in my boat be fall one upon the other so near unto death that few of they have any sense and among all they there be not five that can stand on their foot and when night come there remain no more but the master and myself that can manage the boat and two hour within night the master say unto i that I shall take charge of my boat because he be in such case that he hold it for certainty that he shall die that night and so I take the rudder and midnight be past I go to see if the master be dead who say unto i that sudden he be better and that he will guide the boat until day then sure I find myself in such state that much more willing I will have receive death then see so many man before i in that manner wherein they be and after the master take charge of the boat I rest myself a little but very unquiet because at that time nothing be further from i then sleep and about the morning i think that I hear the noise and roar of the sea because be a very low coast it rage much whereupon when I hear this I call to the master who answer i that he suppose we be now near unto the land and sound we find ourselves in seven fathom and he think it fit that we shall abide at sea until the day appear and so I take a oar and row to the land side which we find one league distant and put the stern to the Sea and be near to the land a wave take we which cast the boat back again into the sea as far as a man may well fling a stone and with the great blow which it give almost all the man who remain there as dead receive their sense again and see we so near unto the land begin to arise and go on their hand and foot and have land we make fire in certain trench and boil some of the Maiz which we have bring and find rainwater and with the heat of the fire the man begin to recover and take strength and the day that we arrive there be the six of November after the man have eat I command Lopez de Ouiedo who be the best able and strong of all the rest that he shall go close to any tree of they that be there at hand and climb up into one of they he shall discover the land where the controller and I come towards they and call unto they and they come near unto we and we endeavour the best we can to secure they so we give they crown and bell and every one of they give i a arrow drown they that coast be very fair the sea cast we all aland on the same coast all tumble in the water and half drown so that we lose not a man but those three who the boat smite under water we which and their food be the root aforesaid dig under water in the indian poor life November and December they have wear but have no fish but at this time and before that they eat root at the end of February they go into other part to seek food because the root begin then to grow and be not very good this nation above all other part of the world love their child and use they best and when it happen that any one of their child die the father mother and kindred with all the people lament he and the mourn mourn for child and lamentation continue one whole year so that every day before the sun arise the parent begin first to lament and after they all the people and they do the same at noon and in the morning and the year be end they accomplish their funeral and honourable rite of burial which they perform unto the dead and then they wash themselves and shift all the apparel which they wear they bewail all their dead in this manner except the age who they esteem not for say they that they have now pass their time and be age disesteem no more good for any thing but occupy the earth and take away the maintenance from infant and little child they use to bury the dead unless they be such as be physician among they physician burn who they burn and while the fire flame they stand all dance with great joy and make powder of the bone and when the year be past wherein they perform the honourable rite unto their dead they all tumble and wallow upon the earth and give that powder of the bone to the kinsfolk to drink in water every one have their proper and peculiar wife the physician be they that have most liberty who may keep two or three wife and among they there be great friendship and conformity when any marry his daughter he that take she bring unto the wife whatsoever he take by hunt or fish even unto the day wherein he be espouse unto she who carry it unto the house of the father without dare to take or eat any thing thereof and afterward they bring food to the house of the father-in-law for he to eat and in all this time neither father-in-law nor mother-in-law enter into their house nor be they to enter in^o their house nor the house of their kindred and if by chance they meet each other in the way they go a crossbow shoot off one from the other and so long time as they thus go far off they hang down their head and cast their eye on the ground for they hold it a wicked and a evil thing to be see and to be speak unto the woman have liberty to converse with the fathers-in-law and other kinsfolk and they of that island have filthy and foolish custom this custom more than fifty league within the Land they have another custom and that be this that when any of their brethren or child die for three month they provide nothing to eat for they of the house where they die but let they die through hunger if the kinsfolk and neighbour provide they not somewhat to eat whereupon at the time that we be there many people die there be very great famine in the most part of the house because they strict observe their custom and ceremony and they who provide food for they it be a very hard time can find but a little and upon this occasion those indian that have i have speak they will make we physician without examine they be make physician we or demand the title of our profession and because they heal the infirmity with blow upon the disease and cure they with that and with their hand they will that we also shall do the like and serve they in any thing whatsoever but we laugh thereat say it be a jest and mockery and that we know not how to heal whereupon they take away our food until we do that which they say and see our unbelief a indian say unto i that I know not what I say because stone and herb that grow in the field have virtue and that he with a hot stone lay it upon the stomach cure the pain and that we who be man must of a certainty have great virtue than all other thing of the world in the end see learned argument ourselves in so great necessity we be constrain to do it yet not hope to help any at all the manner and mean which they observe in cure be this that see themselves sick they send for the physician to who after they be cure they give all that they have and beside procure other thing from their kindred to give they the cure which the physician do unto they be to cut certain gash where the disease or grief be and suck it round about they fear manner of cure it also with fire which among they be hold a very profitable thing and I have prove it and it succeed well after this blow in the place where the grief be they suppose the disease thereby to be remove the mean whereby we cure they be to bless they and blow upon they and say a and a Au^ Mary and pray the best we can unto our lord God that he will give they water nor any thing to eat in the boat so about midnight so hard a gale of wind from the north take they that it drive the boat into the sea before any one see it for he have nothing to relieve he but one flint stone and they know not that he have any other thing beside and when the man who remain on the land see this they go along the coast and find the water so rough they make float with much trouble and pain and so pass over unto the other side and go further they come to the point of a hill at the water side and find indian there who when they see they come put their thing into their Andrea dorantes flee to the Marianes who be they with who Esquivel abide and they themselves report that they have keep Esquivel there who afterward will ha^e flee because a woman have dream that he shall kill a child of she the indian pursue he and slay he and they afterward show Andrea dorante his sword crown book and other thing which he have they have this custom also even to kill the same male child while they sleep and when a cruel custom of the indian who use to kill their male child while they sleep and cast their female child as soon as they be bear to the dog to eat they because they will not marry they to their enemy nor to their kindred the female child be bear they leave they for the dog to eat and cast they away in those place and the reason why they do it be this because they say that all they of the country be their enemy and make very great war with they wherefore if by chance they shall marry their daughter their enemy shall be the more increase who will subject they and hold they all in captivity and for this cause they will rather kill they then have any bear of themselves to become their enemy we demand of they why they marry they not among themselves who answer that it be a beastly thing to marry they unto their kindred and that it be much better to kill they then give they for wife unto their kinsfolk and enemy and they observe this custom and other of their neighbour also call jaguane and no other of that country but they observe the same and when they take wife they get the woman of their enemy and the price which they pay be the best bow that they can get with two arrow and if peradventure they have not a bow they give a net of the wideness of a man arm and as much more in length dorante abode with they and not long after flee from they Castiglio and Estevamico come into the firm land to the jaguanes all they be archer and well ^et although they be not so great as the other which we leave behind and have all their pap and their lip pierce like they their food principal be root of two or three sort penutious die which they seek throughout the whole country which be very harsh and puff up such as eat they they stay two day to roast they and many of they be very bitter and withal they dig they with much pain but the famine in those country be so great that they can live without they and they go two or three league to seek they they sometime kill any wil^e the indian in this province eat serpent viper and other beastly thing by reason of the famine which continual be th^re woman beast whatsoever and at certain time take fish but this be so little and their hunger so great that they eat frog ant egg worm lizard salamander serpent and viper which with their sting kill man they also eat earth wood and whatsoever they can get the dung of wild beast and other thing which I leave to report and I certain believe that if there be stone in that country they will eat they they keep the sharp bone of fish and serpent which they eat to grind they all afterward and so eat that powder the man load not themselves nor carry burden but the old man and woman do all this who be least esteem among they they bear no such love to their child as the other do whereof I have speak before there be some among they who use that sin which be against nature their woman be very sufficient and able to endure labour for of the four and twenty hour of the day and night they have but six hour of rest and all the great part of the night they spend in heat their oven to dry those root which they eat and when the day begin to appear they begin to draw water and carry wood unto their house and give order for other thing which they want the great part of they be great thief because although among they they be well divide yet if the father or the son turn but their head about the one take from the other thief whatsoever he can get they be great and monstrous liar and great drunkard and for that purpose they drink a certain kind of drink they be so well use to run that without rest themselves or stand still at all they run from morning until the evening follow indian which run a whole day to take a deer and tire he with run eftsoon take he alive in the chase nature nur^lings dog life tune-time a deer and in this manner they kill many follow they until they tire they and sometime take they alive their house be of mat set upon four arch and they take they up and remove they every two or three day to seek food they sow nothing at all to be able to have fruit thereof and be a very pleasant and cheerful people and notwithstanding the great hunger they endure they cease not to dance and sport themselves the best time which they have be when they eat tune because than they have no hunger and pass all that time in dance and eat day and night all the time they have they they wring they open they and set they to dry and be thus dry they hang they up in garland like fig and keep they to eat by the way when they return thence they also dry their pill and make powder of they many time while we be with they it so fall out that we continue four day without eat any thing because it be not there to be have to make we merry they tell we that we shall short have tune and shall eat many of they and drink their juice and fill our belly very well and that we shall be very cheerful and content and without any hunger and when they tell we this it be five or six month to the time of tune and when the time come we come to eat tune and by the way we find many fly of three sort very mischievous and noisome and all the rest of the summer they put we to much fly troublesome trouble and to defend we from they we make fire of rot and moist wood that it may not burn but make a smoke but this defence put we to another trouble for all the night we do nothing else but complain of the smoke which come into our eye and also of the great heat noisome remedy which the much fire give we and we go out to sleep by the side thereof and if at any time we can sleep they remember we with their bastinado to return and make the fire burn they who dwell further within the land use a remedy for these fly as intolerable as this and worse that be to say they go with firebrand in their hand burn the field and the wood wheresoever they meet with they to make the fly to fly away and so also they use to dig under the earth for lizard and other such like thing to eat they they use also to ^ill decree compass they with many fire which they also do to take away food from the beast that they may be constrain to go from thence to find it where they will have they for they never settle themselves to dwell but where wood and water be and sometime they load themselves all with this provision and go to seek dear which most common abide where decree hau^^ dry place to avoid huntman there be neither water nor wood and the day they come thither they kill dear and some other hunt game such as they can get and consume all I be fain to fly three time from those master that keep i who all come diligent to seek i that they may kill i but it please our lord God not to suffer they to find i and to preserve i from their hand from i I can not carry it on my shoulder nor trail it along the ground when I find myself in this torment I have no other remedy nor comfort but to think on the passion of our lord jesus Christ and of the blood which he shed for i and consider how much great the torment may be which he suffer through the crown of thorn then that which I endure i contract with those indian make comb bow arrow and themselves to work they sustain very great hunger at other time they make i shave skin and make they thin and the great prosperity that I have among they be the day when they give i any hide to shave in that country observe this for a common custom that if they perceive their woman to be great with child they lie not and liber^ fr^g^t Venus the indian let their child suck (...) will the age of tw^lue year with they until two year be pass after the child be bear to the which they give suck until they be of the age of twelve year that they be now of understanding to provide food for themselves we demand of they for what reason they do thus nourish they who answer we that they do it for the great famine which be in that country where as we ourselves see they be fain to continue sometime three or four day without eat and therefore they let they suck that in that time they may not die through hunger and if notwithstanding some shall escape they will become too delicate and of little strength if by chance it happen that any among they be sick they let they die in those field if he be not a child and all the rest that can go with they remain there but for a child or a brother of they they lay they upon their neck and so they carry they they have all this custom to be separate from their wife when there be no agreement between they and that both they and she may marry again with who they please and this be usual among the young sort but such as have child never forsake their wife and when they contend with other people or be at variance one with another they buffet and beat each o (...) r with cudg (...) l until they be very weary and then they part and sometime the woman part they go between they because the man come not in to part they and what choler or passion soever they have they fight not together with their bow and arrow and after no deadly fight they have buffet and cudgel each other the brawl be end they take their house and woman and go to live in the field separate from the rest until their anger and choler be pass and when they be now pacify it be not needful that other interpose themselves to make peace and friendship because in this manner they make it themselves and if they who be at variance have no wife they go to other of their neighbour who although they be their enemy receive they courteous and do they much flatter kindness and give they such as they have so that when their choler be past they return rich unto their people they be all warlike people and use as great subtlety to defend they from their enemy as they will do if they have be bring up in Italy and in continual war the horse be they that only overcome they and which the indian general fear they who be to fight with they must be use of horse very wary that they know not that they be faint or cowardly and while the battle continue they be to use they the worst they can for if they perceive they to be timorous or coward it be a people that very well know the time to avenge themselves and to take courage and strength from the fear of their enemy when they be shoot in the war and have spend arrow they return every one their way without any pursuit of the enemy although the one part be few and the other many and this be their custom they go many time away shoot clean through with arrow and die not if they touch not the bowel or heart nay they quick heal they they see and hear and have the sharp sense I think of any man in quick sense the world they be very well able to endure hunger thirst and cold as they who be more acquaint there with then likewise they drink another thing which they take from the leaf of tree like unto the mulberry tree and boil it in certain vessel on the fire and after they have boil it they fill the vessel with water and so keep it over the fire and when it have be twice boil they pour it out into certain vessel and cool it with half a gourd and when it gather much ^ome they drink it as hot as they be able to suffer it and while they put it out of the vessel and until they drink it they stand cry who will drink and when the woman perceive these exclamation they present settle themselves not dare once to move although they foolish drinkrite find that they be very well belove and if by chance any of they move they account her shameless and cudgel she and with much choler and anger cast away the water or drink which they have make and if they have drink it they vomit it out again which they do very easy the reason of this their custom they say be this that if when they will drink of that water the woman move themselves from the place where they hear that voice some bad thing may be put into that drink which enter into the body in short space will cause they to die and all the time that that water be boil the vessel must be well close and shut and if peradventure it shall stand uncover and any woman shall come and pass by they cast it away and drink no more of it it be of the colour of saffron and they drink it three day without eat and every day they drink one * * a vessel contain diu^rs gallon and a half and when the woman have their natural purgation they provide no meat but for themselves because no other person will eat of that which she carry in the time that I continue among they I see a most brutish and beastly custom to wit a man who be marry to another and these be certain effeminate and impotent man who go clothe and attire like woman and perform the sodomy office of a woman they carry no bow but bear very great and weighty burden and among they we see many such effeminate person as I have say and they be of great limb and tall than the other man after we depart from they who we leave lament we be with the other at their house and be very well entertain of they who bring we their child that we shall touch their hand and so they give we much meal of Mesquiquez these Mesquiquez be certain fruit which when they be on the tree be very bitter and be of the same sort that the Mesquiquez a fruit of India carobe be and they eat they with the earth and with it they be very sweet and good to eat the manner how they prepare they be this they make a trench in the earth of what depth they please and after they have cast the fruit into this trench they bruise and break they very well with a piece of wood as great as a man leg and three cubit long and after they be mingle with the earth of the trench they take other that be sit and put they into the say trench and return to bruise they a little more and after put they into a vessel like unto a basket and cast so much water thereon as be sufficient to cover it that the water may rise to the top and he that have bruise they taste they in his mouth and if he think they be not sweet and pleasant he demand earth and mingle it therewith and this he do until he find it sweet and so afterward they prepare themselves to sit round and every one put in his hand and take as much as he can and the seed or kernel of those fruit and so the husk they cast upon certain hide and he that have bruise they gather they together and return afterward to put they all in a basket and cast water upon they as at the first and so they return to wring out the juice and water so long as it will drop and likewise they return to put the seed and husk upon the hide and so in this manner they do three or four time far every bruise and they that be find at this banquet which because it be very great remain with their belly much puff up through the earth and water which they drink and of this the indian make we many great feast and use much dance and jollity among themselves for so long time as we stay there and when we sleep in the night six man watch with great diligence and care at the door of the cottage where we abide not cease to come in unto some of we till the sun arise and when we will depart from they certain woman of other people who live further beyond come thither and be inform by they where their house be we depart towards those part although they earnest entreat we that we will not depart for that day because those house be very far from thence and that there be no way to go thither and that the woman who come be weary but rest themselves unto the next day they will afterward go with we and conduct we thither but we dispatch ourselves thence and go away and a little after those woman who come thither with certain other of the former indian come after we but there be no beat way nor path we present lose ourselves and so go four league at the end whereof we come to drink at a water where we find the woman that follow we who tell we what great pain and travail they have take to find we depart thence and bring those woman for our guide we pass a river somewhat late and the water take we up to the breast and may be as broad as that of Seville and it run very strong and at the set of the sun we come to a hundred house of the indian who before we come go all forth to receive we with so vehement shout and loud exclamation the Toupin erasilian use such Marakas or Raeles and have like conceit thereof that it be a fearful thing and give great blow with their hand upon their thigh and bring hollow guord with stone within they which be the instrument of their great jollity and sport and never use they but for their dance and for medicine and none dare to take they in his hand but they and they say that these guord have virtue and come from heaven because they grow not in those country nor do they know from whence they come unless the river bring they when they overflow and the fear and confusion of they be so great that strive to come near unto we and touch we they so thrunge we that it be a wonder that they have not kill we and not suffer we to set our foot on the ground they carry we unto their house and bear we so above ground and the press of people so thrunge we that we enter into the house which they have prepare for we and will not consent that they shall make their festival sport any more with we for that night they pass all that night among themselves in sport and dance and the day follow at a good hour they bring we before all the people of that place that we may touch and bless they as we have do to the rest with who we abide and after this they give many arrow to the woman of another people who be come with they the next day we depart thence and all that people go with we and when we come to the other indian we be very well entertain as of the other and they give we such as they have and dear which they have kill that day among these indian we see a new custom to wit that they who be first with we take the bow and arrow shoe and crown if they have any from they who come to we to be heal and after they have thus take they away from they they bring they before we that we shall heal they and be heal that we shall have they so they depart very well content and say that they be whole after this we depart from they and go unto other of who we be very courteous receive and they bring we their disease person who when we have bless they say they be cure and he that be not whole believe that we can cure he and for that which other tell they who we have heal they make such great sport and dance that they suffer we not to sleep depart from they we go where many other house be and where another new custom begin to wit that entertain every one of we very well they who come with we take all their substance from they and rifle their house without leave they any kind of thing which displease we very much see they so other indian and the day follow we be desirous to depart they will all bring we to their friend who remain on the top of the mountain lay that there be many house and people that they will give we many thing but because it be out of our way we will not go thither and therefore take our journey through the plain near unto the mountain which we suppose shall not be very far from the coast all those people be very poor and miserable wherefore we hold it better to cross over the land because the people that dwell further into the country be better condition and will use we better and we wer^ certain persuade that we shall find a more populous country and of better sustenance and last we therefore do it because cross over the land we see more particularity so that if it shall please our lord God to bring some of we out of that country and to conduct we into the land of the christian we may be able to make relation and report thereof the indian see that we be determine to go whither they will not tell we that there be neither people nor tune nor any other thing to eat and therefore pray we that we will stay there for that day and so we do then they send two indian to discover the people that way which we purpose to go and the next day we depart carry many of they with we and the woman go lade with water and our authority be so great among they that none dare presume to drink mettle under ground and that that bell among they be a thing great esteem and that house be build there and we suppose that it be the south sea for we always know that that sea be always rich than that of the north. so we depart from they and go south Sea through so many sort of nation and diverse language that the memory of man be not able to reckon they and one people always spoil the other and so both they that lose and they who gain remain well content through those valley where we pass every one of they carry a stick or cudgel of three handful long and they go all in troop and if any
