we be angry so that one night I arise and go out to sleep in the open field apart from they but they come present where I be and never sleep all that night with much fear and speak unto i they say that if we will not continue any long angry they will bring we whether we purpose to go although they be certain assure to die by the way nevertheless we always feign that we be yet angry and because their fear be not remove a very strange accident happen that be to say that on the very same day many of they become sick and the day follow eight of they die whereupon through all the country where it be know they be so afraid of we that when they see we they seem even to die as it be for fear so they beseech we that we will not continue angry any long and that we will not cause any more of they to die certain persuade themselves that we kill they only with our will and desire we pray our lord God that he will relieve we and so all those that be sick begin to recover at which time we see a very marvelous thing to wit that the father brethren and wife of they that die be exceed grieve to see they so sick but after they be no lament for the dead dead they show not any sign or token of sorrow nor do we see they lament nor speak one to the other nor make any other sign nor dare they come near unto they until we command they to bury they and for the space of fifteen day and more that they have of we they yet put into the head of those who come late to know we because they shall give we whatsoever they have for they know that we take nothing for ourselves but give every thing to all the land until we come forth at the south sea and the fear wherein they have put we of the great famine which we be they come to the south Sea to pass as sure we pass it for day together as they all this nation come unto we that we shall touch and bless they and they be so importunate herein that they put we to much trouble because the sick and the whole will all go from we bless and it often happen desire of the spaniard blessing that of the woman that come with we some be deliver and as soon as the child be bear they bring they unto we that we shall touch and bless they they accompany we what that thing be and they answer that it come from heaven and question further with they who bring they they answer that certain man bring they which have beard like unto we who come from heaven and come to that river with horse bring lance and sword news of spaniard and two of they pass over with their lance afterwards as cunning as we can we ask they what become of those man so they answer we that they go to the Sea we go through many country and find they all dispeople and not inhabit for the country people go their way fly through the mountain not dare to keep their house nor labour for fear of the christian it great discontent we see the country very fruitful and exceed country dispeople by spaniard pleasant and full of water and goodly river and to see they afterward so solitary and scorch and the people so feeble and weak flee away and all hide and because they sow not in so great famine they maintain themselves only with the bark of tree and root we have our part of this famine in all this journey because they can not so well provide for we be so evil hire that it seem they will all die they bring we cover and bead which they have hide for fear of the christian and give they unto we and declare how at other time the christian have enter and pass through that country and have destroy and burn the people and carry half the man away and all the woman and little child and that such as be able to escape out of their hand flee away we see they so affright that they can not be secure to settle themselves in any place and that they neither will nor can sow nor labour and manure the country nay they rather determine to suffer themselves to die which seem better unto they then to expect to be so ill entreat with so great cruelty as they have be until that time and they seem to be great please with we notwithstanding we fear that be come unto they who be upon the frontier and in war with the christian lest they will use we cruel and make we pay for that which the christian have do unto they but God be please to conduct we where they be they begin to fear and reverence we as the former have do and somewhat more whereat we do not a little marvel whereby gentleness fit than cruelty it may clear appear that to allure this nation to become christian and make they obedient to the imperial majesty they ought to be gentle and courteous use and this be the only and most certain way of all other they bring we to a people that abode on the top of a mountain where they be fain to climb up by reason of the exceed roughness of those place where we find many people gather together for fear of the christian these people receive we with great good will and kindness and give we whatsoever they have and above two thousand burden of Maiz which we give unto those miserable and famish people who follow we and conduct we thither and the day follow we dispatch four messenger through the country as we use to do to the intent that they shall assemble and gather together as many people as they can unto one people which abide three day journey off from thence and have do this we depart with all the people that be there and always find the track and token where the christian have lodge and about midday we find our messenger who tell we that they can not meet with any people because they be all go and flee and hide in the mountain lest the christian shall either kill they or make they slave and that the night before they have see the christian they themselves stand behind certain tree to behold what they do and they see that they lead certain indian in a chain tie from this place which be call the river of Petutan unto the river where Diego Guzman r. from thence with many people who have conduct we whereupon he present send three horseman and fifty indian of those they bring and the negro return with they to guide they but I remain there and controversy with they because they will have make those indian slave who we bring with we and through this displeasure and disdain at our departure we leave many turkish bow which we bring and many budget and arrow and among they five of emerand which we remember not and so we lose they we give the christian many mantle of the hide of cow and other thing which we bring and much ado with the indian to cause they to return to their house and to secure they and make they sow their maiz. they be not willing to go but with we until they leave we with other indian as the custom be for otherwise if they return without be leave with other they fear lest they shall die and come with we they fear not the christian nor their lance this thing great displease the christian who cause a interpreter to speak unto they in their own language and tell they that we be the very same man who for a long time have be terrify and lose and be a people of mean condition and of small force and that they be lord of the country who they be to serve but the indian make little no no account of all this so that among themselves they say one to another that the christian lie because we come from the place where the sun rise and the other christian from the place where the sun go down and that we heal the sick they kill the (@) that be sound and that we go naked and without garment they clothe on (...) back and with lance and that we have not any covetous or insatiable desire so that whatsoever be give we we present give it unto other and have nothing ourselves and the christian intend (...) language and do the like to other in a language which be among they which we understand and those that use it we call which we have find use for above the space of four hundred league of the christian yet with much ado and through our persuasion we make they return unto their house command they to rest satisfy and bring back their people to sow and till the ground which because it be so desolate become now full of wood albeit of it own nature sure it be the best country and more fertile and abundant than any in all those indies for they sow three time in the year and have many fruit and many goodly river and other very good water there be many sign and great token of mine of gold and silver the people be very well condition and serve the christian that be their friend with a very good will they be much better dispose then the people of Mexico and final it want nothing to make it a absolute country the indian be dispatch they tell we that they will do as much as they have command and bring back their people if the christian will suffer they to continue whereupon I say and certain affirm that if they do it not the christian shall be much to blame and after we have send the indian year say unto all they that we find that they shall believe in God and serve he because he be lord of all the thing in the world and that he give a reward and payment unto the good and perpetual punishment of hell fire unto the wicked and that when the good man die he take they up into heaven where afterward they shall never die any more nor suffer hunger or cold or endure any other necessity but find there great glory than can be imagine and they who will not believe nor obey he shall be throw down under the earth in the company of devil into a exceed huge fire which never shall they very well and that we will command that they shall not do they any hurt nor take their counyrie from they but become their good friend and if they will not do it the christian shall use they very cruel and carry they for slave into far and remote country to this they answer the interpreter that they will become very good christian and serve God and demand of they who they adore and to who they sacrifice and of who they ask water for their seed time and health and safety for themselves they answer that they pray unto a man which be in heaven and be demand how they call he they say Aguar and they believe that he create all the world and the thing therein then we question they further whence they know that who answer that their parent tell they so and that of a long time they understand it and know that he send water and all other good thing so we cause the interpreter to tell they that he who they call Aguar we call God and that they also shall call he so and serve he and adore he as we have appoint and they shall find it very good for they they answer that they understand all very well and that they will do so wherefore we command they to descend from the mountain and that they shall live secure and in peace and dwell in the country and build their house and among they make a house for God and set a cross at the entry thereof like unto that which we have there and when the christian shall come they shall go to meet they with the cross without bow and weapon and conduct they to their house and give they such as they have to eat and so they will not do they any harm but will become their friend and the captain give they some of the mantle and use they very well so they depart carry with they the two indian which before be prisoner who we have send as messenger and all this be do in the presence of the secretary of the governor and many other witness now when the indian be return all the rest of that province who be friend unto the christian come to see we and his man and only the seaman remain in the ship which in eight day go up with the tide every day a little bring they up unto the town assoon as the people be come on shore he pitch his camp on the sea side hard upon the bay which go up unto the town and present the captain general Vasques Porcallo with other seven horseman forage the country half a league round about and find six indian which resist he with their arrow which be the weapon which they use to fight withal the horseman kill two of they and the other four escape because the country be cumbersome with wood and bog where the horse stack fast and fall with their rider because they be weak with travel upon the Sea the same night follow the governor with a hundred man in the brigantine light upon a town which he find without councrie be most esteem the cacique answer by the same indian that whereas he say that he be the child of the sun if he will dry up the river he will a most witty and stout answer of the cacique of Quigalta believe he and touch the rest that he be wont to visit none but rather that all those of who he have notice do visit he serve obey and pay he tribute willing or perforce therefore if he desire to see he it be best he shall come thither that if he come in peace he will receive he with special goodwill and if in war in like manner he will attend he in the town where he be and that for he or any other he will not shrink one foot back by that time the indian return with this answer the governor have be take himself to bed be evil handle with fever and be much aggrieve that he be not in case to pass present the river and to seek he to see if he can abate that pride of he consider the river go now very strong in those part for it be near half a league broad and 16. fathom deep and very furious and run with a great current and on both side be many indian and his power be not now so great but that he have need to help himself rather by slight then force the governor feel in himself that the hour approach wherein he be to leave this present life and call for the king officer captain and principal person he name l^ys de aluarado his captain general and present he be swear by all that be present and elect for governor the next day be the one and twenty of May 1542. the death of don Ferdinando de Soto the 21. of May 1542. at G^acoya depart out of this life the valorous such a time as in his sickness he have but little comfort and the danger wherein all his people be of perish in that country which appear before their eye be cause sufficient why every one of they have need of comfort and why they do not visit nor accompany he as they ought to have do Lewis de moscoso determine to conceal his death from the indian because Ferdinando de Soto have make they believe that the christian be immortal and also because they take he to be hardy wise and valiant and if they shall know that he be dead they will be bold to set upon the christian though they live peaceable by they in regard of their disposition and because they be nothing constant and believe all that be tell they the adelantado make they believe that he know some thing that pass in secret among themselves without their knowledge how or in what manner he come by they and that the figure which appear in a glass which he show they do tell he whatsoever they practise and go a witty stratagem about and therefore neither in word nor deed dare they attempt any thing that may be prejudicial unto he as soon as he be dead Lewis de moscoso command to put he secret in a house where he that desire long to see himself in a place where he may sleep his full sleep rather than to conquer and govern a country where so many trouble present themselves present return back that same way that he come when that which be determine be publish to the camp there be many that be great grieve at it for they hold the sea voyage as doubtful for the evil mean they have and as great danger as the the town to seek the brigandine from whence they carry they by water to the river which if they have go by land have be in danger of break and split their keel and to be all undo because that for want of iron the spike be short and the plank and timber be very weak they ship two and twenty of the best horse that be in the camp the rest they make dry flesh of and dress the hog which they have in like manner they depart from Minoya the second day of july 1543. there go from Minoya three hundred twenty and two spaniard in seven brigandine well make save that the plank be thin because the nail be short and be not pitch nor have any deck to keep the water from come in in stead of deck they lay plank whereon the mariner may run to trim their sail and the people may refresh themselves above and below they sail down the river seventeen day which may be two hundred and fifty league journey little more or less and near unto the sea the river be divide into two arm each of they be a league and a half broad by the way the indian set on they slay some and wound many the eighteen of july they go forth to sea with fair and prosperous weather for their voyage they sail with a reasonable good wind that day and the night follow and the next day till evening song always in fresh water whereat they wonder much for they be very far from land but the force of the current of the river be so great and the coast there be so shallow and gentle that the fresh water enter far into the Sea they endure a intolerable storm first and after that the torment of a infinite swarm of moskito which fall upon they which as soon as they have sting the flesh it so infect it as though they have be venomous for the sail which be white seem black with they those which row unless other keep they away be not able to row have pass the fear and danger of the storm behold the deformity of their face and the blow which they give themselves to drive they away one of they laugh at another they meet all together in the creek where the two brigandine be which outgo their fellow there be of the sea like pitch call Copee find a scum which they call Copee which the sea cast up and it be like pitch wherewith in some place where pitch be want they pitch their ship there they pitch their brigandine they rest two day and then eftsoon proceed on their voyage they sail two day more and land in a bay have slay we I march against he and find the information true beside other inormity in sacrifice indian and christian as he have use to do before he be a christian whereupon I condemn he to the fire of they down the river leave at every lodging place a crosse. on the six day we come to the province Cuinao full of Cuinao good town and abound in victual the people have at first arm themselves for resistance but when I send Barius against they they be all flee to the mountain the light horse take some of the slow not without make some defence I send they word not to be afraid but to return to their house and give their obedience which they refuse I march against they with three squadron and send the overseer on one part and captain ognate on the other and I be at their back the overseer find none but woman and child ognate encounter with about one hundred man with their bow and arrow wound slight two horse and three man but many of they be slay other take with woman and child about five hundred which I cause to be keep together lest the indian shall sacrifice they after their wont the cacique be flee to the next province call Cuinaquiro of another signiory and language because he come not at my send I wretched hospitality go to seek he enter that province where be many town and great store of Maiz and fruit we find many people dead sacrifice which have out of the former province retire thither for fear of we with many piece of flesh which they use to eat I send many prisoner to their friend to let they see that I come not to slay they the language of this people none of we can understand the overseer encounter three hundred arm with bow and arrow which the day before have kill four of our indian they set upon we sing and kill a horse but have lose one hundred of their company the rest escape I find my man cut the horse in piece that the enemy may see no sign of he whereby they may know that a horse can die I send the camp master to discover the ford three indian set on he one courageous indian of which have a two hand sword of wood which give he two blow but the indian be slay I move forward and discover many inhabit place another skirmish happen with convers infidel pope and what they ought to do to be save and how the king of Castille be the minister of God in earth and lord of all those part subject to he and that to i in his royal name they be they ought to serve and obey on earth the king of Castille the cacique answer that till that hour he indian simplicity have never know any thing of that which I have speak nor have ever hear of any but i that which I declare but that he now conceive great pleasure to have understand it and that from henceforth he will hold for God the king of Castille and will worship he I answer that he ought not so to do for the king of Castille be a mortal man as we ourselves be but that he be lord and sovereign over we all and give to we of God to rule and govern we and we be to serve and obey he and God above which create heaven and earth and all thing visible and invisible be he which ought to be worship fear and serve above all thing for as much as he give we and of his hand we hold the life and be which we have and he be able to take it from we at his pleasure in this manner he stand advise of that which he ought to do although their wit and capacity be very small and their will much gourd Maiz and such kind of pulse whereof we and they eat so plentiful that there be no speech of the rise of the price of thing or of famine nay rather a great part of the old crop perish oftentimes and they cast away their old Maiz to make room for the new they have great store of Cotten wool whereof they make excellent clothes wherewith they be apparel their apparel Cotten wool be a piece of cloth tie upon their shoulder wherewith as with a cloak they cover their whole their apparel body after the manner of the mexican true it be that though they be all workman yet for the most part of the year they be not cover but go naked yet all of they wear a broad girdle of the say Cotten clothe cunning and artificial wrought with figure of diverse colour in the same which the shell of cockle and oyster join artificial with bone do make moreover they thrust many thread through their ear whereon they hang earring for which purpose they bear the ear of their child as soon as they be bear in many place and hang earring round stone and coral in they so that each ear be lade with fifty of these ornament at least for which cause they always sleep not lie on their side but with their face upward the woman be decent cover from their waste downward be all the rest naked the man as well as the woman wear long hair the woman have it their heir hang down their shoulder the man often bind up and tie in diverse knot they thrust coral in it adorn with diverse feather and cockle shell which add a certain beauty and ornament to the head they wear many round bead of diverse colour about their neck they be of great stature and high than the spaniard by a handful their great stature so that as we sit upright upon our horse without stand on tiptoe they easy can embrace we they be valiant and strong which the war which they their yalour have with the spaniard do easy show wherein though they sustain no small damage yet be they not unrevenged nor without the blood of their adversary when they will fight resolute for their uttermost liberty they denounce and appoint the day of battle their weapon be bow and poison arrow and a kind of club of their weapon hard wood wherewith they need not to strike twice to brain a man they use also ^ertaine short javelin make of red wood so hard and sharp that they be not inferior to our arm spear and as fearful and terrible as they be to their enemy so quiet and peaceable be they among themselves and their neighbour and you shall seldom find a quarrellour or contentious person the spaniard after certain conflict at length make friendship with they leave their country to they but those eight spaniard who I mention before live quiet among they and though they be call lord yet be they eight Spaniard live in Ci^^loa content with such thing as the indian give they offer no violence nor molestation to any man upon our come into these country the indian stir up with the fame of new man come by flock unto our lodging and witness their love with exceed great signification of good will with salutation and word which yet we understand not stay so long with we till they be friendly dismiss by we neither neglect they the opportunity offer upon the first occasion to show how great they affect the christian religion for as soon as we enter into the first village of this province the day follow there assemble a great number of old readiness to hear the gospel and young folk to be baptize which be a great comfort unto we we christen full fourscore boy and girl we raise the mind of the rest with good hope that assoon as they be instruct with necessary doctrine they shall be partaker of the same sacrament we four hundred baptize by franciscan slay there twelve year before difference of language find four hundred christian which have be baptize by the franciscane father which come into these part twelve year past when at length they be slay by the inhabitant be leave destitute of a teacher neither can all of they be instruct by we unless some help be send we for beside that the people be many they also differ in language and tongue although there be two chief and most general we learn two tongue with great celerity which albeit they be not so vulgar and general yet be they more necessary and we have profit so much in three month that we can easy understand the indian when they speak wherefore we begin to instuct in the catechism and with godly speech to exhort the nation to keep they within the compass of their duty and to deliver they of all fear when they see that they receive of we the service instruction in the catechism and form of pray to God not in a strange but in their own language the which together with the catechism they learn with great care and shortness of time and now we have and why do you teach Babylon or to babble in a strange tongue here instead of pray sixteen hundred new christen concubine christen above sixteen hundred as well those of year as boy beside those four hundred which be christen by the aforesaid father almost in their infancy and full twelve year neglect have scarce any show of Christendom but be marry with pagan after their country fashion from many of they we take away their concubine because such be the custom of this nation that they take as many as they be able to keep many of they we likewise marry there be also many more which desire to be baptize but since the people be exceed many and the workman but two only we be not able to sustain the labour the last of November I visit the people of this tract or river and in the space of twelve or thirteen mile there be four thousand indian at the least which use bow and arrow beside woman and child among these be certain of bad name and fame which have familiarity and acquaintance with the devil with who they commit abominable and very horrible familiarity with the devil sin many of they flee into the mountain that their child may not be christen because the devil have report abroad that all they shall die that be baptise not withstand in seven or eight day we christen two hundred and forty child necessity enforce i to 240. child christen leave they and to go to another place to help our neighbour yet I be great desirous to return move with a certain pity because I see this people so strong possess by the devil be utter ignorant of the faith there be now thirteen church in these three river beside those which be erect by little and little neither have we any more holy vestment for they than those which we carry thirteen church in three river about with we and one other furniture of a altar which belong to the spaniard we have never a bell in any of these church we furnish a altar with one cross and certain paper image which be bring hither from culhuacan because we want other furniture which we look from your reverency and it will be very profitable since this nation be so delight culhuacan with outward ornament we celebrate the dedication of a church at Petatlan on the day of the conception of the virgin the mother of God in the same I set up a certain small image consecrate to the conception Petatlan in 25. degree and a half the christianity there teach of the bless virgin we go on procession wherein the boy sing the in the vulgar language I add a prayer and then red mass because the singer be yet ignorant of song and can sing nothing else but amen with a rude and untune voice many of the pagan be present which be invite to this holy day from other place and be almost amaze behold these first beginning wish that the like solemnity may be keep in their village as far as hitherto we be able to gather the indian the inhabitant of these and the neighbour pagan castle where there be great store of people and less diversity of language be quick and prompt tractable and of easy conversion than any that I have hitherto see or know I can wish that I may sometime live private with myself but such be the concourse of comer that they love i not thus quiet and though I be silent yet they minister diverse speech inquire of our thing and rehearse their own and come to we in the night to prayer they be ingenious and docile although they have no teacher by who instruction this force of nature shall be exercise they live in castle and country village in house join near the one to the other and build of chalk and timber which they adore their house with mat and cover of reed in the marriage which they make when they take many wife it seem not inconvenient or indecent unto they to take their sister mother or daughter because they think that this make much for domestical peace and that thereby all emulation may be avoid and though their plurality and incest in marriage they make no account of affinity yet they have exceed great regard of consanguinity they love their child most tender for a certain time and teach they nothing else but such thing as they know themselves and never beat they nor chastise they for any thing and so the bad education of their child form of marriage they live like beast they marry they at their time and this be the form of their marriage the parent of each party meet together and after conference have between they they dance according to their country custom and give hand return home if the bridegroom or bride be under age they stay certain month and sometime a year never see one the other afterward at time convenient the father of the spouse give a house to his daughter and son in law with furniture thereto belong they also make the bridegroom a knight if he be of a worthy family with diverse rite their form of make knight whereof these be the chief ceremony they deliver he a bow and instruct he how to use his new weapon and to show a sign of his industry and ability he be turn out to some young lion or wild beast which when he have kill he be advance to some honour and dignity whereby he excel other which be not knight among the thing belong to policy this be one which they do observe that they adopt other man child for their own adoption but this adoption into another family have very severe and dangerous ceremony for they thrust a stick into their mouth into the bottom of their throat wherewith they be almost choke if it fall out well they vomit up all the meat in their stomach and so they pass over into the right of another man whatsoever time remain from labour and travail they their quietness and kind play spend in a play which be like to dice but consist of diverse sign they play with exceed great moderation and patience of mind be most cunning in this kind of sport no oath be hear among they nor any contention or brabble word though they lose their apparel and all that they have and go home naked as sometime it fall out when they be sick if the disease be sore and dangerous they dig a place for their burial and sometime it stand five or six day open which custom be very profitable to a certain their burial woman for when I come into a certain village and see the ground dig very deep know what the matter be I come unto her lie on her couch and sick and have instruct she in the catechism which I have write in the vulgar tongue in the principle of christian religion I baptize she but she recover now the cause why they open the place of their burial be this that present they may cover the body or ash of he that be dead for sometime they burn the body with all the house and household stuff they sprinkle the sepulchre with a certain dust whereof they make a drink and bring meat with they and after they have weep over the grave they make themselves drink the kinsfolk of the dead make a feast for they that do assist they and these be their funeral the vicar of the church of culiacan which be forty two league from Cinoloa where the foresay father live in his letter send to a certain friend write after this manner in cinaloa the father labour painful in the lord in convert the indian unto the faith so fruitful and happy they perish and do perish all with faith and without sacrament i brother Bartholomew casas or Casaus religious of the order of saint Dominicke which by the mercy of God be come into this court of Spain to sue that the hell may be withdraw from the indies and that these innumerable soul redeem by the blood of jesus Christ shall not perish for evermore without remedy but they may know their creator and be save also for the care and compassion that I have of my country which be Castille to the end that God destroy it not for the great sin thereof commit against the faith and his honour and against our neighbour for certain man sake notable zealous of the glory of God touch with compassion of the affliction and calamity of other followers of this court howbeit that I be purpose to do it but I can not so soon have do it because of my continual occupation I achieve this treatise and summary at valencia the eight of December 1542. the force be mount to the high type of extremity and all the violence tyranny desolation anguish and calamity abovesaid spread over all the indies where there be spaniard although they be more cruel in one part than they be in another and more savage understanding of the mischief and treason that there have be and be commit against those poor people against the will of God and his own for they have always cunning conceal the truth from he will the great city they enter into it slay all that they can take in that day more than three hundred person etc. among diverse the remedy by friar casas bishop of the royal town call Chiapa propound in the assembly of sundry prelate name parson by his majesty commandment gather together in the town of valladolid the year of our lord 1542. for order and reformation to be observe in the indies the eight in order be this ensue which consist upon twenty reason and motion the eight remedy be among all other principal and most in force as without which all the rest be to no purpose for that they all have relation thereunto as every motion to his proper end in whatsoever touch or be of any importance unto your majesty which no man can express in as much as thereupon depend at the least the whole loss or preservation of the indies and the remedy that I speak of be this that your majesty do determine decree command and solemn in your sovereign court ordain by pragmatical saction and royal statute that all the indies as well already subdue as hereafter to be subdue may be insert reduce and incorporate into the royal crown of Castille and Leon to be hold in chief of your majesty as free subject and vassal as they be likewise that they be not give in unto the spaniard but that it stand as a inviolable constitution determination and royal law that they never neither at this time neither hereafter in time to come may be alienate or take from the say royal crown neither that they be give command demise in fee farm by depost commandment or alienation either under any other title call Seine he make league with eight savage king which have be much dispight by the spaniard and be grow as despiteful to they the spaniard be account four hundred strong and have divide themselves into three fort upon the river of May the great begin by the french two small near the river mouth to fortify each thereof with twelve hundred soldier in they well provide for munition three fort Spanish in April 1568. he take these two fort and slay all the spaniard the vindicative savage give he vehement and eager assistance especial Olotocara nephew to Saturiova as they go to the fort he say that he shall die there and therefore desire gourgues to give that to his wife which he will have give himself that it may be bury with he for his better why the savage have their good inter with they welcome to the village of the soul depart this fort be take the spaniard some slay other take and hang on the same tree on which the french hang five of which on of these spaniard confess he have hang and now acknowledge the divine justice in steed of the write which Melendes have hang over they I do not this as to frenchman but as to lutheran gourgues set up another I do not this as to spaniard or mariner but as to traitor robber just requite all and murderer the fort he raze not have man to keep they and in june follow arrive in Rochel come to the king with expectation of reward out of his cabin and they begin to make their tabagie or feast which a feast of this savage Orignac a beast like a ox they make with the flesh of Orignac which be like a ox of bear of seal and bever which be the most ordinary victual which they have and with great store of wild fowl they have eight or ten kettle full of meat in the midst of the say cabin and they be set one from another some six pace and each one upon a several fire the man sit on both side the house as I say before with his dish make of the bark of a tree and when the meat be sodden there be one which divide to every man his part in the same dish wherein they feed very filthy for when their hand be fatty they rub they on their hair or else on the hair of their dog whereof they have store to hunt with before their meat be sodden one of they rise up and take a dog and dance about the say kettle from the one end of the cabin to the other when he come before the great Sagamo he cast his dog perforce upon the ground and then all of they with one voice cry ho ho ho which be do he go and sit he down in his place then immediate another rose up and do the like and so they continue until the meat be sodden when they have end their feast they begin to dance take the head of their enemy in their hand which hang upon the wall behind they and in sign of joy there be one or two which sing moderate their voice by the best disposition which they cause to run and he which be the swift in run have a present all these people be of a very cheerful complexion they laugh for the most part nevertheless they be somewhat melancholy they speak very distinct as though they will make themselves well understand and they stay quick bethink themselves a great while and then they begin their speech again they often use this fashion in the midst of their oration in counsel where there be none but the principal which be the ancient the woman and child be not present all these people sometime endure so great extremity that they be almost constrain to eat one another through the great cold and snow for the beast and these savage endure great famine fowl whereof they live retire themselves into more hot climate I think if any will teach they how to live and to learn to till the ground and other thing they will learn very well for I assure you that many of they be of good judgement and answer very well to the purpose to any thing that a man shall demand of they they have one naughty quality in they which be that they be give to revenge and great liar a people to who you must not give their have quality too much credit but with reason and stand on your own guard they promise much and perform little they be for the most part a people that have no law as far as I can see and inform myself of the say great Sagamo who tell i that they constant believe that there be one God which have make all thing and then I say unto he since they believe in one God only how be it that he send they into this world and from whence come they he answer the belief of the savage i that after God have make all thing he take a number of arrow and stick they in the ground from whence man and woman grow which have multiply in the world until this present and have their original on this fashion I reply unto he that this which he say be false but that indeed there be one God only which have create all thing in the earth and in the heaven see all these thing so perfect without any body to govern this world beneath he take of the slime of the earth and thereof make Adam our first father as Adam sleep God take a rib of the side of Adam and thereof make Eve who he give he for his companion and that this be the truth that they and we have our original after this manner and not of arrow as they believe he say nothing unto i save that he believe rather that which I say then that which he tell i I ask he also whether he believe not that there be any other but one god only he tell i that their belief be that there be one God one son one mother and the sun which be four yet that God be above they all but that the son they believe one God one son one mother and the sun be good and the sun in the firmament because of the good that they receive of they but that the mother be naught and do eat they and that the father be not very good I show he his error according to our faith wherein he give i some small credit I demand of he whether they have not see nor hear say of their ancestor that God come into the world he tell i that he have never see he but that in old time there be five man which go towards the sun set which meet with God who ask they whither go you they say we go to seek our live God answer they you shall find it here they go far without regard what God have say unto they which take a stone and touch two of they with it which be turn into a stone and he say again unto the other three whither go you and they answer as at the first and God say to they again go no further you shall find it here and see that nothing come unto they they go far and God take two staff and touch the two first therewith which be turn into staff and the five stay and will go no turth and God ask he again whither go thou I go to seek my live stay and thou shall find it he stay without go any further and God give he meat and he do eat thereof after he have well feed he return with other savage and tell they all the former story he tell they also that another time there be a man which have store of tobacco which be a kind of herb whereof they take the smoke and that God come to this man and ask he where his tobacco pipe be the man take his tobacco pipe and give it to God which take tobacco a great while after he have take store of tobacco God break the say pipe into many piece and the man ask he why have ceremony but that every one pray in his heart as he think good this be the cause why I believe they have no law among they neither do they know how to worship or pray to God and live for the most part like brute beast and I think in short space they will be bring to be good christian if their country be planten which they desire for the most part savage which speak with the devil they have among enterprise in execution either to kill a french man or any other of their nation they will immediate obey his commandment also they believe that all the dream which they dream be true and indeed there be many of they which say that they have see and dream thing which do happen or shall happen but to speak true of these thing they be vision of the devil which do deceive and seduce they loe this be all their belief that I can learn of they which be brutish and bestial all these people be well proportion of their body without any deformity they be well set and the they paint themselves with a olive colour woman be well shape fat and full of a tawny colour by abundance of a certain paint wherewith they rub themselves which make they to be of a olive colour they be apparel with skin one part of their body be cover and the other part uncover but in the winter they cover all for they be clad with good fur namely with the skin of Orignac their apparel of skin otter bever lea-boore stag and dear whereof they have store in the winter when the snow be great they make a kind of racket which be twice or thrice as big as one of a device to go on the snow with a racket we in France which they fasten to their foot and so go on the snow without sink for otherwise they can not hunt nor travail in many place they have also a kind of marriage which be that when a maid be fourteen or fifteen year old she shall have many servant the marriage of the savage and friend and she may have carnal company with all those which she like then after five or six year she may take which of they she will for her husband and so they shall live together all their life time except that after they have live a certain time together and have no child the man may forsake she and take another wife say that his old wife be nothing worth so that the maid be more free than the marry woman after they be marry they be chaste and their husband for the most part be jealous which give present to the father or parent of the maid which they have marry lo this be the ceremony and fashion which they use in their marriage touch their burial when a man or woman die they make a pit wherein they put all their burial after the tartar manner the good which they have as kettle fur hatchet bow and arrow apparel and other thing and then they put the corpse into the grave and cover it with earth and set store of great piece of wood over it and one stake they set up on end which they paint with red on the top they believe the immortality of the soul and say that when they be dead they go they believe the Champlein have time to view their tillage and the fair land that serve for a ornament to their great extension of water these people be much like to the armouchiquois in their fashion of live they sow indian Maiz and beanes and have quantity of fair grape whereof they make no use and very good root every family have their ground round about their dwelling fort also yet no town make with building of iroquois themselves and as the iroquois do approach Champlein who be arm with a musket charge with two bullet will have set himself forward to aim to make at one of the forward of the iroquois who do brave it challenge his enemy to the combat but the savage of Kebec tell he in their language no do not so for if they once discover you not be the prudence of the savage accustom to see such folk they will forthwith run away and make no stand so shall we loose the glory which we expect of this charge withdraw yourself therefore behind our foremost rank and when we shall be near you shall advance yourself and shoot at those two feather fellow who you see the foremost in the midst of the troop which be find good and execute by the say champlein who with one shot lay they both to the ground as he have relate unto we he who assist he do also his duty but on a sudden all be in flight disorder astonish at such a noise and death so unexpected upon this fear the man of Kebec lose no occasion follow earnest their enemy and kill about fifty of they who fifty of the iroquois slay head they bring back to make therewith merry feast and dance at their return according to their custom these thing so pass Champlein take again his course towards ancient France where he arrive in October 1609. have leave the government of new France to a good reverend old man 1609. call captain pierre and they return to the Azores and after to England arrive at Plymouth octob. 24. master Bartholomew GOSNOLDS letter to his father touch his first voyage to Virginia 1602. my duty remember etc. sir I be in good hope that my occasion will have allow i so much liberty as to have come unto you before this time otherwise I will have write more at large concern the country from whence we late come than I do but not well remember what I have already write though I be assure that there be nothing set down disagree with the truth I think it fit not to go about to add any thing in writing but rather to leave the report of the rest till I come myself which now I hope shall be short and so soon as with conveniency I may in the mean time notwithstanding whereas you seem not to be satisfy by that which I have already write concern some especial matter I have here brief and as well as I can add these few line for your further satisfaction and first as touch that place where we be most resident it be in the latitude of 41. degree and one three part which albeit it be so much to the southward yet be it more cold than those part of Europe which be situate under the same parallel but one thing be worth the note that notwithstanding the place be not so much subject to cold as England be yet do we find the spring to be late there than it be with we here by almost a month this whether it happen accidental this last spring to be so or whether it be so of course I be not very certain the latter seem most likely whereof also there may be give some sufficient reason which now I omit as for the acorn we see gather on heap they be of the last year but doubtless their summer continue long than we we can gather by any thing we can observe in the people or by any trial we have thereof ourselves but that it be as healthful a climate as any can be the inhabitant there as I write before be of tall stature comely proportion strong active and some of good year and as it shall seem very healthful be sufficient proof of the healthfulness of the place first for ourselves thank be to God we have not a man sick two day together in all our voyage whereas other that go out with we or about that time on other voyage especial such as go upon repr^sall be most of they infect with sickness whereof they lose some of the^r man and bring home a many sick return notwithstanding long before we but Verazzano and other as I take it you may read in the book of discovery do more particular entreat of the age of the people in that coast the sassafras which we bring we have upon the land where though we bid little disturbance and reasonable plenty yet for that the great part of our people be employ about the fit of our house and such like affair and a few and those but easy labourer undertake this work the rather because we be inform before our go forth that a ton be sufficient to cloy England and further for that we have resolve upon our return and take view of our victual we judge it then needful to use expedition which afterward we have more certain proof of for when we come to a anchor before Portsmouth which be some four day after we make the land we have not one cake of bread nor any drink but a little vinegar leave f^r these and other reason we return no otherwise lade then you have hear and thus much I hope shall suffice till I can myself come to give you further notice which though it be not so soon as I can have wish yet I hope it shall be in convenient time in the mean time crave your pardon for which the urgent occasion of my stay will plead I humble take my leave 7. septemb 1602. your dutiful son barth gosnold chap. 11 the relation of captain gosnols voyage to the north part of Virginia begin the six and twenty of march 1602. and deliver by Gabriel archer a gentleman in the say voyage the say captain do set sail from Falmouth the day and year above write accompany with thirty two person whereof eight mariner and sailor twelve purpose upon the discovery to return with the ship for England the rest remain there for population the fourteen of April follow we have sight of saint mary a island of the Assoris the three and twenty of the same be two hundred league westward from the say island in the latitude of 37. degree the water in the main ocean appear yellow ocean seem yellow the space of two league north and south where sound with thirty fathom line we after diverse other as pettrel cootes hagbut pengwin murre gannet cormorant gull with many else in our english tongue of no name the eight of the same the water change to a yellowish green where at we which he do according the five we continue our labour when there come unto we ashore from the main fifty savage stout and lusty man with their bow and arrow among they there seem to be one of i only eight person these indian in hasty manner come towards we so as we think fit to make a stand at a angle between the sea and a fresh water I move myself towards he seven or eight step and clap my hand first on the side of my head then on my breast and after present my musket with a threaten countenance thereby to signify unto they either a choice of peace or war whereupon he use i with my own sign of peace I step forth and embrace he his company then all sit down in manner like greyhound upon their heel with who my company fall a barter by this time captain gosnoll be come with twelve alter himself our captain give he a straw hat and a pair of knife the hat awhiles he wear but the knife he behold with great marvel be very bright and sharp this our courtesy make they all in love chap. 12 a voyage set out from the city of Bristol at the charge of the chief merchant and inhabitant of the say city with a small ship and a bark for the discovery of the north part of Virginia in the year 1603. under the command of i MARTIN pringe upon many probable and reasonable inducement use unto sundry of the chief merchant of Bristol by master Richard hakluyt prebendary of saint Augustine the cathedral church of the say city after diverse meeting and due consultation they resolve to set forth a voyage for the far discovery of the north part of Uirginia and first they send the say master hakluyt accompany with one master John angel and master Robert Saltern which have be m. salterne yet live neither be his zeal dead to this action he be now a minister and have both by word and writing to i testify his affection to Virginia m. bring who voyage to the east indies be in the former tome in the say discovery the year before with captain Bar tholomew gosnold to obtain permission of sir Walter Raleigh which have a most ample patent of all those part from queen Elizabeth to intermeddle and deal in that action leave be obtain of he under his hand and seal they speedy prepare a small ship call the speedwell in burden about fifty ton man the same with some thirty man and boy wherein go for master and chief commander in the voyage one Martin bring a man very sufficient for his place and Edmund jones his mate and robert salterne above mention as their chief agent with a bark call the discoverer of six and twenty ton or thereabouts wherein go for master William Browne and Samuel kirkland his mate both good and skilful mariner be thirteen man and a boy in all in that bark the aforesaid ship and bark be plentiful victualy for eight month and furnish with slight merchandize think fit to trade with the people of the country as hat of diverse colour green blue and yellow apparel of coarse kersie and canvas ready make stocking and shoe saw pick-ax spade and shovel axe hatchet hook knife sizzer hammer nail chissel fishhook bell bead bugle looking-glass thimble pin needle thread and such like they set sail from kingrode the twenty day of March. we set sail from Milford haven where the wind have stay we a fortnight in which space April 10. 1603. we hear of queen Elizabeth death the ten of April 1603. in our course we pass by the isle of the acore have first sight of the pike and afterward of the island of Cueruo and flores and after we have run some five hundred league we fall with a multitude of small land on the north coast of Virginia in the latitude of 43. degree the (@) of june which land we find very pleasant to behold adorn with goodly grass and sundry sort of tree as cedar they discover many land good fish place Spruce pines and firre-tree here we find a excellent fish for cod which be better than those of Newfoundland and withal we see good and rocky ground fit to dry they upon also we see no reason to the contrary but that salt may be make in these part a matter of no small importance we sail to the south-west end of these land and there ride with our ship under one of the great one of they we name fox island because we find those kind fox island of beast thereon so pass through the rest with our boat to the main land which lie for a good space north-east and south-west we find very safe ride among they in six seven eight ten and twelve fathom at length come to the main in the latitude of 43. degree and a half we range the same to the south-west in which course we find four inlet the most easterly inlet which upon our search we find to pierce not far into the land the four and most westerly be the best which we row up ten or twelve mile in all these place we find no people but sign of fire and environ our house or barricado wherein be four of our man alone with their musket to keep sentinel who they seek to have come down unto they which they utter refuse and stand upon their guard our master likewise be very careful and circumspect have not pass two with he in the ship put the same in the best defence he can lest they shall have invade the same and cause a piece of great ordnance to be shoot off to give terror to the indian and warning to our man which be fast asleep in the wood at the noise of which piece they be a little awake and begin a little to call for fool and gallant their great and fearful mastiff and full quiet lay themselves down again but be quicken up eftsoon again with a second shoot they rouse up themselves betake they to their weapon and with their mastiff great fool with a half pike in his mouth draw down to their ship who when the indian behold afar off with the mastiff which they most fear in dissemble manner they turn all to a jest and sport and depart away in friendly manner yet not long after even the day before our departure they set fire on the wood where we wrought which we do behold to burn for a mile space and the very same day that we weigh anchor they come down to the shore in great number to wit very near two hundred by our estimation and some of they come in their boat to our ship and will have have we come in again but we send they back and will none of their entertainment about the eight or nine of August we leave this excellent haven at the entrance whereof we find twenty fathom water and ride at our ease in seven fathom be land-locked the haven wind in compass like the shell of a snail and it be in latitude of one and forty degree and five and twenty minute this by the way be not to be forget that our captain fall so much to the northward because he will find high ground where common the best haven be which also fall out to his expectation we also observe that we can find no sassafras but in sandy ground in our return we bring ourselves into the latitude of eight and thirty degree about the acore for certain cause and within five week space come from our port of Uirginia into the sound of England but there of the voyage make to Virginia in the Elizabeth of London a bark of fifty ton by captain Bartholomew Gilbert in the year 1603. write by master THOMAS CANNER a gentleman of Bernard inn his companion in the same voyage upon Wednesday in Easter week the seventeen of April after I have take my leave of some few of my love and dear friend in Bernard inn I ride towards Southampton there to be speak biscuit and some other provision for our bark wherein master Bartholomew Gilbert go as captain which have be in Virginia the year before with captain Bartholomew gosnold after our business be dispatch here we come into Plymouth from whence we put forth the ten of may. and the six and twenty of the same we be in the latitude of 32. degree hope to have have sight of the i will of madera whereof we miss in which course we meet with two or three english man of war the first of june we be in the latitude of 27. degree and hale over towards the land of the west indies and the fifteen of this month towards night we see Land master Gilbert and the master Henry suit dwell within the iron gate of the tower of London take it to be the bermuda be very near the shore they sound many time and have no ground at the last they find good ground in fourteen or fifteen fathom there we cast anchor in the morning we weigh and sound still as we trend by the shore but after we be past a cable length from our road we have no land again in forty or fifty fathom we keep still by the shore not yet be certain what island it be the sixteen in the morning we spy the people come from the shore who when they come near cry out for barter or trade when they come close aboard they make sign and cry out to see our colour which we present put forth in the main top and tell they we be Amigos and that be englishman their friend and brother assoon as they understand we be englishman they be bold to come near we throw they a rope and one come aboard we we trade with they for some tobacco pine-apple Piantanes pompion and such thing as they have we give they bugle knife whistle and such toy here we keep close by the shore when this Canoa have trade with we and utter all they have and drink of our beer be kind use they depart and then present after diverse canoas come we trade and use they as the first one of they tell we that island be Santa Lucia we bestow all that forenoon shake in the they trade a^ Santa Lucia wind for we have no ground to anchor near the shore to trade with they then we set our course for saint Vincent but find a current against we and the wind very scant we doubt we shall not fetch it and that if we do peradventure we may be put to the leeward of dominica and so consequent of Mevis or nieve for which island we be special bind for to out in the same therefore master Gilbert think good to let saint Vincent alone although in it be the best tobacco of all the land yet in the end he put roomer for dominica dominica whereof we have sight the seventeen of june and come close to the shore and present one Canoa come aboard as at Santa Lucia be send with two man belike to discover we and to see what entertainment they shall have we use they kind and so dismiss they there come more full of man with diverse of their commodity the nineteen in the morning be Sunday we anchor in a good road at Mevis and after go on shore to seek master Gilbert with the master and diverse of the company seek far into the wood but find none but one little tree and here and there where one have be cut so we be in doubt to find enough here to load our ship a just plague unto we for profane the sabbath in travel about our worldly business when there be no necessity this day in the evening some go out with the boat unto the shore and bring on board a tortoise so big that four man can not get she into the boat but tie she fast by one great tortoise leg unto the boat and so tow she to the ship when they have she by the ship it be no easy matter to get she on board the next day we go on shore again to search another part of the wood for and then God be thank we find enough this day at night we open our tortoise which have in she about 500 egg excellent sweet meat and so be all the whole fish upon Tuesday in the morning we go all on shore save the carpenter and Thomas and master gilbert man to fell wood and this day we fell good store all the rest of this month and three day more we continue here every day labour sore first in saw down the great tree and saw they again into log portable out of the thick wood to the sea-shoare so in the boat and so to the ship where m. Gilbert his pain profit double as well in example as in work for he be never idle but either search out more tree or fetch drink for the labourer or do one thing or other so that in this just fortnight that we stay here we have get on board some twenty tun within a few day after the tortoise be eat God send we another one of these fish be sufficient meat for twenty man for three or four day if it can be preserve but in that climate no salt can preserve it above two day hardly so long now the wood grow thin and hardly to be find on this island he think it best to stay no long here but to go for Uirginia to search for better store and so upon Sunday the three of july in the afternoon we weigh anchor and sail northwest and by north and that night pass by saint Christopher and another little island Monday the four in the morning we have sight of s. Christopher the island we go into the wood to search for but find none but one tree which he cut and go on board we fight also for fresh water but find none at evening go on abundance of tortoise shore into the bottom of the bay to dray the net and there we get good store of fine fresh fish and much more enough to have lade our boat we shall have get if at every draught we have not have in the net a tortoise which still through and so carry away the fish with they at one draught among the rest we have two in the net a young one and a old on the net hold the young one we weigh and go through between the two land into the main ocean towards our they book long desire country Uirginia distant three hundred and fifty league from we we sail north northwest the seven we run still northwest and north and by west the eight we keep the same course the nine we keep still the same course the wind begin to veer some thing to the southward which have be constant still from the land of the canary unto the land of the west indies and now begin the wind to draw towards the west and then be it as constant the western wind begin there the reason I defer to long consideration the current set out of the gulf of Mexico and from the main shore Sunday the ten we keep still the same course and have now but a small gale almost becalm the eleven we continue the same course with the same small gale we go north. Tuesday the twelve we keep the same course if any at all for for the most part we be becalm Wednesday the thirteen the calm continue the sun be extreme hot in the calm Thursday the fourteen the calm continue as hot as before these day we air our newland fish call poor John which prove ill do for after it be air it rot the soon poor John be burn in the same on Friday the fifteen God send we a reasonable gale the sixteen and seventeen the calm come again Monday we have a good gale and go north and by west and north northwest the nineteen twenty and one and twenty we have a excellent gale and run north northwest then we cast out the lead and look out for land but find no ground nor see no land and therefore we much doubt that the current have set we very far to the leeward of the place which we be bind for be the chesepian bay but that can not be know till it please God to bring we to land in the afternoon about six of the clock we cast out the lead again and have ground in thirty fathom whereof we be ground in 30. fathom glad and thank God know we can not be far from land Saturday the three and twenty in the morning about eight of the clock we see land in the height of 40. degree and odd minute very fine low land appear far off to be full of tall tree and a fine sandy shore but a great siege we see no harbour and therefore coast along to seek one to the northward the wind be at west Sunday the four and twenty the wind be about the north-east we beat hard to fetch a head-land where we think we see a harbour but when we come up with it we perceive a Headland it be none and all our labour lose and therefore the wind be now more full in our tooth at the north-east we consider it be better to put room so that if the wind shall stand than we shall fetch the bay of Chesepian which master Gilbert so much thirst after to seek out the people for sir Walter Raleigh leave near those part in the year 1587. if not perhaps we may find some road or harbour in the way to take in some fresh water for now we have none aboard on Monday the five and twenty of july at night we come near the mouth of the bay the mouth of the chesepian Bay but the wind blow so sore and the sea be so high that the master dare not put in that night into the sea and so continue next day on Wednesday the seven and twenty at night the wind come fair again and we bear again for it all night and the wind present turn again Thursday the eight and twenty consider our extremity for water and wood victual and beer likewise consume very fast we can no long beat for it and therefore run roomer determine for this time to seek it they depart eastward from the mouth of the chesepioc Bay a show of entrance of a river no more Friday the nine and twenty be not far from the shore which appear unto we exceed pleasant and full of goodly tree and with some show of the entrance of a river our captain Baxtholomew Gilbert accompany with master Thomas Canner a gentleman of Bernard inn Richard Harison the master mate Henry kenton our chirurgeon and one Derrick a Dutchman go on shore in the boat from the ship which lie above a mile from the land and with their weapon march up into the country leave two youth to keep the boat but short after the indian set upon they and one or two of they fall down wound in sight of captain Gilbert and four more slay by the indian our young man that keep the boat which have much a do to save themselves and it for some of the indian roam down to they will have hale it on shore which notwithstanding they save and with heavy heart get unto the ship with the loss of their captain and four of their principal man thus be but eleven man and boy in all in the ship though our want of water and wood be great yet we dare not adventure the loss of any more of our small company in this place therefore our master Henry suit take his course home for England by the i^es of the acore and fall first with the pike and afterward enter into our channel have first sight disposition of savage in the virginian masacre and other their deal find too true until by some remissness fit opportunity afford they certain ability to execute the same wherefore we humble give God there be two canoas and in either of they three savage of who two be below at the fire the other stay about the ship for victual and because we can by no mean entice they aboard we give they a can of pease and bread which they carry to the shore to eat but one of they bring back our can again present and stay aboard with the other two for he be young of a ready capacity and one we most desire to bring with we into England have receive exceed kind usage at our hand and therefore we catch five savage two canoas and bow arrow be much delight in our company we ship he and four other two canoas with all their bow and arrow which be the chief substance they possess Saturday the eight of june our captain be desirous to finish all business about this harbour very early in the morning with the pinnace coast five or six league about the land adjoin our captain sound about the land rock and mouth of the harbour and sound all along wheresoever he go he likewise diligent search and sound along before the mouth of the harbour about the rock which show themselves at all time and be a excellent breach of the water so as no sea can come in to offend the harbour this he do to instruct himself and thereby able to direct other that shall happen to come to this place for every where both near the rock and in all sound about the land we never find less water than four or five fathom which be very seldom but seven eight nine and ten fathom be the continual sound by the shore in some place much deep upon clay oaze or soft sand. this day about one a clock afternoon come from the eastward two canoas aboard we wherein be he that refuse to stay with we for a pawn and with he six other savage who two canoas come aboard we from the bashabe we have not see who have beautify themselves after their manner very gallant though their clothing be not different from the former yet they have new paint their face very deep some all black some red with stripe of blue over their upper lip nose and chin one of they wear a kind of coronet about his head make very cunning of a substance like stiff hair colour their ornament of gallantness red broad and more than a handful in depth which he so much esteem as he will not for any truck exchange the same other wear the white feather skin of some fowl round about their head jewel in their ear and bracelet of little white round bone fasten together upon a leather string these make not any show that they have notice of the other before take but we understand they by their speech and sign that they come send from the bashabe and that his desire be we will bring up our ship which they call a quiden to his house be as they point upon the main towards the east from whence they come and that he will exchange with we for fur and tobacco but because we have no desire to discover any further that way and now make what speed we can up the river we let they understand that if their bashabe will come to we he shall be very welcome but we will not remove to he Tuesday the eleven of june we pass up into the river with our ship about six and twenty mile of which be it not of necessity I must report somewhat I have much rather not to we go up into the river with our Ship write then by my relation to detract from the worthiness thereof not be sufficient in word to express the abundant utility and sweet pleasantness it yield for the river beside that it be subject hereafter by ship to bring in all traffic of merchandise the first and chief thing require for a plantation be a bold coast and fair land to fall with the next a safe harbour for ship to ride in the profit of the river saint George island the land fall the first be a special attribute to this Shore be most free from Sands or dangerous rock in a continual good depth with a most excellent landfall as can be desire which be the first island name saint George island for the second by judgement of our captain who know most of the coast of England and most of other country have be experience by implyment in discovery and travail from his childhood and by opinion of other of good judgement in our Ship here be more good harbour for ship of all burden than all England can river in the channel and sound about the land adjoin to the mouth thereof no better ride can be desire for a infinite number of ship the river itself as it run up into the main very nigh forty mile towards the great mountain bear in the breadth of the river for almost 40. mile breadth a mile sometime three quarter and half a mile be the narrow where you shall never have under four or five fathom water hard by the Shore but six seven eight nine and ten fathom at a low water and on both side every half mile very gallant Coves some able to contain almost a hundred sail where the ground be excellent soft oaze with a tough clay under the ground be oaze and clay for anchor hold and where ship may lie without either anchor or cable only moor to the Shore with a Hazur it flow by their judgement sixteen or eighteen foot at a high water what it flow dock to grave and carine ship here be make by nature most excellent place as docke to grave and carine ship of all burden secure from all wind which be such a necessary incomparable benefit that in few place in England or in any other part of Christendom art with great charge can make the like it yield plenty of salmon and other fish of great bigness and assure great probability salmon and store of fish of better thing therein to be find see about the land we have such certain hope of pearl and oar beside all these commodity innative to this river the border land be a the Land most rich neighbour trend all along on both side in a equal plain neither mountainous nor rocky but verge with a green bordure of grass do make tender unto the beholder of her pleasant fertility if by cleanse away the wood she be convert into meadow the wood it bear be no shrubbish fit only for fuel but good tall fir Spruce bird Beech the gentle wind up with our ship in this river any man may conceive with what admiration we all consent in joy many who have be traveller in sundry country and in the most famous river yet affirm they not comparable to this they now behold some that be with sir Walter Raleigh in his voyage to Guiana in the discovery of this river prefer before the river which eccoe fame to the world ear give reason why grande call Rio grande some before the river of Burduna Orleans and breast in France nance and the river of Rhone which although they be great and goodly river yet it be no detraction from they to be account inferior to this which not only yield all the aforesaid pleasant profit but also appear infallible to we free from all imagine inconvenience I will not prefer etc. it before our river of Thames because it be Natale England rich treasure but we all do wish those excellent harbour good deep in a continual convenient breadth and small tide gate to be as well therein for our country good as we find they here beyond our hope in certain for those to who it shall please God to grant this land for habitation which if it have with the other inseparable adherent commodity here to be find then I will bold affirm it to be the most rich beautiful large and secure harbour river that the world afford for if man shall wish or be invent a river subject to all conveniency and free from all danger here they may take a view in a platform frame by nature who in her perfection far exceed all art invention Wednesday the twelve of june our captain man his shallop with seventeen man and we march up into the land above three mile run up to the cod of the river where we land leave six to keep the shallop till our return ten of we with our shot and some arm with a boy to carry powder and match march up into the country towards the mountain which we descry at our first fall with the land and be continual in our view unto some of they the river bring we so near as we judge ourselves when we land to have be within a league of they but we find they not have march well nigh four mile up in the main and pass three great hill wherefore because the weather be parch hot and our man in their armour not able to travel far and return to our pinnace that night we resolve not to pass any further be all very weary of so tedious and laboursome a travel in this march we pass over very good ground pleasant and fertile fit for pasture have but little wood and that oak like stand leave in our pasture in England good and great fit good pasture timber for any use some small birch hazel and brake which may in small time be cleanse with few man and make good errable land but as it be now will feed cattle of all kind with fodder enough for summer and winter the soil be good bear sundry herb grass and strawberry in many place be low thicket like our copiss of small wood and it do all resemble a stately park wherein appear some old tree with high wither top and other flourish with live green bough till we come to the hill upon which do grow exceed tall straight and excellent great timber of sundry kind mast for ship of four hundred timber tree upon the hill ton and at the
