the root of ground we suppose wild hog have dear hare hog range there but we can descry no beast because our noise still chase they from we we be no soon come aboard our pinnace return towards our ship but we espy a Canoa come from the further part of the cod of the river eastward which haste to we wherein with two other be he who we account chief of his company and his come be very earnest importune to have one of our man to go lie with their bashabe or captain as they now term he who be there ashore as they sign and then the next a plot of the savage morning he will come to our ship with fur and tobacco this we perceive to be only a mere device to get possession of any of our man to ransom all those we have take which their natural policy can not so shadow but we do easy discover and prevent these mean be by this savage practise because we have one of his kinsman prisoner as we judge by his most kind usage of he be aboard we together Thursday the thirteen of june by two a clock in the morning because our captain will take the help and advantage of the tide in the pinnace with our company well provide and furnish with armour and shot both to defend and offend we go from our ship up to that we search the western part of the river we set up another crosse. we see no sign that ever Christian have be here before part of the river which trend west into the main to search that and we carry with we a cross to erect at that point which because it be not daylight we leave on shore until our return back when we set it up in manner as the former and this we diligent observe that in no place either about the land or up in the main or along the river we can discern any token or sign that ever any christian have be before which either by cut wood dig for water or set up cross a thing never omit by any christian travailour we shall have perceive some mention leave but to return to our river up into which we then row by estimation twenty mile what profit or pleasure be describe and true verify in the former part of the river be whole double in this for the breadth and depth be such that any ship draw seventeen or eighteen foot water may have pass as far as we go with our shallop and by all our judgement much further because we leave it in so good depth which be so much the more to be esteem of great worth by how much it trend further up into the main for from the place of our ship ride in the harbour at the entrance into the sound to the further point we be in this river by our estimation be not much less than threescore mile from each bank of this river be diverse branch stream run into the main whereby be afford a unspeakable conveniency of transportation profit by the conveniency of easy transportation from place to place which in some country be both very chargeable and not so fit by carriage on wane or horseback here we see store of fish some leap above water which we judge to be salmon for they be great all salmon and great plenty of fish along be a excellent mould of ground the wood in most place especial on the eastern side very thin chief oak and small birch border low upon the river all fit for meadow and pleasant pasture ground of Linschoten with certain occurrent and english act the isle of acore or the flemish land be seven that be Tercera saint Mary saint George Pico and Faiael there be yet two land call flores linscot c. 97. nine land w (...) call acore and Coruo which be not contain under the name of acore but yet at this day be under the government of the same land so that they be in all account nine land they be call acore that be to say sparhawk or hawk because that in their first discovery they find many sparhawk in they whereof they hold the name although at this day there be not any there to be find they be also call the flemish land that be of the netherlander because the first that inhabit the same be netherlander whereof till this time there be a great number and offspring remain that in manner and behaviour be altogether like netherlander and there be yet in the same island a run water that issue out of a hill and so run into the sea whereas yet those issue or offspring of netherlander inhabit and be call Arib^ra do that be the flemish river the principal island of they all be that of Tercera call insula de jesus of Tercera Tercera it be between fifteen or sixteen mile in compass and be altogether a great cliff of land whereby in it there be little room for it be as it be wall round about with cliff but where any strand or sand be there stand a fort. it have no haven nor entrance of water for the security and safety of the ship but only before the chief town call Angra Angra where it have a open haven which in form be like a halfmoon by the portugal call Angra whereof the town have her name it have on the one side in manner of a elbow stick forth two high hill call Bresyl which stretch into the sea so that afar off they seem to be divide from the island those hill be very high so that be upon they a man may see at the least ten or twelve and sometime fifteen mile into the sea be clear weather upon these hill there stand two small stone pillar where there be a sentinel place that continual watch to see what ship be at sea and so to advertise those of the island for that as many ship as he see come out of the west that be from the spanish indies or Brasilia cabo Verde Guinea and the Portugal indies and all other way lie south or west for every ship he set a flag upon the pillar in the west and when the ship which he describe be more than five than he set up a great ancient betoken a whole fleet of ship the like he do upon the other pillar which stand in the east for such ship as come from Portugal or other place out of the east or north part these pillar may be easy see in all place of the town by reason of the highness of the hill so that there be not one ship or sail that be at sea or make towards the island but it be present know throughout all the town and over all the whole island for the watch be not hold only upon those two hill jut into the sea but also upon all corner hill and cliff throughout the island and as soon as they perceive any ship the governor and ruler be present advertise thereof that they may take such order therein as need require upon the further corner into the sea stand a fort right against another fort that answer it so that those two fort do shut and defend the mouth or open haven of the town where the ship lie in the road and so no ship can either go in or come forth without the licence or permission of those two fort this town of Angra be not only the chief town of Tercera but also of all other town within the land thereabouts there in be resident the bishop the governor for the king and the chief place of judgement or tribunal seat of all the land of acore three mile from this town lie another town towards the north call Villa de praya for praya be as much to say as strand because it lie hard by a great strand and for that cause there be little traffic thither as not have any convenient place for ship to come at it yet sometime there come some one that by reason of contrary wind can get before the town of Angra and so by constraint discharge their good in that town which Angra descry from thence be carry by land to Angra and yet some part thereof be spend and use there it be wall and well house but not many people in it and such as be in it do get their live most by husbandry for there be very fair corn land the island be likewise very fruitful and pleasant it have much corn and wine but the wine be not very wine small good to carry into other country thereabouts because it be small and will not long continue so that it be use in the country by the common people but such as be of wealth for the most part drink wine of madera and canaria it abound in flesh fish and all other necessary commodity and meat for man body wherewith in time of need they may help themselves oil there be none but it come out of Portugal also salt pot pan and all kind of earthen vessel chalk and such like be bring thither out of other place for there they be not to be find for fruit they have beside peach of diverse kind and in so great abundance that be be strange cherry plum walnut haslenut chestnut but those not very good of apple pear orange and lemon with all such like fruit there be sufficient of all fruit sort of herb and plant as colewort radish and such like they have at their certain time of the year they have likewise in that island a certain fruit that grow under the earth like radish or other root but the leave or plant be tree like vine but different leaf and grow longwise upon the ground it bear a fruit call that be very good and be so great that it weigh a pound some more some less but little esteem and yet it be a great sustenance and food for the common sort of people it be of good account in Portugal for thither they use to bring it for a present and those of the island by reason of the great abundance do little esteem it there be also another kind of stuff that be sow like corn and be a fruit it grow upon the root of the grass or leaf and be round and as big as a great pease but not so round in eat it taste like earth-nut but hard to bite it be likewise a good meat and much esteem in other place but by reason of the great quantity thereof it be most use to fatten their hog and be call junssa there be also in the island a certain plant which be find in all place thereof in the open field it grow as high as a man and bear no fruit only the root thereof be a substance of the thickness of a root fit to be weave a man two fist and in show as if it be natural golden hair and in handle like soft silk which be use there to stuff and fill their bed in stead of wool and feather and I do certain believe if any man of understanding will take it in hand it will well be weave the princpal traffic of this island be their woad such as we use for die whereof woad much be make in that island and be fetch from thence by englishman scot and frenchman in barter for clothes and other ware who continual traffic into that island and although by reason of the war the englishman be forbid to traffic thither yet under the name of scot and frenchman they have continual trade there the island have not any wild beast or fowl but very few save only canary bird which be there by thousand canary bird where many birder take they and thereof make a daily live by carry they into diverse place it have also wonderful many quail which they call codornisen of tame fowl as hen and gynnie hen be there likewise great store hunt be there little use but only for coney which be very great hare heart partridge venison and such like be not there to be find because of the little respect and care the inhabitant have to breed any such thing fish be very plentiful and of diverse kind and very good in summer there be great store take for in winter they can hardly brook the sea the chief month of winter winter weather for rain and storm be januarie February March and April and also the month of September be common very stormy all the other month it be common good weather the country be very hilly and in some place woody full of bush and tree it be hard to travel because their way for the most part be stony so that for a mile or a mile and a half together man can see no ground but only stone which for sharpness and fashion show like stone point diamond whereby one can hardly tread upon it lest it shall cut through both shoe and foot and yet it be all plant with vine so full and thick that in summer time you can hardly see through it for that the root thereof do grow between the stone so that a man will think it impossible that any thing shall grow therein and which be more in some place it seem impossible for a man to tread upon it be so wild and desert as it show and nothing but hard stone and rock on good ground their vine will not grow but only in the wild and stony place and for that cause they be much esteem the good ground and plain field which in some place be very many especial by villa da praya be sow with corn and woad and they have so much corn that they need not bring any from other place although that beside their inhabitant and natural bear islander they have continual with they fourteen company of spaniard which be all feed and nourish by the corn that grow in the country unless there chance to come a hard and unfruitful year as oftentimes it do for than they be force to help themselves with foreign corn and that especial because of the soldier that lie in the island and yet it be strange that the corn and all other thing in the island continue not above one year and that which be keep above a year be naught and nothing worth and therefore corn will last but a year to keep their corn long than a year they be force to bury it in the earth for the space of four or five month together to the which end every townsman have his pit at one end of the town in the common highway which be appoint for the purpose and every man set his mark upon his pit-stone the corn be but light bury in the earth the hole corn bury within be round and the top thereof so wide that a man may creep in whereunto there be a stone purposely make to cover it which shut it up very close some of the pit be so great as that they may hold two or three last of corn some great and some small as every man have his provision and as soon as the corn be reap and fan which be in july every man put his corn into those pit lay straw under and round about it and then they fill it full or but half full according as their quantity be and so stop it up with the stone which they cover with earth and so let it stand until Christmas when every man that will fetch home his corn some let it lie long and fetch it by little and little as they use it but the corn be as good when they take it out as it be at the first hour that they put it in and although that cart horse and man do common pass over it and also that the rain rain upon it yet there enter not any drop of rain or moisture into it and if the corn be not bury in that manner it will not continue good above four month together but will be spoil and when it have be thus for a long time bury in the earth it will continue the whole year through and then they keep it in chist or make a thing of mat like a coop to preserve it in not once stir or move it and so it continue very good the great commodity they have in the land and that serve their turn best be their ox and I believe they be the great and fair that be to be find in all Christendom g (...) o (...) with unmeasurable great and long horn every ox have his several name like man and although there be a thousand of they in a hear and that one of they be call by his name he present come forth unto his master that call he the land be very high and as it call by their name seem hollow for that as they pass over a hill of stone the ground sound under they as if it be a seller so that it seem in diverse place to have hole under the earth whereby it be much subject to earthquake as also all the other land be for there it be a common thing and all those land for the most part have have i of brimstone for that in many place of Tercera brimstone and saint Michael the smoke and savour of brimstone do still issue forth of the ground and the country round about be all singe and burn also there be place wherein there be hot spring fountain and well the water whereof be so hot that it will boil a egg as well as if it hang over a fire in the island of Tercera about three mile from Angra there be a fountain in a place call Gualua which have a property that all the wood which fall into it by length of time spring (...)ing wood into stone convert into stone as I myself by experience have try in the same fountain by the root of a tree whereof the one half run under that water and be turn into as hard stone as if it be steel and the other part of the root which the water touch not be still wood and root as it shall be the island have great store and excellent kind of wood special cedar tree which grow there in so great number that they make scute cart and cedar common other gross work thereof and be the common wood that they use to burn in those country whereby it be the wood that with they be least esteem by reason of the great quantity thereof there be another kind of wood call Sanguinho and be very fair of a red colour and Sanguinbo wood white and yellow wood another sort that they call white wood be of itself as white as chalk other that be perfect yellow and all natural without any die and therefore there be diverse good workman in Tercera that be skilful in joiners occupation and make many fine piece of work as desk cupboard chist and other such like thing whereof many be carry into Portugal and much esteem there as well for the beauty of the wood as for the workmanship and special the spanish fleet which ordinary refresh themselves in that island do carry much of it from thence for it be the best and fine that be make in all Spain and Portugal although it be not comparable to the desk and fine workmanship of Nurembergh and those countreve but for wood it excel all other country for that they have in the spanish fleet beside their own kind of wood at the least a thousand sort of wood of all colour that man can imagine or devise and so fair that more fair can not be paint there be a certain kind of wood in the island Pico situate and lie twelve mile from Tercera call Teixo a most excellent and princely wood and therefore it be forbid to be a kind of wood as hard as iron cut but only for the king own use or for his officer the wood be as hard as iron and have a colour within as if it be wrought like red Chamlet with the same water and the old it be and the more use the fair it be of colour so that it be worthy to be esteem as in truth it be all those land be inhabit by portugal but since the trouble in Portugal there have inhabitant be diverse spanish soldier send thither and a spanish governor that keep all the fort and castle in their possession although the portugal be put to no charge nor yet hardly use by they but be rather keep short so that not one soldier dare go out of the town with soldier out licence and therefore man may quiet travel throughout the island both day and night without any trouble likewise they will not suffer any stranger to travel to see the country and this order be not bring up by the spaniard but by the portugal themselves stranger before their trouble for they will never permit it and which be more all stranger that come thither be usual appoint a certain street wherein they shall sell their ware and may not go out of that street now it be not so straight look unto but they may go in all place of the town and within the island but not about it to view the coast which notwithstanding be grant unto we by the governor himself who lend we his horse to ride about and give we leave to see all the fort which at this time be not permit to the natural bear islander neither be they so much credit we ride twice about the island which he grant we leave to do by mean of certain particular friendship we have with he neither can the portugal hinder we therein because we be in the king service as factor for the king pepper and for that they account we as natural bear portugal for the governor will willing have have i to have draw a plot of the whole island that he may have send it to the king wherein I excuse myself yet I make he the town with the haven come in and fort of Angra which he send unto the king the like whereof you may in this book behold for the which the governor be great affect unto i and show i much friendship we have in our lodging a french merchant and a scot that willing will have go with we to see the island but can not be suffer for the portugal think that they will take the proportion thereof and so seek to defeat they of their right but return to our matter the land be very good and wholesome air and the disease that be most common in those country though not very plentiful but only here and there one be one sickness call o be that be a kind of bad air that take they and make they altogether lame or half lame of their limb or of some one limb and another sickness the air a disease that be call o Sange that be a certain blood that hasty come upon a man as a swell in the eye or other place of the face or of the body and be as red as blood for as they say it be nothing else but mere blood these be two disease like the plague and be common sickness in those country which grow by reason of the great windiness of the land that be subject to all storm and foul weather and be unreasonable mor which be one of the principal cause of these disease for the wind be there so strong and dangerous that they strong wind consume both the iron and the steel of their house and bring they into powder for I have see iron grate in the king custom house as thick as a man arm and the window of hard free stone which be so consume by the wind that the iron in some place be become as thin as a straw and the stone in like sort and therefore in those country they use to make their roof and painthou^es of stone which they dig in the water out of sand upon the sea coast of those land whereon the wind have not so great a power to consume it and yet that customehouse have not be make above six or seven year before at the most in this island beside the two town there be diverse great village as saint Sebastian saint Barboran altar Gualua Villa with many other parish and hamlet so that for the most part it be build and inhabit save only the place that be wild and full of wood which can hardly be travel much less inhabit their most traffic be as I say before the wood that grow in those country I mean for such as deal in merchandise and the workman that make it but the rest wait for the fleet that come and go to and from the spanish and Portugal indies from Brasilia cabo Verde and Guinea all which country do common come unto Tercera to refresh themselves as lie very fit for that purpose so that all the inhabitant do thereby rich maintain themselves and sell all their ware as well handy work as victual unto those ship and all the land round about do as then come unto Tercera with their ware to sell it there for the which cause the englishman and other stranger keep continual about those land be assure that all ship for want of refresh must of force put into those land although at this time many ship do avoid those land to the great discommodity of the land and the ship from Tercera southeast about seven and twenty or eight and twenty mile lie the island of saint Michael which be about twenty mile long and be likewise full of town and village s. Michael inhabit by portugal for air and all other thing like unto Tercera the chief town be call Gada where there be great traffic of english scot and frenchman only as in Tercera because of the woad which be more abundant in that island then in all the rest of they for that every year there be make above two hundred thousand quintal of wood it have likewise great abundance of corn so that they help to victual all the land that be round about they it have neither haven nor river but only the broad sea and have less safeguard and defence than those which be of Tercera but there they lie not under the commandment of any fort so that many set sail with all the wind and put to sea which in the road of Tercera they may not do and therefore the stranger ship have rather sail to saint michael for there they can not be constrain to do any thing but what they will themselves to do there be also a company of spaniard in a castle that stand by the town of Gada which be make by the spaniard for the defence and maintenance of the same town from the island of saint michael southwards twelve mile lie the island Maria saint Mary which be about ten or twelve mile compass and have no traffic but only of pot earth which the other land fetch from thence it have no woad but be full of all victual like Tercera and inhabit by the portugal there be no spaniard in it because it be a stony country like Tercera and hard to board whereby the inhabitant themselves be sufficient and able enough to defend it while I remain in Tercera the earl of Cumberland come thither to take in fresh water and some other victual but the inhabitant will not suffer he to have it but wound both himself and diverse of his man whereby they be force to depart without have any thing there from Tercera north northwest about seven or eight mile lie a little island call and be but five or six mile in compass a very pleasant and fine island full of all fruit and all other victual so that it not only feed itself but also Tercera and the other land about it and have no other kind of merchandise it be well build and inhabit by portugal and have no soldier in it because it be not able to bear the charge the earl of Cumberland while I lay in Tercera come unto that island where himself in person with seven or eight in his company earl of Cumberland s^^ sup. l. 6. c. 1. go on land ask certain beast hen and other victual with wine and fresh water which they willing give he and therewith he depart from thence without do they any hurt for the which the inhabitant thank he and commend he for his courtesy and keep of his promise from Tercera west northwest eight or nine mile lie the island of saint George it be about twelve mile long but not above two or three mile at the further in breadth it be woody saint George and full of hill it have no special traffic but only some woad and yet very little of it the inhabitant live most by cattle and till of the land and bring much victual to sell in Tercera it have likewise many cedar tree and other kind of wood that from thence be bring unto Tercera and sell unto the joiner which for that occasion dwell only in Tercera from saint George west south-west seven mile lie the island call Fayael which be seventeen or eighteen mile in compass it be one of the best island next unto Tercera and saint Fayael michael it abound in all sort of victual both flesh and fish so that from this island the most part of victual and necessary come by whole carvel unto Tercera it have likewise much woad so that many english ship do traffic thither the principal road and place be the town call there the ship likewise do lie in the open sea under the land as they do before all the other land by this town there lie a fortress but of small importance and because the inhabitant of themselves do offer to defend the island against all enemy the soldier discharge from thence which before that time lie in the fort complain that they be not able to maintain nor lodge they the same time that the earl of Cumberland be in the island of he come likewise to Fayael where at the first time that he come they begin to resist he but by reason of some controversy among they they let he Fayael take take by earl Cumberland land where he raze the castle to the ground and sink all their ordnance in the sea take with he certain carvel and ship that lay in the road with provision of all thing that he want and therewith depart again to Sea whereupon the king cause the principal actor therein to be punish and send a company of soldier thither again which go out of Tercera with all kind of warlike munition and great shot make the fortress up again the better to defend the island trust no more in the portugal in that island be the most part of the netherlander offspring yet they use the portugal language by reason they have be so long conversant among they and those that use the dutch tongue be all dead they be great affect to the netherlander and stranger from Fayael southeast three mile and from saint George south-west four mile and from Tercera south-west and by west twelve mile lie the island call Pico which be more than fifteen mile in length it be so name of a high mountain that stand therein call Pico Pico which be so high that some think it be high than the Pico of canaria when it be clear weather high Hill it may as perfect be see in Tercera as if it be not half a mile from thence and yet it lie above twenty five mile from it for it be at the further end of the island towards Fayael the top of it be see clear and bright but the nether part be cover with cloud and with the horizon whereby the island be much speak of it be very fruitful of all kind of victual like Fayael and have great store of wood as cedar and all other kind and also the costly wood Teixo there they build many carvel and small ship and from thence by reason of the abundance of wood they serve the other land with wood it be also inhabit as the rest be their chief traffic be cattle and husbandry it have much wine and the best in all those land and it have the savore and pleasant orange that be throughout all Portugal so that they be bring into the second of October 1589. at the town of Villa da^ praya in the island of Tercera two man be in a field hard without the town be kill with lightning the nine of c. 99 the same month there arrive in Tercera 14. ship that come from the spanish indies lade with cochenile hides gold silver pearl and other rich ware they be fifty in company when they depart out of the island of havana whereof in their come out of the channel eleven sink in the same channel by foul weather the rest by a storm be scatter and separate one from the other the next day there come another ship of the same company that sail close under the island so to get into the road where she meet with a english ship that have not above three cast piece and the Spaniard twelve they seek a long time together which we be in the island may stand and behold whereupon the governor of Tercera send two boat of musketeer to help the ship but before they can come at she the english ship have shoot she under water and we see she sink into the sea with all her sail up and not any thing see of she about the water the englishman with their boat save the captain and about thirty other with he but not one penny worth of the good and yet in the ship there be at the least to the value of 200000. ducat in gold silver and pearl the rest of the man be drown which may be about 50. person among the which be some friar and woman which the englishman will not save those that they have save they set on land and then they sail away the 27. of the same month the say 14. ship have refresh themselves in the island depart from Tercera towards sivil and come upon the coast of Spain they be take by the english ship that lie there to watch for they two only except which escape away and the rest be whole carry into England about the same time the earl of Cumberland with one of the queen ship and five or six more keep about those land and come oftentimes so close under the island and to the road of Angra that the people on land may easy tell all his man that he have aboard and know such as walk on the hatch they of the island not once shoot at they although they may easy have do it for they be within musket shoot both of the town and fort. in these place he continue for the space of two month and sail round about the land and land in and Fayael as in the description of those land I have already declare here he good luck of the spaniard and hard fortune of the englishman for that within less than two day after the gold and silver be lade again into the spanish ship the earl of Cumberland sail again by that island so that it appear that God will not let they have it for if they have once have fight thereof without doubt it have be they as the spaniard themselves confess in the month of November there as it well appear by this brief discourse in the month of march 1590. there be a blaze star with a tail see in Tercera that continue four night together stretch the tail towards the south (@) in the the seven of August a navy of english ship be see before Tercera be twenty in sir m. Frobisher number and five of they the queen ship their general be one Martin Frobisher as we after have intelligence they come purposely to watch for the fleet of the spanish indies and for the indian ship and the ship of the country in the west which put the islander in great fear special those of Fayael for that the englishman send a trumpet to the governor to ask certain wine flesh and other victual for their money and good friendship they of Fayael do not only refuse to give ear unto they but with a shot kill their messenger or trumpeter which the englishman take in evil part send they word that they be best to look to themselves and stand upon their guard for they mean to come and visit they whether they will or no. the governor make they answer that he be there in the behalf of his majesty of Spain and that he will do his best to keep they out as he be bind but no thing be do although they of Fayael be in no little fear send to Tercera for aid from whence they have certain bark with powder and munition for war with some biscuit and other necessary provision the thirty of August we receive very certain news out of Portugal that there be eighty ship put out of the Carunho lade with victual munition money and soldier to go for Britain to aid the catholic and leaguer of France against the king of Navarre at the same time two netherlands hulk come out of Portugal to queen ship have eighty piece of ordnance and that captain Drake lie with forty ship in the english channel watch for the army of Carunho and likewise that there lie at the cape saint Vincent ten other all that year till the next year because of the great danger they may fall into by the englishman which be no small charge and hindrance to the fleet for that the ship that lie there do consume themselves and in a manner eat up one another by reason of the great number of people together with the scarcity of all thing so that many ship choose rather one by one to adventure themselves alone to get home then to stay there all which fall into the englishman hand whereof diverse of the man be bring into Tercera for that a whole day we can see nothing else but spoil man set on shore some out note of one ship some out of another that pity it be to see all of they curse the englishman and their own fortune with those that have be the cause to provoke the englishman to fight and complain of this ship there die by the 280. man die in one ship in one voyage by one man vanity way two hundred and eighty man according to a note by himself make and send to the cardinal at Lisbon with the name either to lose his life or to arrive in India as indeed he do afterward but to the great danger loss and hindrance of his company that be force to buy it with their life and only for want of provision as it may well be think for he know full well that if he have return back again into Portugal as the other ship do he shall have be cashier from his indian regiment because the people begin already to murmurre at he for his proud and lofty mind and among other thing that show his pride the more behind above the gallery of his ship he cause fortune to be paint and his own picture with a staff stand the say Mathias de Alberkerk in India be a soldier and a captain where he be esteem and account for one of the best of they and much honour and belove of all man as behave himself courteous to every man whereby they all desire that he may be viceroy but when he once have receive his patent with full power and authority from the king to be viceroy he change so much from his former behaviour that by reason of his pride they all begin to fear and curse he and that before he depart out of Lisbon as it be often see in many man that be advance unto state and dignity the twenty of january 1591. ship that shall have go to India and because the ship be come back again that ship be stuff and lade as full of good as possible it may be have likewise in ready money five hundred thousand ducat in 170000. ducat all these ship be carry into England and make good prize in the month of july an. 1591. there happen a earthquake in the island of s. Michael which continue from the six and twenty of july to the twelve of August in which time earthquake most terrible no man dare stay within his house but flee into the field fast and pray with great sorrow for that many of their house fall down and a town call villa Franca be almost clean raze to the ground all the cloister and house shake to the earth and therein some people slay the land in some place rise up and the cliff remove from on place to another and some hill be deface and make even with the ground the earthquake be so strong prodigy that the ship which lay in the road and on the sea shake as if the world will ha^e turn round there spring also a fountain out of the earth from whence for the space of four day there flow a most clear water and after that it cease at the same time they hear such thunder and noise under the earth as if all the devil in hell have be assemble together in that place wherewith many die for fear the island of Tercera shake four time together so that it seem to turn about but there happen no misfortune unto it earthquake be common in those land for about twenty year pass there happen another earthquake where in a high hill that lie by the same town of Villa Franca fall half down and cover all the town with earth and kill many man the five and twenty of August the king armada come out of farol arrive in Tercera be in all thirty ship greenfield himself be wound in his brain whereof afterward he die he be bear into the s^ip call the saint Paul wherein be the admiral of the fleet don Alonso de Barsan there his wound be dress by the spanish surgeon but don Alonso himself will neither see he nor speak with he all the rest of the captain and gentleman go to visit he and to comfort he in his hard fortune wonder at his courage and stout heart for that he show not any sign of faintness nor change of colour but feel the hour of death to approach he speak these word in spanish and say here die I Richard greenfield with a joyful and quiet mind for that I have end my life as a true soldier ought to do that have fight for his country queen religion and honour whereby my soul most joyful depart out of this body and shall always leave behind it a everlasting fame of a valiant and true soldier that have do his duty as he be bind to do when he have finish these or such other like word he give up the ghost with great and stout courage and no man can perceive any true sign of heaviness in he this sir Richard greenfield be a great and a rich gentleman in England and have great yearly revenue of his own inheritance but he be a man very unquiet in his mind and great affect to war in so much as of his own private motion he offer his service to the queen he have perform many valiant act and be great fear in these land and know of every man but of nature very severe so that his own people hate he for his fierceness and speak very hardly of he for when they first enter into the fleet or armado they have their great sail in a readiness and may possible enough have sail away for it be one of the best ship for sail in England and the master perceive that the other ship have leave they and follow not after command the great sail to be cut that they may make away but sir Richard greenfield threaten both he and all the rest that be in the ship that if any man lay hand upon it he will cause he to be hang and so by that occasion they be compel to fight and in the end be take he be of so hard a complexion that as he continue among the spanish captain while they be at dinner or supper with he he will carouse three or four glass of wine and in a bravery take the glass between his tooth and crash they in piece and swallow they down so that often time the blood run out of his mouth without any harm at all unto he and this be tell i by diverse credible person that many time stand and behold he the englishman that be leave in the ship as the captain of the soldier the master and other be disperse into diverse of the spanish ship that have take they where there have almost a new fight arise between the Biscayne and the portugal while each of they will have the honour to have first board she so that there grow a great noise and quarrel among they one take the chief ancient and the other the flag and the captain and every one hold his own the ship that have board she be altogether out of order and break and many of their man hurt whereby they be compel to come into the island of Tercera there to repair themselves where be arrive I and my chamber-fellow to hear some news go aboard one of the ship be a Tercera in good company there sudden rise so hard and cruel a storm that those of the great storm island do affirm that in man memory there be never any such see or hear of before for it seem the sea will have swallow up the land the water mount high than the cliff which be so high that it amass a man to behold they but the sea reach above they and live fish be throw upon the land this storm continue not only a day or two with one wind but seven or eight day continual the wind turn round about in all place of the compass at the least twice or thrice during that time and all alike with a continual storm and tempest most terrible to behold even to we that be on shore much more great hurt than to such as be at sea so that only on the coast and cliff of the island of Tercera there be above twelve ship cast away and not only upon the one side but round about it in every corner whereby nothing else be hear but complain cry lament and tell here be a ship break in piece against the cliff and there another and all the man drown so that for the space of twenty day after the storm they do nothing else but fish for dead man that revenge revenge with the loss of above 100 other ship of the spaniard attend her fate as great a blow as 88 continual come dride on the shore among the rest be the english ship call the revenge that be cast away upon a cliff near to the island of Tercera alive and have his body and head all wound and he be on shore bring we the news desire to be shrive and thereupon present die the revenge have in her diverse fair brass piece that be all sink in the sea which they of the island be in good hope to weigh up again the next summer follow among these ship that be cast away about Tercera be likewise a flyboat one of those that have be arrest in Portugal to serve the king call the white dove the master of she be one Cornelius Martenson of Schiedam in Holland and there be in she one hundred soldier as in every one of the rest there be he be over rule by the captain that he can not be master of his own sail here and there at the mercy of God as the storm drive he in the end come within the sight of Tercera which the spaniard perceive think all their safety only to consist in put into the road compel the master and the pilot to make towards the island although the master refuse to do it say that they be most sure there to be cast away and utter spoil but the captain call he drunkard and heretic and strike he with a staff command he to do as he will have he the master see this and be compel to do it say well than my master see it be the desire of you all to be cast away I can but loose one life and therewith desperate he sail towards the shore and be on that side of the island where there be nothing else but hard stone and rock as high as mountain most terrible to behold where some of the inhabitant stand with long rope and cork bind at the end thereof to throw they down unto the man that they may lay hold upon they and save their life but few of they get so near most of they be cast away and smite in piece before they can get to the wall the ship sail in this manner as I say before towards the island and approach to the shore the master be a old man and full of year call his son that be in the ship with he and have embrace one another and take their last farewell the good old father will his son not to take care for he but seek to save himself for say he son thou be young and may have some hope to save thy life but as for i it be no great matter I be old what become of i and therewith each of these shed many tear as every love father and kind child may well consider the ship fall upon the cliff and brake in piece the father on the one side the son on the other side fall into the sea each lay hold upon that which come next to hand but to no purpose for the sea be so high and furious that they be all drown and only fourteen or fifteen save themselves by swim with their leg and arm half break and out of joint among the which be the master son and four other dutch boy the rest of the spaniard and sailor with the captain and master be drown who heart will not melt with tear to behold so grievous a sight special consider with himself that the great cause thereof be the beastliness and insolency of the spaniard as in this only example may well be see whereby may be consider how the other ship speed as we ourselves do in part behold and by the man that be save do hear more at large as also some other of our countryman that as then be in the like danger can well witness on the other land the loss be no less than in Tercera for on the island of saint George there be two ship cast away on the island of Pico two ship on the island of three ship and beside those there come everywhere round upon the spaniard because they only maintain the so then the gate of hell prevail against their faith catholic and romish religion such and the like blasphemy against God they cease not open to utter without that any man reprove they therein nor for their false opinion but the most part of they rather say and affirm that of truth it must needs be so as one of those indian fleet put out of there be etc. and all send into England whereby it plain appear that in the end God will assure plague the spaniard have already blind they so that they have not the sense to perceive it but still to remain in their obstinate opinion but it be lose labour to strive against God and to trust in man as be foundation erect upon the sand which with the wind be blow down and overthrow as we daily see before our eye and now not long since in many place have evident observe and therefore let every man but look into his own action and take our low-countries for a example wherein we can but blame our own sin and wickedness which do so blind we that we whole forget and reject the benefit of God continue the servant and yoke-slave of Satan God of his mercy open our eye and heart that we may know our only health JAMES by the grace of God etc. whereas our love and well dispose subject sir Thomas gate sir George Summers knight Richard hakluyt clerk prebendary of Westminster edward maria Wingfield Thomas Hannam Raleigh Gilbert esquire William Parker George popham and di^ers other of our love subject have be humble suitor unto we that we will vouch safe unto they our licence to make habitation plantation and to deduce a colony of sundry of our people into that part of America common call Virginia and other part and territory in America either appertain unto we or which now be not actual possess by any christian prince or people situate lie and be all along the sea coast between thirty four degree of northerly latitude from the equinoctial line and forty five degree of the same latitude and in the main land between the same thirty four and forty five degree and the land thereunto adjacent within one hundred mile of the coast thereof and to that end and for the more speedy accomplishment of the say intend plantation and habitation there be desirous to divide themselves into two several colony and company the one consist of certain knight gentleman merchant and other adventurer of our city of London and elsewhere which be and from time to time shall be join unto they which do desire to begin their plantation and habitation in some fit and convenient place between thirty four and forty one degree of the say latitude all alongst the sea coast of Virginia and coast of America aforesaid and the other consist of sundry knight gentleman merchant and other adventurer of our city of Bristol and Exeter and of our town of Plymmouth and other place which do join themselves unto that colony which desire to begin their plantation and habitation in some fit and convenient place between thirty eight and forty five degree of the say latitude all alongst the say coast of Virginia and America as that coast lie we great commend and gracious accept of their desire to the furtherance of so noble a work which may by the providence of almighty God hereafter tend to the glory of his divine majesty in propagate of Christian religion to such people as yet live in darkness miserable ignorance of the true knowledge and worship of God and may in time bring the infidel and savage live in those part to humane civility and to a settle and quiet government do by these our letter patent gracious accept of and agree to their humble and well intend desire and do therefore for we our heir and successor grant and agree that the say sir Thomas gate sir George Summer Richard hakluyt and Edward Maria Wingfield adventurer of our city of London and all such other as be or shall the first colony to be plant betwixt 34. and 41. degree of north latitude they to have all the land etc. for the space of fifty mile west south-west from the place of their first plant and all mine etc the like east north-east with all land for 100 mile in the sea over against they 100 (...) hin the land etc. none to inhabit on the backside without their special licence in writing etc. be join unto they of that colony shall be call the first colony and they shall and may begin their say first plantation and seat of their first abode and habitation at any place upon the say coast of Virginia or America where they shall think fit and convenient between the say thirty four and forty one degree of the say latitude and that they shall have all the land wood soil ground haven port river mynes mineral marsh water fish commodity and hereditament whatsoever from the say first seat of their plantation and habitation by the space of fifty mile of english statute measure all alongst the say coast of Virginia and America towards the west and south-west as the coast lie withal the land within one hundred mile direct over against the same sea coast and also all the land soil ground haven port river mynes mineral wood marsh water fish commodity and hereditament whatsoever from the say place of their first plantation and habitation for the space of fifty like english mile all alongst the say coast of Virginia and America towards the east and north-east as the coast lie together with all the land within one hundred mile direct over against the same sea-coast and also all the land wood soil ground haven port river mynes mineral marsh water fish commodity and hereditament whatsoever from the same fifty mile every way on the sea coast direct into the main land by the space of one hundred like english mile and shall and may inhabit and remain there and shall and may also build and fortify within any the same for their better safeguard and defence according to their best discretion and the direction of the council of that colony and that no other of our subject shall be permit or suffer to plant or inhabit behind or on the backside of they towards the main land without the express licence or consent of the council of that colony thereunto in write first have or obtain and we do likewise for we our heir and successor by these present grant and agree that the say Thomas hanham Raleigh Gilbert William Parker and George popham and all other of the town of Plymouth in the Virginia by the english 1606. write by that honourable gentleman master george percy on Saturday the twenty of December in the year 1606. the fleet fall from London and the five of january we anchor in the down but the wind continue contrary so long that we be force to stay there some time where we suffer great storm but by the skilfulness of the captain we suffer no great loss or danger the many excellent vegetable and live creature yet grass there be little why there be little grass or none but what grow in low marsh for all the country be overgrow with tree who droppings continual turn their grass to weed by reason of the rankness of the ground which will soon be amend by good husbandry the wood that be most common be oak and walnut many of their oak be so tall and straight that they will bear two foot wood with their fruit and a half square of good timber for twenty yard long of this wood there be two or three several kind the acorn of one kind who bark be more white than the other be somewhat sweetish which be boil half a day in several water at last afford a sweet oil which they keep in goard to anoint their head and joint the fruit they eat make in bread or otherwise there be also some elm some black wal-nut tree and some ash of ash and elm elm they make soap-ash if the tree be very great the ash will be good and melt to hard lump but if they be small it will be but powder and not so good as the other of walnut there be two walnut suppose cypress or three kind there be a kind of wood we call cypress because both the wood the fruit and leaf do most some part of the country they be find grow natural in pretty grove there be a assay make to make silk and sure the worm prosper mulberry excellent well till the master workman fall sick during which time they be eat with rat in some part be find some chestnut who wild fruit equalise the best in France Spain chestnut Germany or Italy to their taste that have taste they all plum there be of three sort the red and white be like our hedg^ plum but the other which they call putchamin grow plum as high as Palmeta the fruit be like a meddler it be first green then yellow and red when it be ripe if it be not ripe it will draw a man mouth awry with much torment but when it be ripe it be as delicious as a apricock they have cherry and those be much like a damson but for their taste and colour we they break they between two stone yet some part of the walnut shell will cleave to the fruit then do they dry they again upon a Mat over a hurdle after they put it in a mortar of wood and beat it very the country be natural overgrow with wood to prepare the ground they bruise the bark of the tree near the root how they prepare the ground then do they scorch the root with fire that they grow no more the next year with a crooked piece of wood they beat up the wood by the root and in those mould they plant their corne. their manner be this they make a hole in the earth with a stick and into it they put four grain of wheat and two of beanes these hole they make four foot one from another their woman and child do continual keep it with weed and when it be grow middle high they hill it about like a hop-yard in April they begin to plant but their chief plantation be in May and so they continue till the midst of june what they plant in April they reap in August for May in September for june how they plant in October every stalk of their corn common bear two ear some three seldom any four many but one and some none every ear ordinary have betwixt two hundred and five hundred grain the stalk be green have a sweet juice in it somewhat like a sugar cane which be the cause that when they gather their corn green they suck the stalk for as we gather green pease so do they their corn be green which excel their old they plant also pease which they call ass (...) which be the same they call in Italy their bean be the same the turk call gar (...) s but these they much esteem for dainty their corn they roast in the ear gr^ene and bruise it in a mortar of wood with a polt lap how they use their corne. it in roll in the leaf of their corn and so boil it for a dainty they also reserve the corn late plant that will not ripe by roast it in hot ash the heat thereof dry it in winter they esteem it be boil with beanes for a rare dish they call Paus (...) their old wheat they first steep a night in hot water in the morning pound it in a mortar they use a small basket for their thames than pound again the great and so separate by dash their hand in the basket receive the flower in a platter make of wood scrape to that form with burn and shell temper this flower in water they make it either in cake cover with ash till they be bake and then wash they in fair water they dry present with their own heat or else boil they in water eat the broth with the bread which they call po^ap the grout and piece of the corn remain by fan in a platter or in the wind away the bran they boil three or four hour with water which be a ordinary food they call vstataham^n but some more thrifty than clean do burn the core of the ear to powder which they call pungnough mingle that in their meal but it never taste well in bread nor broth there fish and flesh they boil either very tender or bro^le it so long on hurdle over the fire or else after how they use their fish and flesh the spanish fashion put it on a spit they turn first the one side than the other till it be as dry as their jerkin beef in the west indies that they may keep it a month or more without putrify the broth of fish or flesh they eat as common as the meat in May also among their corn they plant pumpeon and a fruit like unto a muake millen plant fruit but less and worse which they call macock these increase exceed and ripen in the begin of july and continue until September they plant also maracock a wild fruit like a lemon which also increase infinite they begin to ripe in September and continue till the end of October when all their fruit be gather little else they plant and this be do by their woman and child neither do this long suffice they for near three part of the year they only observe time and season and live of what the country natural afford from hand to mouth etc. the mildness of the air the fertility of the soil and the situation of the river be so propitious the commodity in Virginia general tall and straight of a comely proportion and of a colour brown when they be of any age but they be bear white their hair be general black but few have any beard the man wear half their the Barbara head shave the other half long for barber they use their woman who with two shell will grate away the hair of any fashion they please the woman be cut in many fashion agreeable to their year but ever some part remain long they be very strong of a able body and the constitu^on full of agility able to endure to lie in the wood under a tree by the fire in the worst of winter or in the weed and grass in ambuscado in the summer they be inconstant in every the disposition thing but what fear constrain they to keep crafty timorous quick of apprehension and very ingenious some be of disposition fearful some bold most cautelous all savage general covetous of copper bead and such like trash they be soon move to anger and so malicious that they seldom forget a injury they seldom steal one from another lest their conjurer shall reveal it and so they be pursue and punish that they be thus fear i^ certain but that any can reveal their offence by conjuration I be doubtful their woman be careful not to be suspect of dishonesty without the leave of their husband each household know their own land and garden and most live of their own labour for their apparel they be sometime cover with the skin of wild beast which in winter be dress with the the possession their attire hair but in summer without the better sort use large mantle of dear skin not much differ in fashion from the irish mantle some embroider with white bead some with copper other paint after their manner but the common sort have scarce to cover their nakedness but with grass the leaf of tree or such like we have see some use mantle make of turkie-feather so pretty wrought and weave with thread that nothing can be discern feather mantle but the feather that be exceed warm and very handsome but the woman be always cover about their middle with a skin and very shamefaced to be see bare they adorn themselves most with copper bead and paint their woman some have their leg their ornament hand breast and face cunning embroider with diverse work as beast serpent artificial wrought into their flesh with black spot in each ear common they have three great hole whereat the hang chain bracelet or copper some of their man wear in those hole a small green and yellow colour snake near half a yard in length which crawl and lap herself about his neck oftentimes familiar will kiss his lip other wear a dead rat tie by the tail some on their head wear the wing of a bird or some large feather with a rattle those rattle be somewhat like the chape of a rapier but less which they take from the tail of a snake many have the whole skin of a hawk or some strange fowl stuff with the wing abroad other a broad piece of copper and some the hand of their enemy dry their head and shoulder be paint red with the root bray to powder mix with oil this they hold in summer to preserve they from the heat and in winter from the cold many other form of paint they use but he be the most gallant that be the most monstrous to behold their building and habitation be for the most part by the river or not far distant from their building some fresh spring their house be build like our arbour of small young sprig bow and tie and so close cover with mat or the bark of tree very hand some that notwithstanding either wind rain or weather they be so warm as stove but very smoky yet at the top of the house there be a hole make for the smoke to go into right over the fire against the fire they lie on little hurdle of reed cover with a mat bear from the ground their lodging a foot and more by a hurdle of wood on these round about the house they lie head and point one by other against the fire some cover with mat some with skin and some stark naked lie on the ground from six to twenty in a house their house be in the midst of their field or garden which be small plot of ground some twenty some forty some a hundred their garden some two hundred some more some less sometime from two to a hundred of those house frequent with deer beast fish fowl rootes and berry at their hunt they leave their habitation and reduce themselves into company as the tartar do and go to the most desert place with how they hunt their family where they spend their time in hunt and fowl up towards the mountain by the head of their river where there be plenty of game for betwixt the river the ground be so narrow that little have paint and disguise themselves in the fierce manner they can devise they divide themselves into two company near a hundred in a company the one company call their manner of battle the other powhatans either army have their captain these as enemy take their stand a musket shoot one from another rank themselves fifteen a breast and each rank from another four or five yard not in file but in the open betwixt their file so as the rear can shoot as convenient as the Front have thus pitch the field from either part go a messenger with these condition that whosoever be vanquish such as escape upon their submission in two day after shall live but their wife and child shall he prize for the conqueror the messenger be no soon return but they approach in their order on each flank a sergeant and in the rear a officer for lieutenant all due keep their order yet leap and sing after their accustom tune which they use only in war upon the first flight of arrow they give such horrible shout and screech as so many infernal hellhound can not have make they more terrible when they have spend their arrow they join together pretty charge and retire every rank second other as they get advantage they catch their enemy by the hair of the head and down he come that be take his enemy with his wooden sword seem to beat out his brain and still they creep to the rear to maintain the skirmish the monacan decrease the powhatans charge they in the form of a half moon they unwilling to be enclose flee all in a troop to their ambuscado on who they lead they very cunning the monacan disperse themselves among the fresh man whereupon the powhatans retire with all speed to their second which the monacan see take that advantage to retire again to their own battle and so each return to their own quarter all their action voice and gesture both in charge and retire be so strain to the height of their quality and nature that the strangeness thereof make it seem very delightful for their music they use a thick cane on which they pipe as on a recorder for their war they have a great deep platter of wood they cover the mouth thereof with a skin at their music each corner they tie a walnut which meet on the backside near to the bottom with a small rope they twitch they together till it be so tough and stiff that they may beat upon it as upon a Drum but their chief instrument be rattle make of small gourd or pumpion shell of these they have base tenor countertenor meare and treble these mingle with their voice sometime twenty or thirty together make such a terrible noise as will rather affright then delight any man if any great commander arrive at the habitation of a werowance their entertainment they spread a Mat as the turk do a carpet for he to sit upon upon another right opposite they sit themselves then do all with a tuneable voice of shout use he welcome after this do two or more of their chief man make a oration testify their love which they do with such vehemency and so great passion that they sweat till they drop and be so out of breath they can scarce speak so that a man will take they to be (...) ding angry or stark mad such victual as they have they spend free and at night where h^s lodging be appoint they set a woman fresh paint red with Pocones and oil to be his bedfellow their manner of trade be for copper bead and such like for which they give such commodity as they have as skin fowl fish flesh and their country corne. but their victual their trade be their chief riches every spring they make themselves sick with drink the juice of a root they call wighsacan their physic and water whereof they pour so great a quantity that it purge they in a very violent manner so that in three or four day after they scarce recover their former health sometime they be trouble with dropsy swell ache and such like disease for cure whereof their chirurgery they build a stone in the form of a dovehouse with mat so close that a few coal therein cover with a pot will make the patient sweat extreme for swell also they use small piece of touchwood in the form of clove which prick on the grief they burn close to the flesh and from thence draw the corruption with their mouth with this root wighsacan they ordinary heal green wound but to scarify a swell or make incision their best instrument be some splint stone old ulcer or putrify hurt be seldom see cure among they they have many profess physician who with their charm and rattle with a infernal their charm to cure rout of word and action will seem to suck their inward grief from their navel or their grieve place but of our chirurgeon they be so conceit that they believe any plaster will heal any hurt of their religion there be yet in Uirginia no place discover to be so savage in which the savage have not a religion deer and bow and arrow all thing that be able to do they hurt beyond their prevention they adore with their kind of divine worship as the fire water lightning thunder our ordnance piece horse etc. but their chief god they worship be the devil he they call oak and serve he more of fear then love they say they have conference with he their God and fashion themselves as near to his shape as they can imagine in their temple they have his image evilfavoured carve and then paint and adorn with chain copper and bead and cover with a skin in such manner as the deformity may well suit with such a God by he be common the sepulchre of their king their body be first bowel then dry upon hurdle till they be very dry and so about the most of their joint and neck they hang how they bury their king bracelet or chain of copper pearl and such like as they use to wear their inward they stuff with copper bead and cover with a skin hatchet and such trash then lap they they very careful in white skin and so roll they in mat for their winding-sheet and in the tomb which be a arch make of mat they lay they orderly what remain of this kind of wealth their king have they set at their foot in basket these temple and body be keep by their priest for their ordinary burial they dig a deep hole in the earth with sharp stake and the corpse be lap in skin and mat with their jewel they lay they upon stick in the ground and their ordinary burial so cover they with earth the burial end the woman be paint all their face with black coal and oil do sit when they return from the war from hunt and upon many other occasion they have also another sacrifice to the water superstition that they use in storm when the water be rough in the river and sea coast their conjurer run to the water side or pass in their boat after many hellish outcry and invocation they cast tobacco copper Pocones or such trash into the water to pacify that God who they think to be very angry in those storm before their dinner and supper the better sort will take the first bit and cast it in the fire which be all the grace they be know to use every nation in seven or child so every one of the five go through the guard to fetch a child each after other by turn the guard fearless beat they with the bastinado and they patient endure and receive all defend the child answer that the child be not c. smith all dead but the next day they be to drink wighsakon which will make they mad and they be to be keep by the last make black boy in the wilderness where their oak quiyoughcosughe which be there other god will let they have no dear turkey corn nor fish and yet beside be will make a great slaughter among they they think that their werowance and priest which they of the manner of the virginian government although the country people be very barbarous yet have they among they such government as that their magistrate for good command and their people for due subjection and obey excel many place that will be count very civil the form of their commonwealth be a monarchial government one as emperor rule over many king or governor their chief ruler be call powhatan and take his name of the principal place of dwell call powhatan but his proper name be wahunsonacock some country he have which have be his ancestor and come unto he by inheritance as the country call powhatan Arrohateck appamatuke pamavuke youghtanud and mattapanient all the rest of his territory express in the map they report have be his several conquest in all his ancient inheritance he have house build after their manner like arbour some thirty some forty yard long and at every house provision for his entertainment according to the time at Werowcomoco he be seat upon the northside of the river pamavuke some fourteen mile from james town where for the most part he be resident but he take so little pleasure in our near neighbourhood that be able to visit he against his will in six or seven hour that he retire himself to a place in the desert at the top of the river Chickahamania between toughtanund and powhatan a description of powhatan his habitation be call orapack where he ordinary now reside he be of parsonage a tall well proportion man with a sour look his head somewhat gray his beard so thin that it seem none at all his age near sixty of a very able and hardy body to endure any labour his attendance and watch about his person ordinary attend a guard of forty or fifty of the tall man his country do afford every night upon the four quarter of his house be four sentinel each stand from other a flight shoot and at every half hour one from the corpse due guard do hollow unto who every sentinel do answer round from his stand if any fail they present send forth a officer that beat he extreme a mile from orapake in a thicket of wood he have a house in which he keep his kind of his treasury treasure as skin copper pearl and bead which he store up against the time of his death and burial here also be store of red paint for ointment and bow and arrow this house be fifty or sixty yard in length frequent only by priest at the four corner of this house stand four image as sentinel one of a dragon another a bear the three like a leopard and the four like a giantlike man all make euill-fauor'd according to their best workmanship he have as many woman as he will whereof when he lie on his bed one sit at his head his wife and another at his foot but when he sit one sit on his right hand and another on his left as he be weary of his woman he bestow they on those that best deserve they at his hand when he dine or sup one of his woman before and after meat bring he water in a wooden platter to wash his hand another wait with a bunch of feather to wipe they instead of a towel and the feather when he have wipe be dry again his kingdom descend not to his son nor child but first to his brethren whereof he have three namely Opitchapan his successor the title of succession opechancanough and Catataugh and after their decease to his sister first to the elder sister then to the rest and after they to the heir male and female of the elder sister but never to the heir of the male he nor any of his people understand any letter whereby to write or read only the law whereby he rule be custom yet when he list his will be a law and must be obey not only as a king but as half a god they esteem he his inferior king who they call their authority werowance be tie to rule by custom and have power of life and death as their command in that nature but this word werowance which we call and construe for a king be a common word whereby they call all commander for they have but few word in their language and but few occasion to use any officer more than one commander which common they call werowance they all know their several land and habitation and limit to fish foul or hunt in but they the of their land hold all of their great werowance powhatan unto who they pay tribute of skin bead copper pearl dear turkey wild beast and corne. what he command they dare not disobey in the least thing it be strange to see with what great fear and adoration all these people do obey this powhatan for at his foot they present whatsoever he command at the least frown of his brow their great spirit will tremble with fear and no marvel for he be very terrible and tyrannous in punish such as offend he for example he cause certain malefactor to be his manner of punishment bind hand and foot then have many fire gather great store of burn coal they rake these coal round in the form of a cockpit and in the midst they cast the offender to broil to death sometime he cause the head of they that offend he to be lay upon the altar or sacrifice stone and one with club beat out their brain when he will punish any notorious enemy or malefactor he cause he to be tie to a tree and with muscle shell or reed the executioner cut off his joint one after another ever cast what they cut off into the fire then do he proceed with s (...) else and reed to case the skin from his head and face then do they rip his belly and so burn he with the tree and all thus themselves report they execute George cassen their ordinary correction be to beat they with cudgel we have see a man kneel on his knee and at powhatans command two man have beat he on the bare skin till he have fall senseless in a sound and yet never cry nor complain in the year 1608 he surprise the people of Payankatank his near neighbour and subject the occasion be to we unknown but the manner be thus first he send diverse of his man to lodge among they that night than the ambusacode environ all their house and at the hour appoint they all fall to the spoil twenty four man they slay the long hair of their one side of their head with the skin case off with shell or reed they bring away they surprise also the woman the child and the werowance all these triumph at Werowocomoco show they to the english man that then come unto he at his appoitment they expect provision he to betray they suppose to half conquer they by this spectacle of his terrible cruelty and this be as much as my memory can call to mind worthy of note which I have purposely collect to satisfy my friend of the true worth and quality of Virginia yet some bad nature will not stick to slander the country that will slovenly spit at all thing especial in company where they can find none to contradict they who though they be scarce ever ten mile from james town or at the most but at the fall yet hold it a great disgrace that among so much action their action be nothing exclaim of all thing though they never adventure to know any thing nor ever do any thing but devour the fruit of other man labour be for vanity of effeminate planter most part of such tender education and small experience in martial accident because they find not english city nor such fair house nor at their own wish any of their accustom dainty with featherbed and down-pillowe tavern and alehouse in every breathe place neither such plenty of gold and silver and dissolute liberty as they expect have here and their own action be there according some other there be that have yearly stipend to pass to and again for transportation vanity of self-seeking glorioso who to keep the mystery of the excuse which still to maintain their vainglory and estimation from time to time they have use such diligence as make they pass for truth though nothing more false and that the adventurer may be thus witty spirit what will they not affirm in the behalf of our transporter to get victual from their ship or obtain their good word in England to their pass thus the clamour and the ignorance of false informer be spring those disaster that spring in Virginia and our ingenious verbalist be no less plague to we in Virginia than the locust to the egyptian for the labour of thirty of the best only and by that time three ship be provide one of one hundred tun another of forty and a pinnace of twenty the transportation of the company be commit to captain Christopher Newport a mariner well again and then another oration ever lay down so many corn as before till they have twice encircle the fire that do they take a bunch of little stick prepare for that purpose and at the end of every song and oration lay down a stick betwixt the division of the corne. till night neither he nor they do eat or drink and then they feast merry with their best provision three day they use this ceremony thereby to know as they say whether he intend they well or no. the circle of meal signify their country the two circle of corn the sea-bound and the stick his country they imagine the world to be flat
