I have here omit and proceed to the english proceed in those land be bind for the summer land in the ship call the plough we embark the eight and twenty of April 1612. so pass down to Gravesend we anchor at tilbery-hope until the five of may. the wind come taire we put forth and come to the down the six of May where we stay till the nine and then set forward we have a fair and comfortable passage and by God blessing find so direct a course that on the eleven of july in the morning betwixt nine and ten of the clock we descry our hope and desire land and in the afternoon of the same day about three a clock we arrive in a very safe harbour near s. George saint George island island there we land all our man and woman and have be at anchor above a hour before we can hear of our three man which have be leave there as soon as we have land all our three man have stay behind and go not to Virginia harter water and chard company we go all to prayer and give thanks unto the lord for our safe arrival and while we be at prayer we see our three man come row down to we the sight of who do much rejoice we so they welcome we and we the like to they again we sing a psalm and praise the lord for our safe meeting and go to supper the next day be the sabbath day which we dedicate to God in the best manner we can we abide still in the foresay island with all the rest of our company till Monday morning be the thirteen of july then we go up with our ship and company high into the harbour to the place where these three man have plant themselves they have plant corn great store of wheat beanes tobacco and melon with many other good thing for the use of man beside they have wrought upon timber in square and saw of cedar tree for they intend to build a small pinnace to carry they into Virginia be almost out of hope and comfort of our come because cap. Davies time be to have be with they long before we come we be no soon come within a league of the land but a company of fish as it be meet we and never leave we till we be come to a anchor within the harbour and as soon as we commodite of the country fish have pass over our business and all thing safe and in order with a hook and line we take more than our whole company be able to eat so that there be enough to feed many more the next day after the sabbath we go with our net and boat and if we will have load two boat we may and so may you do day by day fish do so abound and there be of these sort mullet breame hog-fish rock-fish and lobster with more sort of other fish which I can name turkle there be of a mighty bigness one Turkle will serve or suffice three or four score at a meal especial if it be a she Turkle for she will have as many egg as will suffice fifty or tortoise great and of great use threescore at a meal this I can assure you they be very good and wholesome meat none of it bad no not so much as the very gut and maw of it for they be exceed fat and make as good Tripes as your beast belly in England and for foul we go the three day of our arrival unto the bird land as we call they and use neither stick nor stone-bow nor gun we take they up with our hand so many as we will that every one of the company be to have fowl some three some four a piece three for a child boy or girl for a man four then reckon what those that serve some fourscore people do amount unto but this be for certain if we will have bring away twice so many more we may some six day after our come we send out for hog so the company which go out hog by reason of their food there and our man stomach extraordinary sweet the weather fruit pear not hurtful bring home some for the meat of they I hold your mutton of England not of so sweet and pleasant a taste for the inclination of the weather consider in what climate it lie we have have for the space of some forty day no rain but very cool and fresh gale of wind yet in the day time very hot but we agree with it very well and not a man that have lie sick or disease but all like well and follow and employ themselves to one business or other for the fruit which the land yield th^y be the mulberry great store and pear which have in they a red liquor as the pomegranate hat or somewhat red but very wholesome if you eat a hundred at one time you shall never surfeit of they if you eat some proportion of they they will bind but if you exceed in eat of they then be they of the contrary operation yet never any that hurt themselves by they eat they never so many it be certain that one man eat above a peck of they in some ten hour and be never the worse we have a kind of Berrie upon the cedar tree very pleasant to eat and for the Palmito tree the top of it be a cedar berry great deal sweet and wholesome than any cabedge in some of our land there grow pepper but not so good as our indian pepper diverse sort of other good thing there be which the several time of the year bring forth one after another pepper but the top of the Palmito tree be in season and good all the year take a hatchet and cut he or a augar and bear he and it yield a very pleasant liquor much like unto your sweet wine palme-liquor it bear likewise a Berrie in bigness of a prune and in taste much like also we have olive grow with we but no great store many other good excellent thing we have grow with we which this short time will not permit i to write of so large as I may but this be of truth that hog turkle fish and fowl do abound as dust of the earth ambergris and pearl for ambergris and pearl we have not have leisure in so few day since our arrival to go look out for the one or to fish for the other but the three man which be leave there have find of they both also they have make a great deal of tobacco and if some will come that have tobacco kill in make it it will be very commodious both to the merchant and to the maker of it silk-spider timber tree and for the silkworm if any be bring over and some of skill to use they there will be very much good do with they for the very spider in these our land do weave perfect fine * * I have omit the rest of this discourse as be better know to late writer silk both yellow and white the timber of the country consist of three sort the one be the cedar very fine timber to work upon of colour red and very sweet the other sort we have no name for for there be none in the company have see the like in other country before we come etc. a copy of the article which master r. more governor deputy of the summer land propound to the company that be there with he to be subscribe unto which both he and they subscribe the second of August in his house 1612. which about the same time he send into England to the worshipful company of the aduenturor we who have here under subscribe our name be by the great goodness of God safe arrive at the summer land with purpose here to inhabit do hereby promise and bind ourselves to the performance of the several article hereafter follow and that in the presence of the most glorious God who have in mercy bring we hither first we do faithful promise and by these present solemn bind ourselves evermore to worship that aforesaid only true and everliving God who have make the heaven and the earth the sea and all that therein be and that according to those rule that be prescribe in his most holy word and ever to continue in that faith into the which we be baptize in the church of England and to stand in defence of the same against all atheist papist anabaptist brownist and all other heretic and sectary whatsoever dissent from the say word and Faith second because the keep of the sabbath day holy be that wherein a principal part of God worship do consist and be as it be the key of all the other part thereof we do therefore in the presence aforesaid promise that we will set apart all our own labour and employment on that day unless it be those that be of mere necessity much more vain and unfruitful practice and apply ourselves to the hear of God word prayer and all other exercise of religion in his word require to the uttermost of our power three see the true worship of God and holy life can be sever we do therefore promise in the presence aforesaid that to the uttermost of our power we will live together in do that which be just both towards God and man and in particular we will forbear to take the most holy name of God in vain in ordinary swear by it or any other thing or by scoff or vain abuse of his most holy word or to use curse or filthy speech or any other thing forbid in god most holy word as also to live together without steal one from another or quarrel one with another or slander one of another and to avoid all thing that stand not with the good estate of a christian church and well govern commonwealth as also to embrace the contrary as justice and peace love and all other thing that stand with the good and comfort of society four whereas we be here together far remote from our native soil of England and yet be indeed the natural subject of our most royal and gracious king JAMES of England Scotland France and Ireland king defender of the faith etc. we do therefore in the presence aforesaid solemn promise evermore to continue the loyal subject of our say sovereign king his heir and successor and never to revolt from he or they unto any other whatsoever but evermore to acknowledge his supreme government five whereas we be send hither by diverse adventurer of the city of London and other part of the realm of England we do here in the presence aforesaid promise to use all diligence for the good of the plantation and not to purloin or embezzle any of the prohibit commodity out of the general estate but to use all faithfulness as it become christian to do as also to be obedient to all such governor or governor or their deputy or deputy as be or shall be by they send to govern we as also to yield all reverence towards the ministry or minister of the gospel send or to be send six and last we do here in presence aforesaid promise the lord assist we that if at any time hereafter any foreign power shall attempt to put we out of this our lawful possession not cowardly to yield up the same but manful to fight as true english man for the defence of the commonwealth we live in and gospel we profess and that while we have breath we will not yield to any that shall invade we upon any condition whatsoever I have think hitherto to have add a letter of m. in bermuda nine month with help of such thing as they save with the sea-ven'ure and of such as they find in the country have build of cedar and rig fit for the sea two vessel a ship and a pinnace and upon the ten of May 1610. depart towards Uirginia leave only two man behind they and carry they store of provision for the relief of the people there upon the four and twenty of May they arrive safe there and short after some of they return to the summer land again for a further supply in the same ship which they have former build there where sir George Summer die his man do not according to his last charge give unto they return to Virginia but frame their course for England leave behind they three man that stay voluntary who short after find in Somerset island which be a part of sandys tribe a very great treasure in ambergris to the value of nine or ten thousand pound sterling there have also be find ambergris since diverse time of the best sort this new discovery of the summer land be thus make know in England to the virginian company by these man which return they sell it to some hundred and twenty person of the same company who obtain a charter from his majesty and so hold it and towards the latter end of April 1612. send thither a ship call the plough with some sixty person to inhabit appoint governor one master Richard Moor a man ingenuous and careful who since die in sir Walter rawlye last voyage to Guiana a place as appear by our modern geographer very rich and spacious but as I say he arrive there about the begin of july and find the foresay three man that stay voluntary very well master Moor spend the three year of his government for the most part in fortify the country and train the people in martial exercise which custom have be continue by his successor he build some nine or ten fort place ordnance and munition in they in his time the lord send upon the country a very grievous scourge and punishment threaten the utter ruin and desolation of it that it come from God I need not strive to prove especial consider it be general rat-plague so acknowledge by we at that time the cause and occasion of it I need not name be very well know to we all that then live there which be about six hundred person think short after much diminish I will only show the thing itself which be a wonderful annoyance by silly rat these rat come at the first out of a ship few in number how vain a thing be man who best wit and industry be triumph over by silly rat great God give we grace to fear thou that we may fear nothing else else shall we fear with Pharaoh frog louse fly grasshopper or with other flea sparrow and ^ yea a few rat in despite of cat dog trap poison shall starve we increase in the space of two year or less so exceed that they fill not only those place where they be first land but swim from place to place spread themselves into all part of the country insomuch that there be no island though sever by the sea from all other land and many mile distant from the isle where the rat have their original but be pester with they they have their nest almost in every tree and in all place their burrowes in the ground like coney to harbour in they spare not the fruit of plant and tree neither the plant themselves but eat they up when we have set our corn they will common come by troop the night follow or so soon as it begin to grow and dig it up again if by diligent watch any of it be preserve till it come to ear it shall then very hardly escape they yea it be a difficult matter after we have it in our house to save it from they for they become noisome even to the person of man we use all diligence for the destroy of they nourish many cat wild and tame for that purpose we use ratsbane and many time set fire on the wood so as the fire may run half a mile or more before it be extinct every man in the country be enjoin to set twelve trap and some of their own accord set near a hundred which they visit twice or thrice in a night we train up our dog to hunt they wherein they grow so expert that a good dog in two or three hour space will kill forty of fifty rat and other mean we use to destroy they but can not prevail find they still to increase against we and this be the principal cause of that great distress whereunto we be drive in the first plant of the country for these devour the fruit of the earth keep we destitute of bread a year or two so that when we have it afterwards again we be so wean from it that we shall easy neglect and forget to eat it with our meat we be also destitute at that time of boat and other provision for fish and moreover master Moor have receive warning from England that he shall expect the Spaniard that year yet they come not but with two ship attempt to come in and have their boat before they to sound the way be shoot at by the say master Moor from king castle and as we suppose one of they strike through whereupon they present depart but as I say this expectation of they cause we though in great necessity to hasten the fortification of the country all these joint but principal the rat be the cause of our distress for be destitute of food many die and we all become very feeble and weak whereof some be so will not other can not stir abroad to seek relief but die in their house such as go abroad be subject through weakness to be sudden surprise with a disease we call the feage which be neither pain nor sickness but as the Feag^ it be the high degree of weakness deprive we of power and ability for the execution of any bodily exercise whether it be work walk or what else be thus take if there be any in company that can minister any relief they will straightways recover otherwise they die there yet many after a little rest will be able to walk again and then if they find any succour be save about this time or immediate before come thither a company of raven which continue with we all the time of this mortality and then depart there be not before that time nor since so far as I hear any more of they see there and this with some other reason of more moment move many to think that there be some other land near the summer land between Uirginia and it and m. Moor in his time with some other of we go forth in a boat so far as then we can convement of purpose to discover it since then it have be endeavour by other and be yet as I hear to be further attempt and howsoever I be persuade for certain cause which I can here relate there be no such thing yet will I not disanimate any from this enterprise for if they find any their labour will be well recompense and though they find none yet may they discover those part so well that the passage to and from Virginia will be more safe and easy but to return from whence we have digress the extremity of our distress begin to abate a little before m. Moor time of government be expire partly by supply out of England of victualland provision for fish and partly by that rest and liberty we then obtain the country be fortify yet the rat increase and continue almost to the end of captain Tuckers time although he be provident and industrious to destroy they but towards the end of his time it please God by what mean it be not well know to take they away insomuch that the wild cat and many dog which live on they be famish and many of they leave the wood come down to the house and to such place where they use to garbage their fish and become tame some have attribute this destruction of they to the increase of wild cat but that be not likely they shall be so sudden increase rather at that time then in the four year before and the chief occasion of this supposition be because they see such company of they leave the wood and show themselves for want of food other have suppose it to come to pass by the coolness of the weather which notwithstanding be never so great there as with we in march nor scarce as it be in April except it be in the wind beside the rat want not feather of young bird and chicken which they daily kill and of Palmeto moss as we call it to build themselves warm nest out of the wind as usual they do neither do it appear that the cold be so mortal to they see they will ordinary swim from place to place and be very fat even in the midst of winter it remain then that as we know God do sometime effect his will without subordinate and secondary cause and sometime against they so we need not doubt but that in the speedy increase and spread of these vermin as also in the preservation of so many of we by such weak mean as we then enjoy and especial in the sudden removal of this great annoyance there be join with and beside the ordinary and manifest mean a more immediate and secret work of God now to proceed m. Moor time of government be expire capt. Tucker succeed arrive cap. Tucker there about mid-may 1616. who likewise govern according to the custom three year which time he spend for the most part in husbandr the country plant and nourish all such thing as be find fit either for trade or for the sustentation and use of the inhabitant wherein he travel with much diligence and good success send to some part of the indies for plant and fruit he also ad^ed to the fortification and make some enclosure in his time viz. in the year 1617. be send a ship and provision with man of skill for the kill of whale but they arrive there too late to wit about the midst of April so that before they can make ready their shallop and fit themselves the principal season for whalefishing be whale pass for the whale come thither in january and depart again towards the latter end of May yet they strike some but find they so lively swift and fierce after they be strike that they can take none they yield great store of oil as appear by one that drive to shore on Somerset island in sandys tribe and by another that we find not far from thence dead upon a rock I also receive by captain Tucker direction from the adventurer to divide the country and to assign to each adventurer his share or portion of land and withal a description with share note touch the manner how they will have it do as they have former determine by Lot which thing I do with all faithfulness and diligence the manner of it do above appear and be more large manifest in a book of the survey of the country exhibit to the right honourable his majesty counsel and the court of adventurer for these part and then begin this which be before as it be a unsettle and confuse chaos I mean as touch a plantation for consider only as a regiment it be otherwise to receive a convenient disposition form and order and to become indeed a plantation for though the country be small yet they can not have be convenient dispose and well settle without a true description and survey make of it and again every man be settle where he may constant abide they know their business and fit their household according they build for themselves and their family not tent or cabin but more substantial house they clear their ground and plant not only such thing as will yield they their fruit in a year or half a year but all such too as will afford they profit after certain year etc. so that in short time after even before expiration of captain Tuckers government the country begin to aspire and near to approach unto that happiness and prosperity wherein now it flourish for may it not just be account happiness and prosperity for man to live where they enjoy the mean of true religion and salvation to wit the sincere ministry of the word and sacrament where the government be good without rigour and oppression the place healthful and temperate where they be free from all extreme care and toil where they have food in abundance and very good with other thing needful to the body and where they have commodity meet for trade by which they better advance their estate all which and more be large verify in the present estate of that colony whatsoever some malicious mind or to evil end suborn may say to the contrary so that there may seem to be a restauration of that golden age so much speak of the governor now there resident be one captain Butler for captain Tucker depart thence in December 1618. leave in his place captain Kendal who also be one that supply the same place in the interim between master Moor time and captain tucker and have spend some nine or ten year in the country but in the year 1619. about midsummer the adventurer send thither as governor for three year according to the custom the say captain Butler and four ship with some five hundred person there be at that time in the country only five hundred more for by the space of four year to wit during the latter part of master Moor government and all the time of captain tucker they have send few thither be almost hopeless of the place by reason of the rat but since there have be send many company more than have come to my knowledge insomuch that I understand the country be now almost full plant and inhabit thus have I brief relate so far forth as have come to my knowledge and remembrance every thing of most note and importance that have befall in the first discovery and plant of these land till this present I have labour to contract myself yet have exceed my intend limit now I must speak something of the country itself which consist of a company of small land situate and form as above appear it lie in the western ocean in that part of the world late discover and call America or the new world vulgar the west indies it have latitude or elevation as be abovesaid 32. degree 25. minute which be almost the same with the maderae or rather more southward the country be round about environ with rock which to the northward westward and southward extend far then have be yet discover by reason of these rock the country be very strong for there be only two place and scarce two except to such as know they well where ship may safe come in and those place be very well fortify but within be room to entertain a royal Fleet. the rock in most place appear at a low water neither be they much cover at a high water for it ebb and flow there not above five foot the shore itself for the most part be a rock so harden by the sun wind and sea that it be not apt to be wear by the wave who violence be also break by the rock before they come at the shore the mould be of diverse colour neither clay nor sand but a mean between the red which resemble clay be worst the whitish resemble sand and the blackish clay be good the brown between they both which they call white because there be mingle with it as it be a white Marle be best under the mould two or three foot deep and sometime less be a kind of white hard substance which they call the rock the tree usual fasten their root in it and draw their nourishment from it neither be it indeed rock or stone nor so hard though for the most part hard than chalk not so white but pumice-like and spongy easy receive and contain much water I have see in some place clay find under it it seem to be engender of the rain water drain through the earth and draw with it of his substance unto a certain depth where it congeal the hard kind of it which be common under the red ground be not so spongy nor retain much water but lie in the ground in quarry as it be thick slate one upon another and there be some chink or crevice betwixt one late and another through which the water have passage so that in such place there be scarce find any fresh water for all or the most part of their fresh water whereof they have good store come out of the sea drain through the sand or through the foresay substance which they call the rock and leave his salt behind it become fresh sometime we dig welles of fresh water within four or five pace of the seaside Wels. sometime further off the most part of they will ebb and flow as the sea do and be level or little high than the superficies of the Sea the air be most common clear very temperate moist with a moderate heat very the air healthful and apt for the generation and nourish of all thing so that there be scarce any thing transport from hence thither but it yield a far great increase and if it be any live thing become fat and better like then here by this mean the country be so replenish with hen and turkeye within the space of three or four year that be neglect many of they forsake the house and become wild and so live in great abundance the like increase there be of hog and other cattle according to their kind there seem to be a continual spring which be the cause that some few thing come not to that maturity and perfection as be requisite and though the tree do shed their leaf yet be they always full of green their corn be the same which they use almost in all part of the west indies to wit Maiz which to such as be use to it be more hearty and nourish then our english wheat and yield a far great increase as a pound sometime of one or two grain of this corn and ^ivers other thing without either plow or dig the ground they have two harvest every year for they set about march which they gather in july and again in August which be ripe in December and little slip of fig tree and vine do usual bear fruit within less than a year after they be plant sometime in half a year the like fertility it have in other thing there be scarce at any time to be perceive either frost or snow nor any extreme heat for temperature of the country there be almost always some wind stir which clear and cool the air their summer and winter observe the same time with we but their long day and night be short than we in England by two hour and almost a half as also their short day and night be as much long than we for their long day and night be about fourteen hour and their short ten when it be noon with we it be morning with they and when it be about five of the clock in the evening with we it be high-noon with they so that while the sun decline with we it rise with they as also it do in Virginia it be apt to thunder and lightning all the year ofttimes more terrible then in England but no man or other live creature have I know hurt by it there be no venomous creature in the country the yellow spider spider which be there make her web as it be of silk and bring forth her young as the alchemist their stone of egg like little ball of quicksilver be not perceive to be any whit venomous yet there be a plant that climb tree like ivy the leaf also of the same colour but in shape like the vine that be somewhat venomous but of no great force there be great store and variety of fish and so good as these part of the world afford not the like which be for the most part unknown to we each man give they name as they best like as one kind they call rocke-fish another grooper other porgie-fish hog-fish angle-fish cavally yellow-tayle spanish makerell mullet bream connie-fish morraye sting-raye flying-fish etc. the like they do by the fowl as cohooe sandbird heron duck and teal pemblicoe castle-booby hawk etc. the country when we first begin the plantation be all overgrow with wood and plant of several kind and to such kind as be unknown to we which be the most part we also give name such as be know retain their old name as cedar Palmetoes black-wood white-wood yellow-wood mulberie-tree stopper-tree laurel and olive-tree mangrowes pepper-tree yellow-bery-weed red-weed these and many other we find natural grow in the country but since it have be inhabit there have be bring thither as well from the indies as from other part of the world sundry other plant as vine of several kind sugarcane figge-tree appletree orange lemon pomegranate Plantanes pines parsnip radish artichoke potato indigo and many other insomuch that it be now become as it be some spacious garden or nursery of many pleasant and profitable thing now if I shall proceed to a more special narration and speak of all these plant bird fish and other remarkable thing particular I can not but be much large than be any way expedient in this place beside I have long since understand that captain Butler the governor there resident have undertake to write of these and the like thing a peculiar treatise this therefore that be speak touch the nature of the country in general shall suffice only to make choice of two particular whereof I will speak not so large as the thing require but so far forth as will be meet and convenient in this place the first shall be the tortoise which they call a turtle which have some affinity and resemblance with fish beast and fowl shall serve instead of a history of they all the other shall be that which they call the prickle peartree which participate in nature and resemble in some thing herb and in other tree shall likewise serve in stead of the natural history of they both and first of the turckle not regard for brevity sake the large discourse of other I will only write what I have see and know myself they be in the shape of their body like a crabfish and have four fin they be as great as three or four man can carry the upper part of they be cover with a great shell which we call a galley-patch weigh as I take it half a hundred weight the flesh that cleave to the inside of this be roast against the fire be excellent meat almost like the marrow of beef but the shell itself hard than horn she have also a shell on her belly not so hard but be boy lead it become soft like the sinew or gristle of beef and good meat these live in the sea spend the spring time and part of the summer about these land but the residue of the year we know not where they be like to fowl in respect of the smallness and fashion of their head and neck which be wrinkle like a turkeye but white and not so sharp bill they also breed their young of egg which they lay they resemble beast in that their flesh be like veal but more hard and solid and they feed always upon grass grow at the bottom of the water neither can they abide any long under water than they hold their breath which the old one will do long but the young one be chase to and fro can continue two minute with out come up to breathe short after their come in the male and female couple which we call coot this they continue some three day together during which time they will scarce separate though a boat come to they nor hardly when they be smite not long after the shee-turckle come up by night upon some sandie bay and further up then the water use to flow she dig a hole with her fin in the sand some two foot deep and there come up several night lay her egg some half a bushel which be about the bigness of a hen egg and round as a ball and each time cover they with sand very curious so that a man shall hardly find the place these egg as it seem be afterward hatch by heat of the sun and then by the providence of God the mean be yet unknown to we be bring out of the earth for we can never perceive that she return any more to they and yet in likelihood they remain not long in the earth after they be hatch because as I have before say they can live without breathe we sometime see of the young one no big than a man hand which some fish will deucure they grow slow and seem to have a very long life they will sleep on the top of the water and be wont to sleep often on the land till the country be people they will also live out of the water some three week and that without meat but mourn and pine away they be very witty be on the land turn upon their back they can no more without some help or advantage recover themselves by which mean when they come on shore to lay their egg they be easy take as also they be when they be coot but otherwise we take they for the most part by night make a great light in a boat to which they will sometime swim and seldom shun so that a man stand ready with a staff in his hand which have at one end a socket wherein be a iron less than a man finger foure-square and sharp with a line fasten to it he strike this iron into the upper shell of the turckle it stick so fast that after she have a little tire herself by swim too and fro she be take by it they will live the head be cut off four and twenty hour so that if you cut the flesh with a knife or touch it it will tremble and shrink away there be no meat will keep long either fresh or salt but leave these we will now come to speak of the prickle pear which be a fruit grow in these land in such place as be scarce fit for any thing else namely upon rock and cliff and common by the sea side as if the salt-water do somewhat help to the generation and nourish of they the tree seem to grow certain year before it bear fruit and then to continue bear very many year have almost all the year long fruit upon it and although we call this a tree yet have it scarce any body or branch but consist in a manner whole of leaf and fruit soft and brittle but we will give you a large history of the creature from captain Smith in the next chapter chap. 18 and exercise to that service chap. 19 brief intelligence from Virginia by letter a supplement of french-virginian occurrant and their supplantation by sir SAMVEL argal in right of the english plantation the late alteration of Virginia government be unknown to none and most know of the frequent complaint both by private letter and by petition to his majesty now lest any shall hereupon think Virginia to be unworthy of such our care and cost I have out of one of the planter private letter transcribe a few word of grievance and yet a magnify of the country that the english may be more blame for want of providence than the region for defect of nature best gift other thing I can allege from other but my meaning be to amend thing not to quarrel they and to awaken the care of good man rather than to recite the fault of the bad in one letter date dec. 22. last past he have these word the intolerable rate we pay here for commodity as ten pound sterling a hogshead of meal sixteen shilling a gallon of Alicante three pound sterling a hen and eight chicken etc. and so according to he mention in other letter 3. s. a pound of butter 6. d. money for a pint of milk 10 s. or 12. s. a day for a workman carpenter beside meat and lodging these rate for every thing else last the heavy taxation that be lay upon we free man for build of castle pay of public debt for the not gather of sassafras etc. so that it will come to my share with that that be pay and that that be to pay in corn and tobacco to at least twenty or five and twenty pound sterling this year so that when I have pay this and pay my faithless servant their wage I shall scarce have good tobacco enough leave to buy myself for the next year a pint of aquavitae etc. thus you see I neither warrant nor except against the truth but present the worst quarrel parallel with the best complaint of great prize of thing not arise from plenty of money as you read before in the conquest of Peru but from I know not what ill habit and indisposition of that colony and lest any man shall withdraw his heart hand or purse therefore from that worthy work I have out of the same man letter deliver a commendation of the country the letter be write and date 22. march 1624. and contain for substance none other then what before you have read in other yet be more suitable to this time and purpose as late news and fit directory to the physician of that estate that at last the english honour may be vindicate against so base peril from savage and base quarrel from and among our own God prosper his majesty care and make those which be therein employ not to seek their own good by hasty return much less other their fellow adventurer evil by calumny and undermine but Virginia prosperity of which nature prosperity be thus relate by one querulous of his own loss and cross his word be these now concern the state of the country so much as I have observe I will relate unto you first the country itself I must confess be a very pleasant land rich in commodity and fertile in soil to produce all manner of plant herb and fruit I have see here myself both carrot turnip cabbage onion leek garlic time Parseley pompion Muskmilion and watermilion rare fruit and exceed wholesome here be also strawberry I have lie down in one place in my corn field and in the compass of my reach have fill my belly in the place and for mulberry I can when I list go and gather a bushel at a time here be also a cool fruit grow wild on the ground much resemble a great walnut with the green rind on it which reserve in it three admirable good taste namely of strawberry rosewater and sugar they be a exceed great comfort to i in my last year sickness and be admirable good against the bloud flux english wheat and barley will grow here exceed well I have see here grow as good english wheat as ever I see in England in all my life for timber we have the oak ash poplar black walnut white walnut pines gum tree the pine here afford admirable good pitch and tar and serve split out in small piece in many place of this land instead of candle but it will smear one worse than a link here be also pear tree which yearly bring forth pear but there be a tree that pass all fruit tree which we call by the name of a Prissurmon tree which bear a plum much about the bigness of a pear plum I do think it be one of the rare fruit in the world when they be ripe they eat natural of themselves from the tree better than any preserve plum I ever taste in England the beast that this land be plentiful store withal be dear bear in some part beaver otter fox hare squirrel roccounes Possucins name strange to you yet be they singular good meat the roccoun taste as well as pig flesh indian dog here be as good meat with we as your english lamb english cattle here increase and thrive very well as cow hog goat and poultry foul here be abundance as swan brant goose turkey heron crane eagle fish hawk bussard duck and mallard Sheldrake dapchicke partridge leave sick and weak with very small mean the indian round about we peaceable and friendly the country very pleasant and temperate yield natural of itself great store of fruit as uine of diverse sort in great abundance there be likewise walnut chestnut small-nut and plum with much variety of flower root and herb no less pleasant than wholesome and profitable no place have more goose-berry and strawberry nor better timber of all sort you have in England do cover the land that afford beast of diverse sort and great flock of turkey quail pigeon and partridge many great lake abound with fish fowl beavers and otter the sea afford we as great plenty of all excellent sort of sea-fish as the river and isle do variety of wild fowl of most useful sort mynes we find to our think but neither the goodness nor quality we know better grain can be then the indian corn if we will plant it upon as good ground as a man need desire we be all freeholders the rend day do not trouble we and all those good blessing we have of which and what we list in their season for take our company be for most part very religious honest people the word of God sincere teach we every sabbath so that I know not any thing a content mind can here want I desire your friendly care to send my wife and child to i where I wish all the friend I have in England and so I rest your love kinsman William hilton from the west country go ten or twelve ship to fish which be all well fraught proof 13. 1622 those that come first at Elbow make seventeen pound a single share beside beaver otter and Martin skin but some of the rest that come to the same port that be already furnish so glut the market their price be abate yet all return so well content they be a prepare to go again there be go from the west of England only though the indian continue their wont friendship yet be we more wary of they then before for their hand have be imbrue in much english blood only by too much confidence but not by force here I must entreat a little your favour to digress they do not kill the english because they be christian but for their weapon and commodity that be rare novelty but now they fear we may beat they out of their den which lion and tiger will not admit but by force but must this be a argument for a Englishman or discourage any either in Virginia or new England no ^or I have try they both for Virginia I keep that country with thirty eight and have not to eat but what we have from the savage when I have ten man able to go abroad our commonwealth be very strong with such a number I range that unknown country fourteen week I have but eighteen to subdue they all with which great army I stay six week before their great king habitation till they have gather together all the power they can and yet the dutchman send at a needless excessive charge do help powhatan how to betray i of their number we be uncertain but those two honourable gentleman captain George Percy and captain Francis west two of the phittiplace and some other such noble gentleman and resolute spirit bear their share with i and now live in England do see i take this murder Opechankanough now their great king by the long lock on his head with my pistol opechancanough take in ^he midst of his army as Atabalipa be by Picarra at his breast I lead he among his great force and before we part make he fill our bark of twenty tun with corne. when their own want be such I have give they part again in pity and other have buy it again to plant their field for wrong a soldier but the value of a penny I have cause powhatan send his own man to james town to receive their punishment at my discretion it be true in our great extremity they shoot i slay three of my man and by the folly of they that flee take i prisoner yet God make pocahontas the king daughter the mean to deliver i and thereby teach i to know their treachery to preserve the rest it be also my chance in single combat to take the king of Paspahegh prisoner and by keep he force his subject to work in chain till I make all the country pay contribution have little else-whereon to live twice in this time I be their precedent and none can say in all that time I have a man slay but for keep they in that fear I be much blame both there and here yet I leave five hundred behind i that through their confidence in six month come most to confusion as you may read at large in the description of Virginia when I go first to those desperate design it cost i many a forget pound to hire man to go and procrastination cause more run away then go but after the ice be break come many brave voluntary notwithstanding since I come from thence the honourable company have be humble suitor to his majesty to get vagabond and condemn man to go thither nay so much scorn be the name of Virgnia some do choose to be hang ere they will go thither and be yet for all the worst of spite detraction and discouragement and this lamentable massacre there be more honest man now suitor to go than ever have be constrain knave and it be not unknown to most man of understanding how happy many of those callumner do think themselves that they may be admit and yet pay for their passage to go now to Virginia and have I but mean to transport as many as will go I may have choice of ten thousand that will glad be in any of those new place which be so base contemn by ungrateful base mind to range this country of new England in like manner I have but eight as be say and among their bruit condition I meet many of their silly encounter and without any hurt God be thank when your west country man be many of they wound and much torment with the savage that assault their ship as they do say themselves in the first year I be there 1614 and though master hunt then master with i do most base in steal some savage from that coast to sell when he be direct to have go for Spain yet that place be so remote from capawuck where epenew shall have fraught they with gold over that his fault can be no cause of their bad success however it be allege for a excuse I speak not this out of vain glory as it may be some gleaner or some be never there may censure i but to let all man be assure by those example what those savage be that thus strange do murder and betray our country man but to the purpose what be already write of the healthfulness of the air the richness of the soil the goodness of the wood the abundance of fruit fish and fowl in their season they still affirm that have be there now near two year and at one draught they have take one thousand base and in one night twelve hogshead of herring they be build a strong fort they hope short to finish in the interim they be well provide their number be about a hundred person all in health and well near sixty acre of ground well plant with corn beside their garden well replenish with useful fruit and if their adventurer will but furnish they with necessary for fish their want will quick be supply to supply they this sixteen of October be go the paragon with sixty seven person and all this be do by private man purse and to conclude in their own word shall they write of all plenty they have find they think they shall not be believe for the twenty six sail of ship the most I can yet understand be m. make wonderful return in fur thus you may see plain the yearly success from new England by Virginia which have 1622. be so costly to this kingdom and so dear to i which either to see perish or but bleed pardon i though it passionate i beyond the bound of modesty to have be sufficient able to foresee it and have neither power nor mean how to prevent it by that acquaintance I have with they I may call they my child for they have be my wife my hawk my hound my card my dice and in total my best content as indifferent to my heart as my left hand to my right and notwithstanding all those miracle of disaster have cross both they and i yet be there not one Englishman remain as God be thank there be some thousand I will yet begin again with as small mean as I do at the first not for that I have any secret encouragement from any I protest more than lamentable experience for all their discovery I can yet hear of be but pig of my own sow nor more strange to i then to hear one tell i he have go from Billings gate and discover Greenwich Gravesend Tilberry Quinborow Lee and Margit which to those do never hear of they though they dwell in England may be make seem some rare secret and great country unknown except the relation of master Dirmer but to return it be certain from Cannada and new England within these six year have come near 20000. beaver skin now have each of those ship transport but some small quantity of the most increase beast fowl fruit plant and seed as I project by this time their increase may have be sufficient for a thousand man but the desire of present gain in many be so violent and the endeavour of many undertaker so negligent every one so regard their private gain that it be hard to effect any public good and impossible to bring they into a body rule or order unless both authority and money assist experience it be not a work for every one to plant a colony but when a house be build it be no hard matter to dwell in it this require all the best part of art judgement courage honesty constancy diligence and experience to do but near well your homebred engross projector shall find there a great difference betwixt say and do but to conclude the fish will go forward if you plant it or no whereby a colony may be transport with no great charge that in a short time may provide such fraught to buy of we there dwell as I will hope no ship shall go or come empty from new England the charge of this be only salt net hook line knife irish rug course cloth bead glass and such like trash only for fish and trade with the savage beside our own necessary provision who endeavour will quick defray all this charge and the savage have entreat i to inhabit where I will now all these ship till this last year have be fish within a square of two or three league and not one of they all will adventure any further where questionless five hundred sail may have their fraught better than in island new find land or elsewhere and be in their market before the other can have their fish in their ship because new England fish begin with February the other not till mid may the progression hereof tend much to the advancement of Virginia and the bermuda who empty ship may take in their fraught there and will be a good friend in time of need to the inhabitant of new find land etc. chap. 4 a relation or journal of a plantation settle at Plymouth in new England and proceed thereof print 1622. and here abbreviate WEdnesday the six of September the wind come east north-east a fine small gale we loose from Plymouth have be kind entertain and courteous use sep. 6. 1620. by diverse friend there dwell and after many difficulty in boisterous storm at length by God providence upon the nine of November follow by break of the day we espy land which we deem to be cape cod and so no. 9 cape Cod. afterward it prove upon the eleven of November we come to a anchor in the bay which be a good harbour and pleasant bay circle round except in the entrance which be about four mile over from land to land compass about to the very sea with Oakes pine juniper saffafras and other sweet wood it be a harbour wherein 1000 sail of ship may safe ride there we relieve ourselves with wood and water and refresh our people while our shallop be fit to coast the bay to search for a habitation there be the great store of fowl that ever we see and every day we see whale play hard by we of which in that place if we have instrument and mean to take they we may have make a very rich return which to our great grief we want our master and his mate and other experience in fish profess we may have make three or four thousand pound worth of oil they prefer it before greenland whalefishing and purpose the next winter to fish for whale here for cod we assay but find none there be good store no doubt in their season neither get we any fish all the time we lay there but some few little one on the shore we find great mussel and very fat and full of sea pearl but we can not eat they for they make we all sick that do eat as well sailor as passenger they cause to cast and scour but they be soon well again the bay be so round and circle that before we can come to anchor we go round all the point of the compass we can not come near the shore by three quarter of a english mile because of shallow water which be a great prejudice to we for our people go on shore be force to ill land wade a bow shoot or two in go aland which cause many to get cold and cough for it be many time freeze cold weather this day before we come to harbour observe some not well affect to unity and concord but give some appearance of faction it be think good there shall be a association and agreement that we shall combine together in one body and to submit to such government and governor as we shall by common consent agree to make and choose and set our hand to this that follow word for word in the name of God amen we who name be underwrite the loyal subject of our dread sovereign lord king james by the grace of God of great Britain France and Ireland king defender of the faith etc. have undertake for the glory of God and advancement of the christian faith and honour of our king and country a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern part of Virginia do by these present solemn and matual in the presence of GOD and one of another covenant and combine ourselves together in a civil body politic for our better order and preservation and furtherance of the end aforesaid and by virtue hereof to enact constitute and frame such just and equal law ordinance act constitution office from time to time as shall be think most meet and convenient for the general good of the colony unto which we promise all due submission and obedience in witness whereof we have here under suscribe our name cape cod eleven of November in the year of the reign of our sovereign lord king JAMES of England France and Ireland 18. and of Scotland 54. 1620. the same day so soon as we can we set ashore fifteen or sixteen man well arm with some to fetch wood for we have none leave as also to see what the land be and what inhabitant they can meet with they find it to be a small neck of land on this side where we lay be the bay and the further side the sea the ground or earth sand hill much like the down in Holland but much better the crust of the earth a spit depth excellent black earth all wood with oak pine saffafras juniper birch holly vine some ash walnut the wood for the most part open and without under-wood fit either to go or ride in at night our people return but find not any person nor habitation and lade their boat with juniper which smell very sweet and strong and of which we burn the most part of the time we lay there Monday the thirteen of November we unship our shallop and draw she on land to mend and repair she have be force to cut she down in bestow she betwixt the deck and she be much open with the people lie in she which keep we long there for it be sixteen or seventeen day before the carpenter have finish she our people go on shore to refresh themselves and our woman to wash as they have great need but while we lie thus still hope our shallop will be ready in five or six day at the further but our carpenter make slow work of it so that some of our people impatient of delay desire for our better furtherance to travail by land into the country which be not without appearance of danger not have the shallop with they nor mean to carry provision but on their back to see whether it may be fit for we to seat in or no and the rather because as we sail into the harbour there seem to be a river open itself into the main land the willingness of the person be like but the thing itself in regard of the danger be rather permit then approve and so with caution direction and instruction sixteen man be set out with every man his musket sword and corslet under the conduct of captain Miles Standish unto who be adjoin for counsel and advise William Bradford Stephen Hopkins and Edward tilley Wednesday the fifteen of November they be set a shore and when they have order themselves in order of a single file and march about the space of a mile by the sea they espy five or six people with a dog come towards they who be savage who when they sight of savage see they run into the wood and whistle the dog after they etc. first they suppose they to be master jones the master and some of his man for they be a shore and know of their come but after they know they to be indian they march after they into the wood lest other of the indian shall lie in ambush but when the indian see our man follow they they run away with might and main and our man turn out of the wood after they for it be the way they intend to go but they can not come near they they follow they that night about ten mile by the trace of their footing and see how they have come the same way they go and at a turn perceive how they raune up a hill to see whether they follow they at length night come upon they and they be constrain to take up their lodging so they set forth three sentinel and the rest some kindle a fire and other fetch wood and there hold our rendezvous that night in the morning so soon as we can see the trace we proceed on our journey and have the track until we have compass the head of a long creak and there they take into another wood and we after they suppose to find some of their dwelling but we march through bough and bush and under hill and valley which tear our very armour in piece and yet can meet with none of they nor their house nor find any fresh water which we great desire and stand in need off for we bring neither beer nor water with we and our victual be only biscuit and Holland cheese and a little bottle of aquavite so as we be sore a thirst about ten a clock we come into a deep valley full of brush wood-gaile and long grass through which we find little path or tract and there we see a deer and find spring of fresh water of which we be hearty glad and a dear and water sit we down and drink our first new England water with as much delight as ever we drink drink in all our life when we have refresh ourselves we direct our course full south that we may come to the shore which within a short while after we do and there make a fire that they in the ship may see where we be as we have direction and so march on towards this suppose river and as we go in another valley we find a fine clear pond of fresh water be about a musket shoot broad and twice as long there grow also many small vine and fowl and dear haunt there there grow much sassafras from thence we go on and find much plain ground about fifty acre fit for the blow and some sign where the indian have former plant their corn after this some think it best for nearness of the river to go down and travail on the sea sand by which mean some of our man be tire and lag behind so we stay and gather they up and strike into the land again where we find a little path to certain heap of sand one whereof be cover with old mat and have a wooden thing like a mor^er whelm on the top of it and a earthen pot lay in a little hole at the end thereof we muse what it may be dig and find a bow and as we think arrow but they be rot we suppose there be many other thing but because we deem they grave sepulcher we put in the bow again and make it up as it be and leave the rest untouched because we think it will be odious unto they to ransack their sepulcher we go on further and find new stubble of which they have get corn this year and many walnut tree full of nut and great store of strawberry and some vine pass thus a field or two which be not great we come to another which have also be new get and there we find where a house have be and four or five old plank lay together also we find a great kettle which kettle and corn find have be some ship kettle and bring out of Europe there be also a heap of sand make like the former but it be new do we may see how they have padle it with their hand which we dig up and in it we find a little old basket full of fair indian corn and dig further and find a fine great new basket full of very fair corn of this year with some six and thirty goodly ear of corn some yellow and some red and other mix with blue which be a very goodly sight the basket be round and narrow at the top it hold about three or four bushel which be as much as two of we can lift up from the ground and be very handsome and cunning make but whilst we be busy about these thing we set our man sentinel in a round ring all but two or three which dig up the corne. we be in suspense what to do with it and the kettle and at length after much consultation we conclude to take the kettle and as much of the corn as we can carry away with we and when our shallop come if we can find any of the people and come to parley with they we will give they the kettle again and satisfy they for their corne. so we take all the ear and put a good deal of the loose corn in the kettle for two man to bring away one staff beside they that can put away into their pocket fill the same the rest we bury again for we be so lade with armour that we can carry no more not far from this place we find the remainder of a old fort or palizado which as we conceive have be make by some christian this be also hard by that place which we think have be a river unto which we go and find it so to be divi^ing it f^^re into two arm by a high bank stand right by the cut or mouth which come from the sea that which be next unto we be the less the other arm be more than twice as big and not unlike to be a harbour for ship but whether it be a fresh river or only a indraught of the sea we have no time to discover for we have commandment to be out but two day here also we see two canoas the one on the one side the other on the other side we can not believe it be a C^noa t^ll we ca^e they return near it so we return leave the further discovery hereof to our s (...) an^ (@) that night back again to the fresh water pond and there we make our rendezvous that night make a great fire and a baricado to wind ward of we and keep good watch with three sentinel all night every one stand when his turn come while five or six inch of match be burn it prove a very rainy night in the morning we take our kettle and sink it in the pond and trim our musket for few of they will go off because of the wet and so coast the wood again to come home in which we be shrewd puzzle and lose our way as we wander we come to a tree where a young spirit be bow down over a bow and some acorn strew underneath Stephen Hopkins say it have be to catch some deer so as we be look device to catch dear at it William Bradford oe in the rear when he come look also upon it and as he go about it give a sudden jerk up and he be immediate catch by the leg it be a very pretty device make with a rope of their own make and have a noose as artificial make as any roper in England can make and as like we as can be which we bring away with we in the end we get out of the wood and be fall about a mile too high above the creak where we see three buck but we have rather have have one of they we also do spring three couple of partridge and as we come along by the creak we see great flock of wild goose and duck but they be very fearful of we so we march some while in the wood some while on the sand and other while in the water up to the knee till at length we come near the ship and then we shoot off our piece and the long boat come to fetch we master jones and master carver be on the shore with many of our people come to meet we and thus we come both weary and welcome home and deliver in our corn into the store to be keep for indeed before she be full fit for there be two day work after bestow on she there be appoint some four and twenty man of our own and arm then to go and make a more full discovery of the river before
