till the sun begin to draw low and then we haste out of the wood that we may come to our shallop by that time we have do and our shallop come to we it be within night and we feed upon such victual as we have and betake we to our rest after we have set out our watch about midnight we hear a great and hideous cry and our sentinel call arm arme. so we bestir ourselves and shoot off a couple of musket and noise cease we conclude that it be a company of wolf and fox for one tell we he have hear such a noise in Newfoundland about five a clock in the morning we begin to be stir upon a sudden we hear a great and strange cry which we know to be the same voice though they vary their note one of the company be abroad come run in and cry they be man indian indian and withal their arrow come fly among we our man run out with all speed to recover their arm the cry of our enemy be dreadful especial when our man run out to recover their arm their note be after this manner woath woach ha ha hach woach our man be no soon come to their arm but the enemy be ready to assault they there be a lusty man and no whit less valiant who be think to be their captain stand behind a tree within half a musket shoot of we and there let his arrow fly at we he stand three shot off a musket at length one take as he say full aim at he after which he give a extraordinary cry and away they go all we follow they about a quarter of a mile but we leave six to keep our shallop for we be careful of our business we take up eighteen of their arrow which we have send to England by master jones some whereof be head with brass other with heart horn and other with eagle claw many more no doubt be shoot for these we find be almost cover with leaf yet by the special providence of God none of they either hit or hurt we on Monday we find a very good a good harbour harbour for our ship we march also into the land and find diverse corn field and little run brook a place very good for situation so we return to our ship again with good news to the rest of our people which do much comfort their heart this harbour be a bay great than cape cod compass with a goodly land and in the bay two fine land uninhabited wherein be nothing but wood Okes pine wal-nut Beech sasifras vine and other tree which we know not this bay be a most hopeful place innumerable store of fowl and excellent good and can but be of fish in their season skote cod Turbot and herring we have taste of abundance of Mufles the great and best that ever we see crab and lobster in their time infinite it be in fashion like a Cikle or fish-hooke the eighteen we go along the coast in the wood some seven or eight mile but see not a indian nor a indian house only we find where former have be some inhabitant and where they have plant their corn we find not any navigable river but four or five small run brook of very fresh water that all run into the Sea the land for the crust of the earth be a spit depth excellent black mould and fat in some place two or three great oak but not very thick pine walnut Beech ash birch hasell holley asp sasifras in abundance and vine every where cherry-tree plum-tree and many other which we know not many kind of herb we find here in winter as strawberry leave innumerable Sorrell Yarow carvel brook-lime liver-wort water-cress great store of leek and onion and a excellent strong kind of flax and hemp here be sand gravel and excellent clay no better in the world excellent for pot and will wash like soap and great store of stone though somewhat soft and the best water that ever we drink and the brook now begin to be full of fish that night many be weary with march we go aboard again the nineteen of December after our land and view of the place so well as we can we come to a conclusion by most voice to set on the main land on the first place on a high ground where there be a great deal of land clear and have be plant with corn three or four year ago and there be a very sweet Brook run under the hill side and many delicate spring of as good water as can be drink and where we may harbour our shallop and boat exceed well and in this brook be much good fish in their season on the further side of the river also much corn ground clear in one field be a great hill on which we point to make a platform and plant our ordnance which will command all round about from thence we may see into the bay and far into the sea and we may see thence cape Cod. Saturday the three and twenty so many of we as can go on shore fell and carry timber to provide themselves stuff for building Monday the five and twenty we go on shore some to fell timber some to see some to rive and some to carry so no man rest all that day Monday the five and twenty be Christmas day we begin to drink water aboard but at night the master cause we to have some beer and so on board we have diverse time now and then some beer but on shore none at all we take notice how many family they be will all single man that have no wife to join with some family as they think fit that so we may build few house which be do and we reduce they to nineteen family to great family we allot large plot to every person half a pole in breadth and three in length and so lot be cast where every man shall lie which be do and stake out we think this proportion be large enough at the first for house and garden to impale they round consider the weakness of our people many of they grow ill with cold for our former discovery in frost and storm and the wade at cape Cod have bring much weakness among we which increase every day more and more and after be the cause of many of our death Friday and Saturday we fit ourselves for our labour but our people on shore be much trouble and discourage with rain and wet that day be very stormy and cold we see great smoke of fire make by the indian about six or seven mile from we as we conjecture Thursday the four of januarie captain Miles Standish with four or five more go to see if they can meet with any of the savage in that place where the fire be make they go to some of their house but not late inhabit yet can they not meet with any as they come home they shoot at a eagle and kill she which be excellent meat it be hardly to be discern from mutton Tuesday the nine of janury be a reasonable fair day and we go to labour that day in the build of our town in two row of house for more safety we divide by lot the plot of ground whereon to build our town after the proportion former allot we agree that every man shall build his own house think by that course man will make more haste than work in common the common house in which for the first we make our rendezvous be near finish want only cover it be about twenty foot square some shall make mortar and some gather thatch so that in four day half of it be thatch frost and foul weather hinder we much this time of the year seldom can we work half the week on the twelve day John goodman and Peter Browne at dinner time take their meat in their hand and will go walk and refresh themselves so go a little off they find a lake of water and have a great mastiff bitch with they and a spaniel by the water side they find a great d^ere the dog chase he and they follow sofar as they lose themselves and can not find the way back they wander all that afternoon be wet and at night do freeze and snow they be slender apparel and have no weapon but each one his cycle nor any victual they range up and down and can find none of the savage habitation when it draw to night they be much perplex for they can find neither harbour nor meat but in frost and snow be force to make the earth their bed and the element their cover and another thing do very much terrify they they hear as they think two lion roar exceed for a long time together and a three that they think be very near they so not know what to do they resolve to climb up into a tree as the safe refuge though that will prove a intolerable cold lodging they stand at the tree root that when the lion come they may take their opportunity of climb up the bitch they be fain to hold by the neck for she will have be go to the lion but it please God so to dispose that the wild beast come not so they walk up and down under the tree all night it be a extreme cold night so soon as it be light they travel again pass by many lake and brook and wood and in one place where the savage have burn the space of five mile in length which be a fine champion country and even in the afternoon it please God from a high hill they discover the two isle in the bay and so that night get to the plantation be ready to faint with travel and want of victual and almost famish with cold John goodman be fain to have his shoe cut off his foot they be so swell with cold and it be a long while after ere he be able to go the house be fire occasional by a spark that fly into the thatch which instant burn it all up but the roof stand and little hurt the most loss be master carver and William bradfords who then lie sick in bed and if they have not rise with good speed have be blow up with powder but through God mercy they have no harm the house be as full of bed as they can lie one by another and their musket charge but bless be God there be no harm do Monday the fifteen day it rain much all day that they on shipboard can not go on shore nor they on shore do any labour but be all wet Tuesday Wednesday Thursday be very fair sun-shiny day as if it have be in April and our people so many as be in health wrought cheerful the ninteenth day we resolve to make a shed to put our common provision in of which some be already set on shore but at noon it rain that we can not work this day in the evening John goodman go abroad to use his lame foot that be pitiful ill with the cold he have get have a little spaniel with he a little way from the plantation two great wolf run after the dog the dog run to he and betwixt his leg for succour two great wolf he have nothing in his hand but take up a stick and throw at one of they and hit he and they present run both away but come again he get a pail board in his hand and they sit both on their tail grin at he a good while and go their way and leave he Saturday the seventeen day in the morning we call a meeting for the establish of military order among ourselves and we choose Miles Standish our captain and give he authority of command in affair Saturday the three of march the wind be south the morning misty but towards noon warm and fair weather the bird sing in the wood most pleasant at one of the clock it thunder which be the first we hear in that country it be strong and great clap but short thunder but after a hour it rain very sad till midnight Wednesday the seven of march the wind be full east cold but fair Friday the sixteen there present himself a savage which cause a alarm he very bold come all alone and along the house straight to the rendezvous where we intercept he not conference with savage suffer he to go in as undoubted he will out of his boldness he salute we in english and bid we welcome for he have learn some break english among the englishman that come to fish at monhiggon and know by name the most of the captain commander and master that usual come he be a man free in speech so far as he can express his mind and of a seemly carriage we question he of many thing he be the first savage we can meet withal he say he be not of those part but of morattiggon and one of the sagamore or lord thereof have be eight month in these part it lie hence a day sail with a great wind and five day by land he discourse of the whole country and of every province and of their sagamore and their number of man and strength the wind beginning to rise a little we cast a horsemans coat about he for he be stark naked only a leather about his waist with a fringe about a span long or little more he have a bow and two arrow the one head and the other unheaded he be a tall straight man the hair of his head black long behind only short before none on his face at all he a^ked some beer but we give he strong-water and biscuit and butter and cheese and pudding and a piece of a mallerd all which he like well and have be acquaint with such among the english he tell we the place where we now live be call Patuxet and Patuxet people all dead of a plague that about four year ago all the inhabitant die of a extraordinary plague and there be neither man woman nor child remain as indeed we have round none so as there be none to hinder our possession or to lay claim unto it all the afternoon we spend in communication with he we will glad have be rid of he at night but he be not willing to go this night than we think to carry he on shipboard wherewith he be well content and go into the shallop but the wind be high and water scant that it can not return back we lodge that night at Steven Hopkins house and watch he the next day he go away back to the masasoyt from masasoyt whence he say he come who be our next border neighbour they be sixty strong as he say the nausite be as near southeast of they and be a hundred strong and those be they of nausite who our people be encounter as we before relate they be much incense and provoke against the english and about eight month ago slay three englishman and two more hardly escape by flight to monhiggon they be sir Ferdinando Gorge his man as this savage tell we as he do likewise of the huggery that be fight that our discoverer have with the nausite and of our tool they be take out of the wood which we will he shall be bring again otherwise we will right ourselves these people be ill affect towards the english by reason of one hunt a master of a ship who deceive the people and get they under colour of truck hunt wickedness with they twenty out of this very place where we inhabit and seven man from the nausite and carry they away and sell they for slave like a wretched man for twenty pound a man that care not what mischief he do for his profit Saturday in the morning we dismiss the savage and give he a knife a bracelet and a ring he promise within a night or two to come again and to bring with he some of the massasoyt our neighbour with such beaver skin as they have to truck with we Saturday and Sunday reasonable fair day on this day come again the savage and bring with he five other tall proper man they have every man a deer skin on he and the principal of they have a wild cat skin or such like on the one arm they have most of they long hose up to their groyne close make and above their groyne to their waist another leather they be altogether like the irish-trouse they be of complexion like our english gipsy no hair or very little on their face on their head long hair to the shoulder only cut before some truss up before with a feather broad wise like a fan another a fox tail hang out these leave according to our charge give he before their bow and arrow a quarter of a mile from our town we give they entertainment as we think be fit they they do eat liberal of our english victual they make semblance unto we of friendship and amity they sing and dance after this manner like S^u^ge^ describe antic they bring with he in a thing like a bow-case which the principal of they have about his waist a little of their corn pound to powder which put to a little water they eat he have a little tobacco in a bag but none of they drink but when he list some of they have their face paint black from the forehead to the chin four or five finger broad other after other fashion as they like they bring three or four skin but we will not truck with they all that day but wish they to bring more and we will truck for all which they promise within a night or two and will leave these behind they though we be not willing they shall and they bring all our tool again which be take in the wood in our man absence so because of the day we dismiss they so soon as we can but samoset our first acquaintance either be sick or feign himself so and will not go with they and stay with we till Wednesday morning then we send he to they to know the reason they come not according to their word and we give he a hat a pair of stocking and shoe a shirt and a piece of cloth to tie about his waist Thursday the 22. of march be a very fair warm day about noon we meet again about our public business but we have scarce be a hour together but samoset come again and the only native of where we now inhabit who be one of the twenty captive that by hunt be carry away and have be in England and dwell in Cornhill with master John slanie a merchant and hard by with quadequina his brother and all their man they can not well express in english what they will but after a hour the king come to the top of a hill over against we and have in his train with he which we do which be Edward Winsloe to know his mind and to signify the mind and will of our governor which be to have trade and peace with he we send to the king a pair of knife and a copper our messenger make a speech unto he that king JAMES salute he with word of love and peace and do accept of he as his friend and alley and that our governor desire to see he and to trocke with he and to confirm a peace with he as his next neighbour he like well of the speech and hear it attentive though the interpreter do not well express it after he have eat ^nd drink himself and give the rest to his company he look upon our messenger sword and armour which he have on with intimation of his desire to buy it but on the other side our messenger show his unwillingness to part with it in the end he leave he in the custody of quadequina his brother and come over the brook and some twenty man follow he leave all their bow and arrow behind they we keep six or seven as hostage for our messenger cap. Standish and m. williamson meet the king at the brook with half a dozen musketeer they salute he and he they so one go over the one on the one side and the other on the other conduct he to a house then in building where we place a green rug and three or four cushion then instant come our governor with a drum and trumpet after he and some few musketeer after salutation our governor kiss his hand the king kiss he and so they sit down the governor call for some strong water and drink to he and he drink a great draught that make he sweat all the while after he call for a little fresh meat which the king do eat willing and do give his follower then they treat of peace which be first that neither he nor any of he shall injure or do hurt to any of our people second and if any of his do hurt to any of we he shall send the offender that we may punish he three the agreement of peace between we and Massasoyt that if any of our tool be take away when our people be at work he shall cause they to be restore and if we do any harm to any of he we will do the like to they four if any do unjust war against he we will aid he if any do war against we he shall aid we five he shall send to his neighbour confederates to certify they of this that they may not wrong we but may be likewise comprise in the condition of peace six that when their man come to we they shall leave their bow and arrow behind they as we shall do our piece when we come to they last that do thus king JAMES will esteem of he as his friend and Ally all which the king seem to like well and it be applaud of his follower be no appearance of danger the next morning diverse of our people come over to we hope to get some victual as we imagine some of they tell we the king will have some of we come see he captain Standish that be at war with he against who he think we may be some strength to he for our piece be terrible unto they this morning they sta^ed till ten or eleven of the clock and our governor bid they send on with our common business from which we have be so often hinder by the savage come and conclude both of military order and of some law and order as we think behooveful for our present estate and condition and likewise choose our governor for this year which be master John carver a man well approve among we it seem good to the company for many consideration to send some among they to Massasoyt a journey to Packanokik the habitation of the great king Massasoy^ the great commander among the savage border about we partly to know where to find they if occasion serve as also to see their strength discover the country prevent abuse in their disorderly come unto we make satisfaction for some conceive injury to be do on our part and to continue the league of peace and friendship between and we they of our victual not doubt but we shall have enough where ere we come there we lodge in the open field for house they have none though they spend the most of the summer there the head of this river be report to be not far from the place of our abode upon it be and have be many town it be a good length the ground be very good on both side it be for the most part clear thousand of man savage seek lobster and send our two interpreter to speak with they the channel be between they where they tell they what we be and for what we be come will they not at all to fear we for we will not four pledge for they in the boate. they bring we to their Sachim or governor who they call jyanough a man not exceed twenty six year of age but very personable gentle courteous and fair condition indeed not like a savage save for his attire his entertainment be answerable to his part and his cheer plentiful and various one thing be very grievous unto we at this place there be a old woman who we judge to be no less than a hundred year old which come to see we because she never see english yet can not behold we without break forth into great passion weep and cry excessive we demand the reason of it they tell we she have three son who when master hunt be in these part go aboard his ship to trade with he and he carry they captive into Spain for at that time be carry away also by which mean she be deprive of the comfort of her child in her old age we tell they we be sorry that any Englishman shall give they that offence that hunt be a bad man and that all the english that hear of it condemn he for the same but for we we will not offer they any such injury though it will gain we all the skin in the country so we give she some small trifle which somewhat appease she after dinner we take boat for nauset jyanough and two of his man accompany we ere we come to nauset the day and tide be almost spend in so much as we can not go in with our shallop but the Sachim or governor of deliver and the manner of the messenger carriage relate he signify to the governor that to send the rattle snake skin in that manner import enmity and that it be no better than a challenge hereupon after some deliberation the governor stuff the skin with powder and shot and send it back return no less defiance to Conavacus assure he if he have ship now present thereby to send his man to nanohigganset the place of his abode they shall not need to come so far by land to we yet withal show that they shall never come unwelcome or unlooked for this message be send by a indian and deliver in such sort as it be no small terror to this savage king insomuch as he will not once touch the powder and shot or suffer it to stay in his house or country whereupon the messenger refuse it another take it up and have be post from place to place a long time at length come whole back again in the mean time know our own weakness notwithstanding our high word and lofty look towards they and still lie open to all casualty have as yet under God no other defence than our arm we think it most needful to impale our town which with all expedition we accomplish in the month of February and some few day take in the top town empale of the hill under which our town be seat make four bulwark or ietty without the ordinary circuit of the pale from whence we can defend the whole town in three whereof be gate and the four in time to be this be do captain Standish divide our strength into four squadron or company appoint who he think most fit to have command of each and at a general muster or train appoint each his place give each his company give they charge upon every alarm to resort to their leader to their appoint place and in his absence to be command and direct by they that do according to his order each draw his company to his appoint place for defence and there together discharge their musket after which they bring their new commander to their house where again they grace they with their shot and so depart fear also lest the enemy at any time shall take any advantage by fire our house captain Standish appoint a certain company that whensoever they see or hear fire to be cry in the town shall only betake themselves to their arm and shall enclose the house or place so endanger and stand aloof on their guard with their back towards the fire to prevent treachery if any be in that kind intend if the fire be in any of the house of this guard they be then free from it but not otherwise without special command long before this time we promise the people of Massachuset in the country for my consort and hobbamocke for our guide so we set forward and lodge the first night at namasket where we have friendly entertainment the next day about one of the clock we come to a ferry in conbatant country where upon discharge of my piece diverse indian come to we from a house not far off there they tell we that massassowat be dead and that day bury and that the dutch will be go before we can get thither have hove off their ship already this news strike we blank but especial hobbamocke report of massassowats death who desire we may return with all speed I tell he I will first think of it consider now that he be dead combatant be the most like to succeed he and that we be not above three mile from mattapuyst his dwell place although he be but a hollow-hearted friend towards we I think no time so fit as this to enter into more friendly term with he and the rest of the sachims thereabout hope through the blessing of God it will be a mean in that unsettle state to settle their affection towards we and though it be somewhat dangerous in respect of our personal safety because myself and hobbamocke have be employ upon a service against he which he may now fit revenge yet esteem it the best mean leave the event to God in his mercy i resouled to put it in practice if master hamden and Hobbamock dare attempt it with i who I find willing to that or any other course may tend to the general good so we go towards Mattapuyst in the way hobbamocke manifest a trouble spirit break forth into these speech neen etc. his commendation my love Sachim my love Sachim many have I know but never any like thou and turn he to i say while I live I shall never see his like among the indian say he be no liar he be not bloody and cruel like other indian in anger and passion he be soon reclaim easy to be reconcile towards such as have offend he rule by reason in such measure as he will not scorn the advice of mean man and that he govern his man better with few stroke than other do with many true love where he love yea he fear we have not a faithful friend leave among the indian show how he ofttimes restrain their malice etc. continue a long speech with such sign of lamentation and unfeigned sorrow as it will have make the hard heart relent at length we come to mattapuy and go to the Sachimo for so they call the sachims place though they call a ordinary house Witeo but combatant the Sachim be not at home but at Puckanokick which be some five or six mile off the squa-sachim for so they call sachims wife give we friendly entertainment here we inquire again concern massassowat they think he dead but know no certainty whereupon I hire one to go with all expedition to puckanokick that we may know the certainty thereof and withal to acquaint combatant with our there be about half a hour before sunsetting the messenger return and tell we that he be not yet dead though there be no hope we shall find he live upon this we be much reviue and set forward with it distemper we that be well and therefore unlike to ease he that be sick about he be six or eight woman who chafe his arm leg and thigh to keep heat in he when they have make a end of their charm one that the governor hear of his sickness be sorry for the same and though by reason of many business he can not come himself yet he send i with such thing for he as he think most likely to do he good in this extremity and whereof if he please to take I will present give he which he desire and have a confection of many comfortable conserve on the point of my knife I give he some which I can scarce get through his tooth when it be dissolve in his mouth he swallow the juice of it whereat those that be about he much rejoice say he have not swallow any thing in two day before then I desire to see his mouth which be exceed fur and his tongue swell in such manner as it be not possible for he to eat such meat as they have his passage be stop up then I wash his mouth and scrape his tongue and get abundance of corruption out of the same after which I give he more of the confection which he swallow with more readiness then he desire to drink I dissolve some of it in water and give he thereof within half a hour this wrought a great alteration in he in the eye of all that behold he present after his sight begin to come to he in the mean time I inquire how he sleep and when he go to stool they say he sleep not in two day before and have not have a stool in five then I give he more and tell he of a mishap we have by the way in break a bottle of drink which the governor also send he say if he will send any of his man to Patuxet I will send for more of the same also for chicken to make he broth and for other thing which I know be good for he and will stay the return of the messenger if he desire this he take marvelous kind and appoint some who be ready to go by two of the clock in the morning against which time I make ready a letter declare therein our good success the state of his body etc. desire to send such thing as I send for and such physic as the surgeon dare administer to he he request i that the day follow I will take my piece and kill he some fowl and make he some they date come among we the month of April be now come on all hand we begin to prepare for corne. and because there be no corn leave before this time save that be preserve for seed be also hopeless an. 1623. of relief by supply we think best to leave off all other work and prosecute that as most necessary and because there be no small hope of do good in that common course of labour that former we be in for that the governor that follow man to their labour have nothing to give man for their necessity and therefore can not so well exercise that command over they therein as former they have do especial consider that self-love wherewith every man in a measure more or less love and prefer his own good before his neighbour and also the base disposition of some drone that as at other time so now especial will be most burdenous to the rest it be therefore think best that every man shall use the best diligence he can for his own preservation both in respect of the time present and to prepare his own corn for the year follow and bring in a competent portion for the maintenance of public officer fisherman etc. which can not be free from their call without great inconvenience this course be to continue till harvest and then the governor to gather in the appoint portion for the maintenance of themselves and such other as necessity constrain to exempt from this condition in the midst of April we begin to set the weather be then seasonable which much encourage we give we good hope of after plenty the set season be good till the latter end of may. but it please God for our further chastisement to send a great drought insomuch as in six week after the late set there scarce fall any rain so that the stalk of that be first set begin to send forth the ear before it come to half growth and that which be late not like to great drought yield any at all both blade and stalk hang the head and change the colour in such manner as we judge it utter dead our bean also run not up according to their wont manner but stand at a stay many be parch away as though they have be soorch before the fire now be our hope overthrow and we discourage our joy be turn into mourn to add also to this sorrowful estate in which we be we hear of a supply that be send unto we many month since which have two repulse before be a three time in company of another ship three hundred league at sea and now in three month time hear no further of she only the sign of a wrack be see on the coast which can not be judge to be any other than the same these and the like consideration move not only every good man private to enter into examination with his own estate between God and his conscience and so to humiliation before he but also more solemn to humble ourselves together before the lord by fast and prayer to that end a day be appoint by public authority and set a part from all other employment hope public fast. that the same god which have stir we up hereunto will be move hereby in mercy to look upon we and grant the request of our deject soul if our continuance there may any way stand with his glory and our good but oh the mercy of our God who be as ready to hear as we to ask for though in the morning when we assemble together the heaven be as clear and the drought as like to continue as ever it be yet our exercise continue some eight or nine gracious dew hour before our departure the weather be overcast the cloud gather together on all side and on the next morning distil such soft sweet and moderate shower of rain continue some fourteen day and mix with such seasonable weather as it be hard to say whether our wither corn or droop affection be most quicken or reviue such be the bounty and goodness of our God of this the indian by mean of Hobbamock take notice who be then in the town and this exercise in the midst of the week say it be but three day since Sunday and therefore demand of a boy what be the reason thereof which when he know and see what effect follow thereupon he and all they admire the goodness of our god towards we that wrought so great a change in so short a time show the difference between indian conjuration their conjuration and our invocation on the name of God for rain they being mix with such storm and tempest as sometime in stead of do they good it lay the corn flat on the ground to their prejudice but we in so gentle and Tomson a scot his plantation Tomson a Scotchman who also that spring begin a plantation twenty five league north-east from we near smith isle at a place call pascatoquack where he like well now also hear we of the three repulse that our supply have of their safe though dangerous return into England and of their preparation to come to we so that have these many sign of God favour and acceptation we think it will be great ingratitude if secret we shall smother up the same or content ourselves with private thanksgiving for that which by private prayer can day of thanks not be obtain and therefore another solemn day be set apart for that end wherein we return glory honour and praise with all thankfulness to our good God which deal so gracious with we who name for these and all other his mercy towards his church and choose one by they be bless and praise now and evermore amen in the latter end of july and the beginning of August come two ship with supply unto we two ship who bring all their passenger except one in health who recover in short time who also notwithstanding all our want and hardship bless be God find not any one sick person among we at the plantation the big ship call the Anne be hire and there again freight back from whence we set sail the ten of September the lesser call the little james be build for the company at their charge she be now also fit for trade and discovery to the southward of cape cod and almost ready to set sail who I pray God to bless in her good and lawful proceed a few thing I think meet to add hereunto which I have observe among the indian both touch their religion and sundry other custom among they and first whereas myself and other in former letter which come to the press against my their religion the meaning of the word ^^e^tan I think have reference ^o antiquity for chise be a old man and ki^hchise a man that exceed in ag^ will and knowledge write that the indian about we be a people without any religion or knowledge of any god therein I err though we can then gather no better for as they conceive of many divine power so of one who they call Kiehtan to be the principal maker of all the rest and to be make by none he they say create the heaven earth sea and all creature contain therein also that he make one man and one woman of who they and we and all mankind come but how they become so far disperse that know they not at first they say there be no Sachim or king but Kiehtan who dwell above the heaven whither all good man go when they die to see their friend and have their fill of all thing this his habitation lie westward in the heaven they say thither the bad man go also and knock at his door but he bid they Quachet that be to say walk abroad for there be no place for such so that they wander in restless want and penury never man see this kiehtan only old man tell they of he and bid they tell their child yea to charge they to teach their posterity the same and lay the like charge upon they this power they acknowledge to be good and when they will obtain any great matter meet together and cry unto he and so likewise for plenty victory etc. sing dance feast give thanks and hang up garland and other thing in memory of the same another power they worship who they call Hobbamock and to the nothward of we Hobbamoqui their devil this as far as we can conceive be the he they call upon to cure their wound and diseale when they be curable he persuade they he send the same for some conceive anger against they but upon their call upon he can and do help they but when they be mortal and not curable in nature than he persuade they Kiehtan be angry and send they who none can cure insomuch as in that respect only they somewhat doubt whether he be simple good and therefore in sickness never call upon he this hobbomock appear in sundry form unto they as in the shape of a man a dear a fawn a eagle etc. but most ordinary a snake he appear not to all but the chief and most judicious among they though all of they strive to attain to that hellish height of honour he appear most ordinary and be most conversant with three sort of people one I confess I neither know by name nor office direct of these they have few but esteem high of they and think that no weapon can kill they another they call by the name of Powah and the three pniese the office and duty of the Powah be to be exercise principal in call upon the devil and Powah or priest cure disease of the sick or wound the common people join with he in the exercise of invocation but do but only assent or as we term it say amen to that he say yet sometime break out into a short musical note with he the Powah be eager and free in speech fierce in countenance and join many antic and laborious gesture with the same over the party disease if the party be wound he will also seem to suck the wound but if they be curable as they say he touch it not but a skooke that be the snake or Wobsacuck that be the eagle sit on his shoulder and lick the same this none see but the Powah who tell they he do it himself if the party be otherwise disease it be account sufficient if in any shape he but come into the house take it for a undoubted sign of recovery and as in former age Apollo have his temple at Delphos and Diana at Ephesus so have I hear they call upon some as if they have their residence in some certain place or because they appear in those form in the same in the powahs speech he promise to sacrifice many skin of beast kettle hatchet bead knife and other the best thing they have to the fiend if he will come to help the party disease but whether they perform it I know not the other offering practice I have see be necessary call at some time to be with their sick and have use the best argument I can make they understand against the same they have tell i I shall see the devil at those time come to the party but I assure myself and they of the contrary which so prove yea themselves have confess they never see he when any of we be present in desperate and extraordinary hard travel in childbirth when the party can be deliver by the ordinary mean they send for this Powah though ordinary their travel be not so extreme as in our part of the world they be of a more hardy nature for on the three day after childbirth I have see the mother with the infant upon a small occasion in cold weather in a boat upon the Sea many sacrifice the indian use and in some case kill child it seem they be various in their religious worship in a little distance and grow more and more cold in their worship to sacrifice Kiehtan say in their memory he be much more call upon the nanohigganset exceed in their blind devotion and have a great spacious house wherein only some few that be as we may term they priest come thither at certain know time resort all their people and offer almost all the riches they have to their god as kettle skin hatchet bead knife etc. all which be cast by the priest into a great fire that they make in the midst of the house and there consume to ash to this offering every man bring free and the more he be know to bring have the better esteem of all man this the other indian about we approve of as good burn offering the devil keep his servant poor and wish their sachims will appoint the like and because the plague have not reign at nanohigganset as at other place about they they attibute to this custom there use the paniese be man of great courage and wisdom and to these also the devil appear more familiar then to other and as we conceive make covenant with they to preserve their knight pniese valorous counselor they from death by wound with arrow knife hatchet etc. or at least both themselves and especial the people think themselves to be free from the same and though against their battle all of they by paint disfigure themselves yet they be know by their courage and boldness by reason whereof one of they will chase almost a hundred man for they account it death for whosoever stand in their way these be high esteem of all sort of people and be of the sachims council without who they will not war or undertake any weighty business in war their sachims for their more safety go in the midst of they they be common man of great stature and strength and such as will endure most hardness and yet be more discreet courteous and humane in their carriage then any among they scorn theft lie and the like base deal and stand as much upon their reputation as any man and to the end they may have store of these they train up the most forward and likely boy from their childhood in great hardness and make they abstain from dainty meat observe diverse order prescribe to the end that when they be of age the devil may appear to they cause to drink the juice of sentry and other bitter herb till they cast which they must disgorge into bitter trial the platter and drink again and again till at length through extraordinary press of nature it will seem to be all blood and this the boy will do with eagerness at the first and so continue till by reason of faintness they can scarce stand on their leg and then must go forth into the cold also they beat their shin with stick and cause they to run through bush stump and bramble to make they hardy and acceptable to the devil that in time he may appear unto they their sachims can be all call king but only some few of they to who the rest resort Sachim or lord for protection and pay homage unto they neither may they war without their knowledge and approbation yet to be command by the great as occasion serve of this sort be massassowat our friend and Conanacus of our suppose enemy every Sachim take care for the widow and fatherless also for such as be age and any way maim if their friend be dead or not able to provide for they a Sachim will not take any to wife but such a one as be equal to he in birth otherwise they say their seed will in time become ignoble and though they have many other wife yet be they no other than concubine or servant and yield a kind of obedience to the principal who order the family and they in it the like their man observe also and will adhere to the first during their life but put away the other at their pleasure this government be successive and not by choice if the father die before the son or daughter be of age than the child be commit to the protection and tuition of some one among they who rule in his stead till he be of age but when that be I know not every Sachim know how far the bound and limit of his own country extend and that be his own proper inheritance out or that if any of his man desire land to set their corn he give they as much as they can use and set they in their bound in this circuit whosoever hunt if any kill any venison bring he his fee which be four part of the same if it be kill on the land but if in the water than the skin thereof the great sachims or king know not their own bound or limit of land as well as the rest all traveller or stranger for the most part lodge at the sachims when they come they tell they how long they will stay and to what place they go during which time they receive entertainment according to their person but want not once a year the pniese use to provoke the people to (...) bestow much corn on the Sachim to that end they appoint a certain time and place near the sachims dwelling where the people bring many basket of corn and make a great stack thereof there the pniese stand ready to give thanks to the people on the sachims behalf and after acquaint the Sachim therewith who fetch the same and be no less thankful bestow many gift on they when any be visit with sickness their friend resort unto they for their comfort and continue with they oftentimes till their death or recovery if they die they stay a certain time to mourn fo^ the dead mourn for they night and morning they perform this duty many day after the burial in a most doleful manner insomuch as though it be ordinary and the note musical which they take one from another and altogether yet it will draw tear from their eye and almost from we also but if they recover then because their sickness be chargeable they send corn and other gift unto they at a certain appoint time whereat they feast and dance which they call Commoco when they bury the dead they sow up the corpse in a mat and so put it in the earth if the party burial be a Sachim they cover he with many curious mat and bury all his riches with he and enclose the grave with a pale if it be a child the father will also put his own most special jewel and ornament in the earth with it also he will cut his hair and disfigure himself very much in token of sorrow if it be the man or woman of the house they will pull down the mat and leave the frame stand and bury they in or near the same and either remove their dwell or give over housekeeping the man employ themselves whole in hunt and other exercise of the bow except at some time they take some pain in fish the woman live a most slavish life they carry all woman slavery their burden set and dress their corn gather it in and seek out for much of their food beat and make ready the corn to eat and have all household care lie upon they the young sort reverence the elder and do all mean office whilst they be together although they be stranger boy and girl may not wear their hair like man and woman but be distinguish thereby a man be not account a man till he do some notable act or show forth such courage and resolution manhood as become his place the man take much tobacco but for boy so to do they account it odious all their name be significant and variable for when they come to the state of man and woman name they alter they according to their deed or disposition when a maid be take in marriage she first cut her hair and after wear a cover maid and wife on her head till her hair be grow out their woman be diverse dispose some as modest as they will scarce talk one with another in the company of man be very chaste also yet other some light lascivious and wanton if a woman have a bad husband or can affect he and there be war or opposition between that and any other people she will run away from he to the contrary party and there live where they never come unwelcome for where be most woman there be great plenty when a woman have her monthly term she separate herself from all other company and live certain day in a house alone after which she wash herself and all that she have touch or use and be again receive to her husband bed or family for adultery the husband will beat his wife and put she away if he please some common strumpet there be as well as in other place but they be such as either never marry or adultery and whoredom widow or put away for adultery for no man will keep such a one to wife in matter of unjust and dishonest deal the Sachim examine and punish the same in case of theft for the first offence he be disgraceful rebuke for the second beat by the Sachim theft with a cudgel on the naked back for the three he be beat with many stroke and have his nose slit up ward that thereby all man may both know and shun he if any man kill another he must likewise die for the same the Sachim not only pass the sentence upon malefactor murder but execute the same with his own hand if the party be then present if not send his own knife in case of death in the hand of other to perform the same but if the offender be to receive other punishment he will not receive the same but from the Sachim himself before who be naked he kneel and will not offer to run away though he beat he never so much it be a great disparagement for a man to cry during the time of his correction then be his offence and punishment cry a coward note as for their apparel they wear breech and stocking in one like some irish which be make of dear skin and have shoe of the same leather they wear also a deer skin loose about apparel they like a cloak which they will turn to the weather side in this habit they travel but when they be at home or come to their journey end present they pull of their breech stocking and shoe wring out the water if they be wet and dry they and rub or chafe the same though these be off yet have they another small garment that cover their secret the man wear also when they go abroad in cold weather a otter or fox skin on their right arm but only their bracer on the left woman and all of that sex wear string about their leg which the man never do the people be very ingenious and observative they keep account of time by the moon and winter or summer they know diverse of the star by name in particular they know the witty people their Arts. note north-star and call it mask which be to say the bear also they have many name for the wind they will guess very well at the wind and weather before hand by observation in the heaven they report also that some of they can cause the wind to blow in what part they lift can raise storm and tempest which they usual do when they intend the death or destruction of other people that by reason of the unseasonable weather they may take advantage of their enemy in their house at such time they perform their great exploit and in such season when they be at enmity with any they keep more careful watch then at other time as for the language it be very copious large and difficult as yet we can attain to any great measure thereof but can understand they and explain ourselves to their understanding language by the help of those that daily converse with we and though there be difference in a hundred mile distant of place both in language and manner yet not so much but that they very well understand each other and thus much of their life and manner in stead of record and chronicle they take this course where any remarkable act be do in memory of it either in the place or by some pathway near adjoin they make a round register hole in the ground about a foot deep and as much over which when other pass by behold they inquire the cause and occasion of the same which be once know they be careful to acquaint all man as occasion serve therewith and lest such hole shall be fill or grow up by any accident as man pass by they will oft renew the same by which mean many thing of great antiquity be fresh in memory so that as a man travel if he can understand his guide his journey will be the less tedious by reason of many historical discourse will be relate unto he for that continent on which we be call New-england although it have ever be conceive by the english to be a part of the main land adjoin to Virginia yet by relation of the country the indian it shall appear to be otherwise for they affirm confident that it be a island and that either the dutch or french pass through from sea to sea between we and Uirginia and drive a great trade in the same the name of that inlet of the sea they call mohegon which I new England a island take to be the same which we call hudsons river up which master Hudson go many league and for want of mean as I hear leave it undiscovered for confirmation of this their opinion be thus much though Virginia be not above a hundred and fifty league from we yet they never hear of powhatan or know that any english be plant in his country save only by we and who go into a english ship thither and therefore it be the more probable because the water be not passable for they who be very adventurous in their boates. then for the temperature of the air in almost three year experience I can scarce distinguish new England from old England in respect of heat and cold frost snow rain wind etc. some object because our plantation lie in the latitude of two and forty it must needs be much ^otter I confess I can give the reason of the contrary only experience teach we that if it do exceed England it be so little as must require better judgement to discern it and season for the winter I rather think if there be difference it be both sharp and long in new England then old and yet the want of those comfort in the one which I have enjoy in the other may deceive my judgement also but in my best observation compare our own condition with the relation of other part of America I can conceive of any to agree better with the constitution of the english not be oppress with extremity of heat nor nip with bite cold by which mean bless be God we enjoy our health notwithstanding those difficulty we have undergo in such a measure as will have be admire if we have live in England with the like mean the day be two hour long than here when it be at the short day and as much short when it be at the long the soil be variable in some place mould in some clay and other a mix sand etc. the soil chief grain be the indian may or ginny-wheat the seedtime begin in the midst of April corn and continue good till the midst of may. our harvest begin with September this corn increase in great measure but be inferior in quantity to the same in Virginia the reason I conceive be because Uirginia be far hot than it be with we it require great heat to ripen but whereas it be object against new England that corn will not there grow except the ground be manure with fish I answer that where man set with fish as with we it be more easy so to do then to clear ground and set without some five or six year and so begin a new as in Virginia and elsewhere not but that in some place where they can be take with ease in such abundance the indian set four year together without and have as good corn or better than we have that set with they though indeed I think if we have cattle to till the ground it will be more profitable and better agreeable to the soil to sow wheat rye barley pease and oat then to set may which our indian call Ewachim for we have have experience that they like and thrive well and the other will not be procure without good labour and diligence especial at seedtime when it must also be watch by night to keep the wolf from the fish till it be rot which will be in fourteen day yet man agree together and take their turn it be not much much may be speak of the benefit that may come to such as shall here plant by trade with the indian for fur if man take a right course for obtain the same for I dare presume upon that small experience I have have to affirm that the english dutch and french return yearly many thousand pound profit by trade only from that island on which we be seat tobacco may be there plant but not with that profit as in some other place neither be it profitable there to follow it though the increase be equal because fish be a better and rich commodity and more necessary which may be and there be have in as great abundance as in any other part of the world witness the west-country merchant of England which return incredible gain yearly from thence and if they can so do which here buy their salt at a great charge and transport more company to make their voyage then will sail their ship what may the planter expect when once they be seat and make the most of their salt there and employ themselves at lest eight month in fish whereas the other fish but four and have their ship lie dead in the harbour all the time whereas such ship as belong to plantation may take freight of passenger or cattle thither and have their lade provide against they come I confess we have come so far short of the mean to raise such return as with great difficulty we have preserve our life insomuch as when I look back upon our condition and weak mean to preserve the same I rather admire at God mercy and providence in our preservation then that no great thing have be effect by we but though our beginning have be thus raw small and difficult as thou have see yet the same god that have hitherto lead we through the former I hope w^ll raise mean to accomplish the latter chap. 5 scotia the king patent to sir WILLIAM ALEXANDER knight non^ this scale contain 150 english league the three and twenty of june they loose from saint john harbour in Newfoundland an. 1623. and sail towards new Scotland where for the space of fourteen day they be by fog and contrary wind keep back from spy land till the eight of july thereafter that they see the west part of cape Breton and so till the thirteen day they sail to and fro alongst the coast till they come the length of port mutton where they discover three very pleasant harbour and go a shore in one of they which they call Luke bay where they find a great way up to a very pleasant river be three fathom Luke Bay deep at low water at the entry thereof and on every side of the same they do see very delicate meadow have rose white and red grow thereon with a kind of wild lily which have a very dainty smell the next day they resolve to coast alongst to discover the next harbour which be but two league distant from the other where they find a more pleasant river be four fathom water at a low water with meadow on both side thereof have rose and lily grow thereon as the other have they find within this river a very fit place for a plantation both in regard that it be natural apt to be fortify and that all the ground beweene the two fit place for a plantation river be without wood and be good fat earth have several sort of berry grow thereon as gooseberry strawberry Hyndberry Rasberry and a kind of red-wineberry as also some sort of grain as pease some ear of wheat barley and rye grow there wild the pease grow every where in abundance very big and good to eat but taste of the fitch this river be call port jolly from whence they coast alongst to port negro be port jolly port negro 12. league distant where all the way as they sail alongst they find a very pleasant country have grow every where such thing as they do see in the two harbour where they have be they find like wise in every river abundance of lobster and cockle and other small fish and also they find not only in the river but all the coast alongst number of several sort of wild-fowl as wild-goose black-duck woodcock herron pigeon and many other sort of fowl which they know not they find likewise as they sail alongst the coast abundance of great God with several other sort of great fish the country be full of wood not very thick and the most part oak the rest fir-tree Spruce birch and many other sort of wood which they have not see before have discover this part of the country in regard of the voyage their ship be to make to the strait with fish they resolve to coast alongst from Luke bay to port the mutton be four league to the east thereof where they encounter with a Frenchman that in a very short time have a great voyage have furnish one ship away with fish and have never so many ready as to load his own ship and other and have take a view of this port which to their judgement they find no way inferior to the rest they have see before they resolve to retire back to Newfoundland where their ship be to receive her load of fish the twenty of july they loose from thence and the seven and twenty thereof they arrive at saint john harbour in Newfoundland and from thence sail alongst the bay of conception where they leave the ship and dispatch themselves home in several ship that belong to the west part of England and do intend this next spring to set forth a Quibequesson river the description of the country of Mawooshen discover by the english in the year 1602. 3. 5. 6. 7. 8. and 9 MAwooshen be a country lie to the north and by east of Uirginia between the degree of 43. and 45. it be forty league broad and fifty in length lie in breadth east and west and in length north and south it be border on the east side with a country the people whereof they call tarrantine on the west with epistoman on the north with a great wood call Senaglecoune and on the south with the main ocean sea and many land in Mawooshen it seem there be nine river whereof the first to the east be call Quibiquesson on which there be one town wherein dwell two Sagamos or lord the one call the other Abermot in this town be fifty house and 150. man the name of which town be this river run far up into the main at the head thereof there be a Sagamo lake of a great length and breadth it be at the fall into the sea ten fathom deep and half a a great lake mile over the next be pemaquid a goodly river and very commodious all thing consider it be ten fathom 2. P^maquid river water at the entrance and forty mile up there be two fathom and a half at low water it be half a mile broad and run into the land north many day journey where be a great lake of 18. league long and four broad in this lake be seven great land towards the far a great lake end there falleeh in a river which they call acaconstome where they pass with their boat thirty day journey up and from thence they go over land twenty day journey more and then come to another river where they have a trade with Anadabis or Anadabijon with who the frenchman have have commerce for a long time near to the north of this river of pemaquid be three town the first be Upsegon where bashabe their chief lord do dwell and in this three town town be sixty house and 250. man it be three day journey within the Land the second be caiocame the three shasheekeing these two last town be opposite one to the other the river bashabe caiocame divide they both and they be two day journey from the town of bashabe in (...) dwell and in shasheoke bowant two Sagamos subject to bashabe upon both side of this river up to the very lake for a good distance the ground be plain without tree or bush but full of long grass like unto a pleasant meadow which the inhabitant do burn once a year to have fresh feed for their deer beyond this meadow be great wood whereof more shall be speak hereafter the river of pemaquid be four day journey from the mouth of Quibiquesson the three river be call Ramassoc and be distant from the mouth of pemaquid four day journey it be twenty fathom at the entrance and have a mile over it run into the land three 3. Ramassoc day journey and within less than a day journey of the dwell of bashabe upon this river there be a town name Panobscot the lord whereof be call Sibatahood who have in his town panobsc^t a town 4. apanawapeske fifty house and eighty man the four river apanawapeske lie west and by south of Ramassoc at the entrance whereof there be twenty fathom water and it be a mile broad it run up into the country five day journey and within three day of the mouth be two town the one call meecombe where dwell Aramasoga who have in his town fifty house and eighty man the other be chebegnadose who lord be skanke and have thirty house and ninety man the mouth of apanawapeske be distant from Ramassoc three day journey to the south-west four day journey there be another excellent river in the entrance whereof be twenty fathom water and it be a quarter of a mile broad it run into the land 5. Apanmensek two day journey and then there be a great fall at the head whereof there be a lake of a day journey long and as much in breadth on the side of this lake there be a straight and at the end of a l^ke that straight there be another lake of four day journey long and two day journey broad wherein there be two land one at the one end and another at the other end I shall have tell you another lake all the lake full of fish beef and sweet rat 6. Aponeg that both these lake as also the rest former speak of do infinite abound with fresh water fish of all sorts^ as also with diverse sort of creature as otter beef sweet rat and such like the six river be call apponick on which there be three town the first be call Appisham where dwell abochigishic the second be Mesaqueegamic where dwell Amniquin in which there be seventy house and eighty man the three be matammiscowte in which be eighty house and ninety man and there dwell narracommique to the westward of this there be another river call aponeg it have at the entrance ten fathom 7. Aponeg water and be a mile broad it run up into a great sound of fresh water upon the east side of this river there be two town the one call Nebamocago the other call Ashawe in the first dwell mentaurmet and have in his town 160. household and some 300. man in the second dwell Hamerhaw and have in his town eighty household and seventy man on the west side there be another town call Neredoshan where be 120. household and 100 man there be a Sagamo or lord call Sabenaw three day journey from aponeg to the westward there be a goodly river call Sagadohoc the entrance whereof be a mile and a half over hold that breadth a day journey and then 8. John Guy of Bristol do write a treatise to animate the english to plant there a write copy whereof I have a. 1610. it please his most excellent majesty to grant a patent for a plantation part whereof the whole may seem too long for our purpose we have insert chap. 7 the beginning of the patent for Newfoundland and the plantation there make by the english 1610. deliver in a letter date thence from m. GVY to m. slany also of the weather the three first winter and of captain WESTON with other remarkable occurrent JAMES by the grace of GOD of great Britain France and Ireland king defendor of the faith etc. to all people to who these present shall come greeting know you whereas diverse our love and well dispose subject be desirous to make plantation to inhabit and to establish a colony or colonies in the southern and eastern part of the country and i will or land common call Newfoundland unto the coast and harbour whereof the subject of this our realm of England have for the space of fifty year and upward yearly use to resort in no small number to fish intend by such plantation and inhabit both to secure and make safe the say trade of fish to our subject for ever and also to make some commendable benefit for the use of mankind by the land and profit thereof which hitherto from the beginning as it seem manifest have remain unprofitable and for better performance of such their purpose and intention have humble beseech our regal authority and assistance we be well assure that the same land or country adjoin to the foresay coast where our subject use to fish remain so destitute and desolate of inhabitant that scarce any one savage person have in many year be see in the most part thereof and well know that the same lie and be so vacant be as well for the reason aforesaid as for many other reason very commodious for and our dominion and that by the law of nature and nation we may of our royal authority possess ourselves and make grant thereof without do wrong to any other prince or state consider they can just pretend any sovereignty or right thereunto in respect that the same remain so vacant and not actual possess and inhabit by any christian or other whosoever and therefore think it a matter and action well beseem a christian king to make true use of that which God from the beginning create for mankind and therefore intend not only to work and procure the benefit and good of many of our subject but principal to increase the knowledge of the omnipotent God and the propagation of our christian faith have gracious accept of their say intention and suit and therefore do of our special grace certain knowledge and mere motion for we our heir and successor give grant and confirm by these present unto our right dear and right well-beloved cousin and counsellor Henry earl of Northampton keeper of our privy seal and to our trusty and right well-beloved sir Laurence tanfield knight chief baron of our exchequer sir John dodridge knight one of our sergeant at law sir Francis Bacon knight our solicitor general sir Daniel Dun sir Walter cope sir Piercivall Willoughby and sir John Constable knight John weld esquire William freeman Ralph freeman
