common call new find land which be situate lie and be to the southward of the parallel line to be conceive to pass by the cape or hedland common call or know by the name of bonewist inclusive which cape or hedland be to be northward of the bay common call Trinity bay and also which be situate lie and be to the eastward of the meridian line to be conceive to pass by the cape or headland common call or know by the name of cape Maria or cape saint Mary inclusive which cape or headland be to be eastward of the bay common call the bay of Placentia together with the sea and land lie within ten league of any part of the sea coast of the country aforesaid and also all those country land and land common call newfound land which be situate between forty and six degree of northerly latitude and two and fifty degree of the like latitude and also all the land soil ground haven port river mine as well royal mine of gold and silver as other mine mineral pearl and precious stone wood quarry marsh water fish hunt hawk fowl commodity and hereditament whatsoever together with all prerogative jurisdiction royalty privilege franchise and preeminency within any the say territory and the precinct there of whatsoever and thereto or there about both by sea and land be or in any sort belong or appertain and which we by our letter patent may or can grant and in as ample manner and sort as we or any of our noble progenitor have heretofore grant to any company body politic or corporate or to any adventurer or adventurer undertaker or undertaker of any discovery plantation or traffic of in or into any foreign part whatsoever and in as large and ample manner as if the same be herein particular mention and express nevertheless our will and pleasure be and we do by these present express and declare that there be save and reserve unto all manner of person of what nation soever and also to all and every our love subject which do at this present or hereafter shall trade or voyage to the part aforesaid for fish etc. April 27. a. reg. 8. master JOHN GVY his letter to master slany treasurer and to the counsel of the Newfoundland plantation right worshipful it may please you to understand that it be the ten day of this month of May before the bark of Northam call the consent arrive here in Newfoundland notwithstanding that a ship of Bristol call the lioness come to this country the second of May in a month space and the trial of Dartmouth arrive here before in sixteen day by reason of which voyage in eight day stay of the aforesaid bark nothing can be do to take any of the place desire all be possess before so that the ship that come whereof as yet there be no news be to trust to the place here which be reserve for she which I hope will prove a good place some year as great a uoyage have be make here as in any place in this land God send she hither in safety I have not yet see any of the country to the southward or northward of this bay of conception since this spring because I expect daily the arrival of the bark and think it not fit to be absent herehence until she be arrive and dispatch but present upon her departure no time God will shall be lose the care that be take to require general the fisherman to assist we and to supply our want if any shall be be most joyful fisherman kind assistance and comfortable to we which be most willing accomplish by the most part of those which I have yet see yet God be praise such be the state of all thing with we as we be in no want of victual but have a great remainder as you shall after understand the state of the autumn and winter be in these part of Newfoundland after this manner in state of the weather in autumn and winter I have by i a write journal declare the wind and weather of every day from 24. November 1610. till the last of April 1611. but thought it will seem tedious the substance thereof be here contain moderate Frosta both the month of October and November there be scarce six day wherein it either freeze or snow and that so little that present it be thaw and melt with the strength of the sun all the residue of the afore say two month be both warm and dry than in England in December we have sometime fair weather sometime frost and snow and sometime open weather and rain for in the latter end it be rainy and be open weather all these three month the wind be so variable as it will every fortnight visit all the point of the compass the most part of january and February unto the middle of march the frost continue the wind be for the most part westerly and now and then northerly notwithstanding three or four time when the wind be at south it begin to thaw and do rain that which fall in this season be for the most part snow which with the heat of the sun will be consume in the open place within a few day that which abode long be in February during this time many day the sun shine warm and bright from morning to night notwithstanding the length of this frosty weather small brook that do run almost in level with a slow course be not the whole winter three night over freeze so thick as that the ice can bear a dog to go over it which I find by good proof for every morning I go to the brook which run by our house to wash the snow be never above eighteen inch thick general out of the drift so that the fear of want wood or water never take hold of we for albeit we make no provision for they yet at a minute of a hour warning we be furnish where there be lake of fresh water that stand still and do not run there be remain freeze able to bear a man almost three month and be not dissolve until the middle of April but where the air have entrance and issue cut of they there be no frost when the wind in the winter time in England be at the north-east one month together the frost be great and the cold more sharp than it be here at all there be no month in all the winter spring that some of our company do not travel in either by land or by water and lie abroad and drink water in place distant two three four and five league from our habitation and sometime lie in the wood without fire and receive no harm when April come our spring begin and the first that do bud be the small or the Corinth tree our company be not let in work abroad and in the wood and open air fifteen day the wholewinter we never want the company of raven and small bird so that the doubt that have be make of the extremity of the winter season in these part of Newfoundland be find by our experience causeless and that not only man may safety inhabit here without any need of stove but navigation may be make to and fro from England to these part at any time of the year concern the healthfulness of these country we have be now more than ten month upon this voyage of nine and thirty person which be all our number which winter here there be want only healthfulness four whereof one Thomas Percy Sawyer die the eleven of December of thought have slay a man in Rochester which be the cause be unknown unto i until a day before he die that he come this voyage and one other call John morris Tyler miscarry the first of February by reason of a bruise the three call Marmaduke Whittington be never perfect well after he have the small homicide die for thought pox which he bring out of Bristol with he who die the fifteen of February and the four call william stone have at the first only a stiffness in one of his knee keep his bed ten week and will never stir his body which laziness bring he to his end who die the thirteen of April of the rest four or five have be sick some three month and some four month who now be better than they be except one all of they if they have bad as good will to work as they have good stomach to their victual will long since have be recover one Richard Fletcher that be master pilot here and a director of the fish report unto i that he be one of the company consist of forty person that go in a drumbler of Ipswich call the amity to the north part of Ireland about eleven year ago from London in the late queen service under the charge of one captain Fleming and continue there the space of two year in which time two and thirty die of the scurvy and that only eight of they return home whereof the say Richard Fletcher be one so that the accident of death or sickness of any person in these our part of Newfoundland be not to argue any unhealthfulnesse of this country no more than Ireland be to be discredit by the loss of those two and thirty man notwithstanding that there be to be have fresh victual and many other help which this country as yet have not but in good time may have from the six of October until the sixteen of may our company have be employ in make of a storehouse to hold our provision and a dwell house for our habitation which be finish about the employment of the colony first of December with a square enclosure of one hundred and twenty foot long and ninety foot broad compass these two house and a work house to work dry in to make boat or any other work out of the rain and three piece of ordnance be plant there to command the harborough upon a platform make of great post and rail and great pole sixteen foot long set upright round about with two flanker to scour the quarter a boat about twelve tun big with a deck be almost finish to sail and row about the headland six fish boat and pinness a second see pit at the fresh lake of two mile in length and the six part of a mile broad stand within twelve score of our habitation to see the timber to be have out of the fresh lake in keep two pair of sawyer to see plank for the say building in rid of some ground to sow corn and garden seed in cut of wood for the collier in col of it in work at the smith forge iron work for all needful use in cost both by land and sea to many place within this bay of conception in make the frame of timber of a far great and fair house then that which as yet we dwell in which be almost finish and diverse other thing we have sow all sort of grain this spring which prosper well hitherto our goat have live here all this winter english corn fowl and cattle prosper there and there be one lusty kid which be yean in the dead of winter our swine prosper pidgen and coney will endure exceed well our poultry have not only lay egg plentiful but there be eighteen young chicken that be a week old beside other that be a hatch the fear of wild beast we have find to be almost needless our great ram-goate be miss fifteen day in October and come home well again and be yet well with we if the industry of man and presence of domestical cattle be apply to the good of this country of Newfoundland there will short arise just cause of contentment to the inhabitant thereof many of our master and seafaring man see our safety and hear what a mild winter we have and that no ice have be see fleeting in any of the bay of this country all this year notwithstanding that then meet one hundred and fifty league off in the sea great store of land of ice do begin to be in love with the country and do talk of come to take land here to inhabit fall in the reckon aswell of the commodity that they may make by the bank fish as by the husbandry of the land beside the ordinary fish at the green bay where some of our company be a fish in November they report there be great store of good ground without wood and there be a thousand acre together which they say may be mo^ed this year meadow there be great store of deer whereof they see some diverse time and twice they come within shoot of they and the greyhound who be lusty have a course but can not get upon they but near unto cape Razo dear Revonse and trepasse there be great quantity of open ground and stag it be most likely that all the sack will be depart out of England before the return of this our bark which shall not make any matter because I be now of opinion that nothing shall be send hither before the return of the ship from fish for as concern send of cattle it will be best that it be defer until the next spring and concern victual in regard of the quantity we have of it remain of old together with that that be come now as with the dry fish that here we may be store with I be in good hope there will not want any to last till this time twelve month and according to the victual which shall be find at the end of the fish the number of person that shall remain here all the next winter shall be fit that there shall not want notwithstanding about Alhollantide or the begin of December a ship may be send such a one as our Fleming be with salt from Rochel for at any time of the winter ship may as well go and come hither as when they do especial before january this summer I purpose to see most place between cape raze Placentia and and at the return of the fish ship to entertain a fit number of man to maintain here the winter and to set over they and to take the care of all thing here with your patience one master William colton a discreet young man and my brother Philip Guy who have winter with i and have promise i to undertake this charge until my return the next spring or till it shall be otherwise dispose of by you and then together with such of the company as be willing to go home and such other as be not fit long to be entertain here I intend to take passage in the fish ship and so return home and then between that and the spring to be present to give you more ample satisfaction in all thing and to take such further resolution as the importance of the enterprise shall require wherein you shall find i always as ready as ever I have be to proceed and go forward God will and because at my come home it will be time enough for i to lay before you my opinion touch what be to be undertake the next year I will forbear now to write of it because you shall be the soon advertise of our welfare and because such of the company as be send home both for their own good and that the unprofitable expense of victual and wage may coase I have lade little or nothing back that the say company may the better be at ease in the hold only there be send three hogshead of charcoles where 1 be they be of burch no. 2o. be of pine and Spruce no. 3o. be of fir be the light wood yet it make good coal and be use by our smith I send they because you shall see the goodness of each kind of Cole also I send you a hogshead of the skin and fur of such beast as have be take here the particular whereof appear in the bill of lade while I be write I have news of the vineyard the ship which you send to fish to have be in company with another ship that be arrive on this side of the bank and that the master intend to go to Farillon or fer-land God send she in safety so pray God for the prosperity of your worship and the whole company with hope that his divine majesty which have give we so good a beginning will always bless our proceed my duty most humble remember I take my leave date in cupers cove the sixteen of May 1611. I have also a journal of the wind and weather from the latter end of August 1611. till june 1612. write by master William Colston and deliver to master John Guy governor of the english colony in newfoundland at his return from England thither june the seven 1612. by which it appear that the weather be somewhat more intemperate than it have be the year before but not intolerable nor perhaps so bad as we have it sometimes in England their dog kill a wolf otter sable etc. captain easton a pirate be troublesome to the english and terrible to the french there of who I have add this letter for the diary of the weather and occurrent each day will be very tedious to master JOHN slany treasurer and other of the council and company of the Newfoundland plantation the twenty nine of july 1612. right worshipful by my last of the seventeen of june I write you of the estate then of all matter here by the holland ship which I hope be long since safe arrive together with master Colston who have I doubt not make by word of mouth full relation of all matter because the proceed of one captain Peter easton a pirate and his company since be most fit to be know before I touch our plantation business you shall understand what they have be unto this time until the seventeen of this present the say captain easton remain in harbour grace there trim and repair his ship and command not only the carpenter of each ship to do his business but have take victual munition and necessary from every ship together with about one hundred man out of the bay to man his ship be now in number six he purpose to have before he go as be say cut of the land five hundred man while he remain there two several company to the number of about one hundred and eighty person to each company be discontent steal away from he in a shallop and take two ship that be fish in Trinity bay one belong to barnstable and one other to Plymouth and so intend to begin to be new bead of that damnable course of life as I sail from hence towards renoose in a small bark I fall into one of their hand and one of my company be hurt with a musket there be one of their crew that winter with i here the first year by who mean and because I be in the bark they make show that they be sorry that they have meddle with we and so they depart from we without come aboard that which they seek after be man to increase their number before the say captain Eastons departure he send three ship into Trinity bay to store himself with victual munition and man who be say to be worse use than the ship here he take much ordnance from they the say easton be late at saint jones and be now as far as I can learn at Feriland where he take his pleasure and thereabouts the rest be to meet he it be give out that we will send one captain Haruy in a ship to Ireland to understand news about his pardon which if he can obtain in i^ (...) rge and ample manner as he expect than he give out that he will come in otherwise it be think that he will get protection of the duke of Florence and that in his course herehence he will hover about the westward of the land of the Azores to see whether he can light upon any of the plate fleet or any good rich booty before his come in albeit he have so prevail here to the strengthen of himself and encourage of other to attempt the like hereafter yet be there that course take as I hope shall be it be a most easy matter to repress they I have also a diary of the winter weather and observation of occurrent from August 1612. till April 1613. December be very full of snow for I dare not present the whole and the freshwater lake be freeze over and the frost and snow by the ten of that month as in any part of the two former place january be much mild till the fourteen from thence it be very frosty their beer be freeze and they drink half water a ill remedy to cold the cattle do not well thrive as come out of a country not so cold and therefore iresh cattle where the winter be warm be not so fit to be transport hither George davis die of the scurvy and after he Edward garten Edward hartland John Tucker and one and twenty be sick most of the scurvy the whole colony be sixty two February be much warm and more temperate toby and Grigge die in march the rest recover turnip be find as good to recover from the scurvy as the Aneda tree to jacques Cartiers company Nicholas gyve wife be deliver of a lusty boy march 27. the easterly wind and some current bring land of ice from the north sea which make the weather cold that spring then in the depth of winter when the same wind blow namely east and northeast those land be blow into the bays and the wind from they even in April very sharp and the snow on the ten of April as thick as any time that year in October John Guy with thirteen other in the endeavour and five in the shallop go upon discovery a^ mount eagle bay they find store of scurvygrass on a island in the south bottom of Trinity bay which they call savage harbour they find savage house no people in they in one they find a copper kettle very bright you shall have it as one of they write copper kettle it in his own term a fur gown of elk skin some seal skin a old sail and a fish reel order be take that nothing shall be diminish and because the savage shall know that some have be there every thing be remove out of his place and bring into one of the cabin and lay orderly one upon the other and the kettle hang over they wherein there be put some biscuit and three or four amber bead this be do to begin to win they by fair mean this time of the year they live by hunt for we find twelve elke hoof that be late kill a little piece of flesh be bring away which be find to be a beaver cod which be forthcoming to be see their house there be nothing but pole set in their house describe round form meet all together aloft which they cover with dear skin they be about ten foot broad and in the middle they make their fire one of they be cover with a sail which they have get from some christian. all thing in this manner leave every one return by the moonlight go by the brink of the lake unto the entrance of the make way and a little before they come thither they pass by a new savage house almost finish which be make in a square form with a small roof and so come to the bark they have two kind of oar one be about four foot long of one piece of fir the other be about ten foot long make of two piece one be as long big and their oar round as a half pike make of Beech wood which by likelihood they make of a biskin oare the other be the blade of the oar which be let into the end of the long one slit and whip very strong the short one they use as a paddle and the other as a oar the thirty without any further business with the savage we depart thence to the northern side of Trinity bay and anchor all that night under a island the one and thirty we row unto a harbour which now be call All-hallows which have adjoin unto it very high land November the six two canoas appear and one man alone come towards we with a flag in his hand of a wolf skin shake it and make a loud noise which we take to be for a parley whereupon a white flag be put out and the bark and shallop row towards they savage which the savage do not like of and so take they to their canoas again and be go away whereupon the bark wheaze unto they and flourish the flag of truce and come to anchor which please they and then they stay present after the shallop land master Whittington with the flag of truce who go towards they then they row into the shore with one Canoa the other stand aloof off and land two man one of they have the white skin in his hand and come towards master Whittington the savage make a loud speech and shake the skin which be answer by master Whittington in like manner and as the savage draw near he throw down the white skin on the ground the like be do by master Whittington whereupon both the savage pass over a little water stream towards master Whittington dance leap and sing and come together the foremost of they present unto he a chain of leather full of small periwinkle shell a spit knife and a feather that stack in his ear the other give he a arrow without a head and the former be requite with a linen cap and a hand towel who put present the linen cap upon his head and to the other he give a knife and after hand in hand they all three do sing and dance upon this one of our company call Francis tipton go ashore unto who one of the savage come run and give he a chain such as be before speak of who be gratify by Francis tipton with a knife and a small piece of brass then all four together dance laugh and make sign of joy and gladness sometime strike the breast of our company and sometime their own when sign be make that they shall be willing to suffer two of our company more to come on shore for two of they more to be land and that bread and drink shall be bring ashore they make likewise sign that they have in their canoas meat also to eat upon this the shallop row aboard and bring John Guy and master teage a shore who present they with a shirt two table napkin and a hand-towell give they bread butter and reason of the sun to eat and beer and aquavitae to drink and one of they blow in the aquavitae bottle that make a sound which they fall all into a laugh at after master Croote and John Crouther come ashore who they go to salute give they shell chain who bestow glove upon they one of the savage that come last ashore come walk with his oar in his hand and seem to have some command over the rest and behave himself civil for when meat be offer he he draw off his Mitten from his hand before he will receive it and give a arrow for a present without a head who be requite with a dozen of point after they have all eat and drink one of they go to their Canoa and bring we deer flesh dry in the smoke or wind and draw his knife from out of his neck he cut every man a piece and that favour very well at the first meeting when sign be make of meat to eat one of the savage present run to the bank side and pull up a root and give it to master Whittington which the other savage perceive to be dirty take it out of his hand and go to the water to wash it and after divide it among the four it taste very well he that come ashore with the oar in his hand go and take the white skin that they hail we with and give it to master Whittington and present after they do take our white flag with they in the Canoa and make sign unto we that we shall repair to our bark and so they put off for it be almost night in the two canoas there be eight man if none be woman for common in every Canoa there be one woman they be of a reasonable stature of a ordinary middle size they go bareheaded wear their hair somewhat long but round they have no beard behind they have a great lock of hair plait with feather like a hawk lure with a feather in it stand their fashion upright by the crown of the head and a small lock plait before a short gown make of stag skin the fur innermost that run down to the middle of their leg with sleeve to the middle of their arm and a beaver skin about their neck be all their apparel save that one of they have shoe and mitten so that all go barelegged and most barefoot they be full eye of a black colour the colour of their hair be diverse some black some brown and some yellow and their face something flat and broad red with ochre as all their apparel be and the rest of their body they be broad breasted and bold and stand very upright their Canoa be about twenty foot long and four foot and a half broad in the middle aloft their canoas and for their keel and timber they have thin light piece of dry fir rend as it be lathe and instead of board they use the outer burch bark which be thin and have many fold sow together with a thread make of a small root quarter they will carry four person well and weigh not one hundred weight they be make in form of a new moon stem and stern alike and equal distant from the great breadth from the stem and stern here rise a yard high a light thin staff whip about with small root which they take hold by to bring the Canoa ashore that serve instead of rope and a harbour for every place be to they a harbour where they can go ashore themselves they take a land with they their Canoa and will never put to sea but in a calm or very fair weather in the middle the Canoa be high a great deal then in the bow and quarter they be all bear from the keel to the portlesse not with any circular line but with a right line they have make a tilt with a sail that they get from some christian and pitch a dozen pole in the ground veer on which be hang diverse fur and chain make of shell which at that instant we fall not in the reckon to what intent it be do but after it come to our mind as hereafter you shall pereeive the seven day we spend in wash and in observation there and thereof take out of his print book it it well know that my breed and course of life have be such as that I have long time set many people on work and spend most of my day in travel special in merchandize and sea-voyage I have be often in France Spain Italy Portugal Savoy Denmark Norway Spruceland the canary and Soris land and for the Newfoundland it be almost so familiar know to i as my own country in the year 1588. I serve under the then lord admiral as captain in a ship of my own set forth at my charge against the spanish armado and after such time as that service be end take my leave of his honour I have his favourable letter to one sir Robert in the county of Devon knight whereby there may be some course take that the charge as well of my own ship as also of two other and a pinnace with the victual and man therein employ shall not be any way burdensome to i wherein there be such order give by the then right honourable lord of the privy counsel that the same be well satisfy which service be to be see record in the book at white-hall now to express some of my voyage to the Newfoundland which make most for the present purpose my first voyage thither be about forty year since in a worthy ship of the burden of three hundred ^un set forth by one master Cotton of South-hampton we be bind to the grand bay which lie on the northside of that land purpose there to trade then with the savage people for who we carry sundry commodity and to kill whale and to make train oil as the Biscayne do there yearly in great abundance but this our intend voyage be overthrow by the indiscretion of our captain and faint-heartedness of some gentleman of our company whereupon we set fail from thence and bare with Trinity harbour in Newfoundland where we kill great store of fish deer bear beaver seales otter and such like with abundance of sea-fowle and so return for England we arrive safe at South-hampton in a voyage to that country about six and thirty year since I have then the command of a worthy ship of two hundred and twenty tun set forth by one master Crook of South-hampton at that time sir Humphrey Gilbert a Devonshire knight come thither with two good ship and a pinnace and bring with he a large patent from the late most renown queen Elizabeth and in her name take possession of that country in the harbour of saint john whereof I be a eyewitness he fail from thence towards Virginia and by reason of some unhappy direction in his course the great ship he have strike upon shelf on the coast of Canadie and be there lose with most part of the company in she and he himself be then in a small pinnace of twenty tun in the company of his vice-admiral one captain hay return towards England in a great storm be overwhelm with the sea and so perish in another voyage I make thither about four and thirty year past wherein I have the command of a good ship partly my one at that time own sir Bernard drake of Devonshire knight come thither with a commission and have diverse good ship under his command he there take many Portugal ship lade with fish and bring they into England as prize omit to speak of other voyage I make thither during the late queen reign I will descend to late time in the year 1611. be in Newfoundland at which time that famous archpirate Peter easton come there and have with he ten sail of good ship well furnish and very rich I be keep eleven week under his command and have from he many golden promise and much wealth offer to be put into my hand as it be well know I do persuade he much to desist from his evil course his entreaty then to i be that I will come for England to some friend of he and solicit they to become humble petitioner to your majesty for his pardon but have no warrant to touch such good I give he think for his offer only I request he to release a ship that he have take upon the coast of Guinnie belong to one captain rash of Foy in Cornwall a man who I know but only by report which he according release whereupon I provide man victual Portugal voyage a. 1589. sir JOHN Norris and sir FRANCIS Drake general write as be think by colonel Antony Wingfield employ in the same voyage former publish by his friend to who it be write and here abbreviate have determinate purpose to put on this habit of a soldier I grow doubtful whether to employ my time in the war of the low-countries which be in auxiliary manner maintain by her majesty or to follow the fortune of this voyage which be a adventure of she and many honourable personage in revenge of unsupportable wrong offer unto the estate of our country by the castilian king in argue whereof I find that by how much the challenger be repute before the defendant by so much be the journey to be prefer before those defensive war for have the duke of Parma his turn be to defend as it be his good fortune to invade from whence can have proceed that glorious honour which these late war have lay upon he or what can have be say more of he then of a though never so valiant in a private duel even that he have do no more than by his honour he be tie unto for the gain of one town or any small defeat give more renown to the assailant than the defence of a country or the withstand of twenty encounter can yield any man who be bind by his place to guard the same whereof as well the particular of our age especial in the Spaniard as the report of former history may assure we which have still lay the fame of all war upon the inuader and do not we in these day live obscure in Flanders either not have where withal to manage any war or not put on arm but to defend themselves when the enemy shall procure they whereas in this short time of our adventure we have win a town by escalade batter and assault another overthrow a mighty prince power in the a brief rehearsal of the August be in Cadiz attend upon my most honourable good lord I talk with certain of the religious man such as I find learn whereof indeed there be some though not very many I talk also with the bishop of cusco there a grave age comely man and be of late choose to that bishopric he be as then to have go to the indies have not we then take he prisoner and so stay his journey for that time it please the lord general to deal exceed favourable with this say bishop of cusco for it be their good pleasure to give he his free passage without any ransom and therewithal to let he to understand that they come not to deal with churchman or unarmed man or with man of peace weakling and child neither be it any part of their meaning to make such a voyage for gold silver or any other their wealth and riches etc. but that their only come be to meet with their dishonourable practice and manifold injury and to deal with man of war and valour for the defence of the true honour of England and to let they to understand that whensoever they attempt any base-conceited and dishonourable practice to their sovereign queen their mistress that it shall be revenge to the uttermost etc. in this mean space chap. 14 the voyage to the isle of Azores under the conduct of the right honourable ROBERT earl of Essex 1597. @. i. the relation thereof by the say earl and other commissioner i the general have by her majesty gracious favour the charge of her fleet and army set out of Plymouth in june 1597. do both promise myself and give hope to her majesty that I shall be able to defeat the king of Spain fleet command by the adelantado if I meet they at sea or destroy it in the harbour of ferol if I find they there as also to master and take all fleet of treasure or of the east or west indian fleet that I shall find upon the sea in their way to Spain and last that I shall take in the island of tercea which I hold a action of equal importance to the other with this confidence I go out and to these end but none of these three be perform it may be doubt whether we have not through weakness or negligence fail of success for which we make answer that if our whole carriage be examine from the first hour to the last it shall appear that we have strive to attain to every one of these with as much obstinate constancy as any man in the world can do and that only the powerful hand of God do bind our hand and frustrate all our endeavour the first for the enterprise of ferel we go out of Plymouth the three of june and stier direct for that port and when most extreme storm and contrary wind meet with we we cross with wind and storm beat it up till all our fleet be scatter and many of our ship in desperate case and because I the general think my too soon give over will not only deprive the fleet of our principal ship but absolute defeat the journey I force my company first to abide the continual increase of a most dangerous leak which I make light of because I see that with labour of man I can free the ship as fast as the leak do grow second I make they endure the crake of both my main and fore mast the one in two place the other in three so as we still look danger of the admirallship when they shall be carry by the board which be not enough to make i bear up because I know whensoever I shall loose they both I can with jury mast by God favour carry the ship home and I continue so long that my ship Okam come all out her seam open she deck and upper work give way her very timber and main beam with she labour do tear like lathe so as we look hourly when the Orlope will fall and the ordnance sink down to the keel then do those few who before I have win to stand with i all protest against i that if I do not within a minute of a hour bear up the helm I do wilful cast away the ship and whole company then only I suffer myself to be overcome and when I come to Plymouth half her majesty they put in to Plymouth ship and more than half the principal officer by sea and by land be put in before i for the extremity their ship be in and when we be all of we gather together again at Plymouth and have repair all the ship but my own which be send home to chatham to be new build then be we keep in by continual storm and contrary wind till our victual which be at first but for three month be in a manner all spend and the sickness in the sickness fly boat that carry the land army grow so great that I have order from her majesty to discharge the land force all but the thousand old soldier which be draw out of the low order to discharge land force country by which mean though we be disable to land at ferol to beat the land army there and take in the force which be the certaive way to command the adelantado fleet yet I the general offer her majesty to send in certain ship of fire and to second they with the saint Matthew and saint Andrew and some great flye-boate and merchant ship with which I will destroy the most of the enemy principal ship and leave all the queen own english build ship at the mouth of the harbour to assure our retreat by this mean I shall hazard to loose but two great cartes which before I have win and for the adventure of those defeat the enemy whole navy which counsel be allow though with restraint of my own go in with those two ship and a absolute bar to hazard any other we go out the second time to put this project in
